No, because there is no perishing; one passes through the form of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Furthermore, as long as the collection of causes and conditions remains together and uninterrupted, and no cause for arising is obtained, it therefore persists for a long time.
Regarding the four lines on "wandering about": ordinary worldlings, in accordance with worldly convention, [perceive this].
King Pāli guards the subtlest details, protecting the hidden qualities (*guṇa*) of an Arhat.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:

"In this regard, there are four kinds of bhikṣus: those of powerful memory and wisdom, those who proclaim wisdom, and those who, though compliant, are as stubborn and dull as a block of wood, matching even a single phrase."
When these words were spoken, what was their meaning?
Some explained it thus:
"A person of powerful memory and wisdom understands the meaning as soon as the words are uttered."
As for those who are easily transformed: if a bhikṣu extinguishes himself in accordance with that Dharma, the World-Honored One also knows this.
He proclaims wisdom and speaks so that they may understand immediately.
As he has said: "Bhikṣus, form is not yours; it is not yours. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are not yours."
The World-Honored One has also said:
"One who complies with a stubborn and dull-witted person may be led to compliance by means of various methods of inducement.
How does a bhikṣu [comply] with regard to form?"
"Whatever forms there may be, they are all entirely the four great elements and that which is derived from the four great elements," as explained at length.
Even those who are dull-witted and of uniform capacity do not understand the meaning.
Some say: those who possess strong memory and wisdom are of sharp faculties, for their minds know one another;
those who possess analytical wisdom are of medium faculties;
Those who are compliant have soft faculties;
those who are stubborn and recalcitrant, even if they master a single phrase, have no faculties at all.
Or it is said thus:
Those of powerful memory and wisdom are those who, through their past lives, sought the power of liberation.
Those who proclaim wisdom are those who, through their past lives, sought gentle liberation.
Those who are dull-witted and uniform in their single utterance are those who, throughout their past lives, did not seek liberation.
Furthermore, a person of powerful memory and wisdom may understand immediately upon being questioned, such as when the Venerable Śāriputra remained silent when questioned.
A person of distributed wisdom, however, understands only after analyzing and clarifying the matter, such as when the Venerable Pukkusāti thoroughly examined the principles of the meaning.

To be compliant with others means to study the higher training in ethical discipline at the appropriate time, to subdue the mind at the appropriate time, and to study the higher training in wisdom at the appropriate time; this is what that refers to.
Those who train in their natural disposition gradually study the precepts, gradually receive instruction, and accept them for practice, just as the Venerable Rāhula gradually attained the Way.
As for those who are stubborn and dull-witted, even when they receive a single phrase, they neither understand its meaning nor comprehend the profound Dharma.
By what means does a bodhisattva, during his previous lives, not bypass the stages to attain realization?
Some say it is because of their solemn vow.
By means of this vow, one shall appear in the world as a Buddha; those not yet crossed over shall be crossed over, and those not yet liberated shall be made liberated.
Or it is said: the Bodhisattva reflects and contemplates, and with a mind of wisdom, constantly makes this aspiration, saying:
To deliver all sentient beings, some say:
"The Bodhisattva has attained all-knowledge and is thus self-perfected; yet, for the sake of sentient beings, he does not bypass the stages in equal measure to realize the fruit."
Furthermore, because their faculties were not yet mature, they did not simultaneously transcend [the stages] to realize the fruit.
For what reason did the householder Anāthapiṇḍada make offerings to the four Tathāgatas, yet not go forth under those Buddhas to study the Path?
Some may say:
"By reason of this oath, because of that vow, one should make offerings to other Tathāgatas.
Others may say: [the same].
The power and influence of his kinsmen could not remove his feelings of affection;
some even said:
"That householder’s mind always delights in tranquility, he is fond of giving, and he is of dull faculties."
Because of their tranquility, they possess the merit of not falling into the evil realms and obtain great rewards everywhere.
Those of dull faculties do not perceive the affliction of domestic entanglements; for this reason, they do not leave the household life to become śramaṇas.
Furthermore, that elder was excessively prone to lustful thoughts and constantly delighted in employing various means among the female attendants.
Since all Buddhas attain the path of the noble ones (ārya-mārga) through their past actions, for what reason would he not have been born as a male, which is contrary to the principles of the Dharma?
Some say: "Because the various sense faculties are deficient, it is therefore not consistent with the Dharma and its meaning. Others say:
The mind races toward myriad ends and fails to attain samādhi; therefore, it does not accord with the Dharma and its meaning.
Or it may be said:
it obstructs the true retribution of past karmic conditions, such that one receives this physical form without relying on wisdom.

Furthermore, it obstructs and binds the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and being covered by those fetters (*saṃyojana*), one cannot find rest; the mind lacks shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*).

Moreover, the World-Honored One said: "There are three things for which a stūpa should be built: for a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha; for a bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted (*āsravakṣaya*); and for a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin*)."
For what reason do those training as pratyekabuddhas not enter these three matters?

Some explain it thus: this is the Buddha’s exhortatory speech; when he speaks of the Buddha, he speaks of the pratyekabuddha, and when he speaks of the bhikṣu whose outflows are exhausted, he speaks of one in training (*śaikṣa*). Among them, there may be some whose outflows are exhausted; furthermore, they too are included in that number.
It is for the sake of these sentient beings that its profound meaning is revealed; this exhortatory discourse is as previously explained.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:

"In this regard, monks, there are six types of arhats: the arhat subject to falling away (*parihāṇadharman*), the one who guards mindfulness (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the one who protects [the dharma] (*anurakṣaṇādharman*), the one who abides [in his state] (*sthitidharman*), the one who discriminates [the dharma] (*pratividhanadharman*), and the one whose dharma is free from doubt (*akopyadharman*)."
What is the distinction here?
Some explain it as follows:

regarding the various faculties of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), there are the categories of superior-superior, medium-superior, inferior-superior; medium-medium, superior-medium, medium-inferior; and inferior-superior, medium-inferior. One who is established in the lowest of these—the "inferior-inferior"—is called an Arhat of the "subject to falling away" (*parihāṇadharman*).
The superior-inferior accomplishment refers to Arhats who preserve the Dharma through mindfulness.
The middle-inferior accomplishment refers to Arhats who protect the Dharma.
The middle-middle accomplishment refers to Arhats who abide for the duration of a kalpa.
The middling-superior accomplishment refers to the Arhat who discriminates dharmas.
The three superior accomplishments refer to the Arhat free from doubt.

Among these, the Śrāvakas possess the lower and middle superior accomplishments; the Pratyekabuddhas possess the middle and upper superior accomplishments; and the Tathāgatas possess the uppermost superior accomplishment.
Some explain it thus:

Suppose there is a person who applies skillful means to create karma, yet is neither diligent nor possesses sharp faculties. By means of that skillful karma, despite being undiligent and having dull faculties, he seeks to realize and attain the liberation of equanimity; however, due to his lack of diligence and dull faculties regarding that skillful means, he subsequently regresses from that liberation of equanimity. This is called an Arhat of the "regressive" type (*parihāṇadharman*).

It is like a person who, through skillful means, with great diligence, and with dull faculties, attains the realization of the liberation of mind through equanimity by means of those skillful means, great diligence, and dull faculties; he then maintains that liberation of mind through equanimity by means of skillful means, diligence, and dull faculties. This is called an Arhat who guards the Dharma.

It is like a person who constantly and most earnestly applies skillful means, yet possesses dull faculties; through that constant and most earnest application of skillful means despite his dull faculties, he realizes the liberation of mind through equanimity. That liberation of mind through equanimity, attained by one who constantly and most earnestly applies skillful means despite his dull faculties, neither increases nor decreases; this is called an Arhat abiding in the aeon (*kalpa*).

It is like a person who constantly and most earnestly applies skillful means and possesses sharp faculties; because he constantly and most earnestly applies skillful means with sharp faculties, he attains the realization of equanimous liberation of mind, and through that constant and most earnest application of skillful means with sharp faculties, he attains freedom from doubt. This is called an Arhat who has distinguished the Dharma.

It is like a person who constantly and most earnestly applies skillful means and possesses keen faculties; because they constantly and most earnestly apply skillful means with keen faculties, they attain the realization of the liberation of mind through the absence of doubt. This is called an Arhat of the "dharma of no-doubt."

Furthermore, if a person relies upon the power of others to immediately realize the liberation of mind through equanimity, then this liberation of mind through equanimity is like a weak patient who attempts to rise but, lacking someone to support them, falls back onto the bed; such a one is called an Arhat of the nature of falling away (*parihāṇadharman*).

If there is another person whose even-minded liberation is not yet firm, who merely fears losing their mind and seeks death by harming themselves with a blade, this is called an Arhat who is mindful of the Dharma.
Furthermore, if there is a person who possesses equanimous liberation and guards that equanimous liberation,
thinking: "I am able to guard this for as long as life lasts, maintaining it and nurturing it according to the occasion," such a one is called an Arhat who guards the Dharma.

Furthermore, if there is a person whose mind is liberated with equanimity, who transcends dull faculties and abides in middling faculties, therefore their equanimous liberation of mind is non-retrogressive and neither increases nor undergoes death; this is called an Arhat abiding in the kalpa.

If there is another person whose mind is equally liberated, who from the beginning has attained benefit and acquired the faculties, and who relies on external power to attain freedom from doubt, this is called an Arhat who discriminates the dharmas.

Furthermore, if there is a person who, by means of their own power, initially attains superior faculties and dwells in equal liberation, knowing for themselves the proper time [for final realization], this is called an Arhat of the "Dharma Without Doubt."
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said: "Ānanda!
Vaiśālī is exceedingly pleasant and boundless; Vāṣaṭamī is also exceedingly joyful; the Cāpāla Shrine is also exceedingly joyful; and Gautamī’s Nigrodha Park is also exceedingly joyful."
Jambudvīpa possesses manifold pleasures beyond compare, and its population is flourishing; for what reason did the World-Honored One speak thus?
Or perhaps it was said so because, by entering meditative concentration, he caused the bhikṣus to give rise to hopes for bliss.
Some say: "The city of Vaiśālī is exceedingly pleasant and boundless; grain is abundant and cheap, and alms are easily obtained.
Vatsapūri is also exceedingly pleasant and boundless; its people are harmonious and submissive, and they do not encounter suffering or calamity."

At the Cāpāla Monastery, the site where the Wheel of Dharma was turned, and at the Nyagrodha tree of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī, there were various seats and implements, and the place was quiet with few distractions.
On the continent of Jambudvīpa, there are many kinds of gardens and fruits; its various peoples are flourishing, wise, and their deeds are luminous.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One also manifested the removal of all fetters and attachments, extinguishing various desires so that they were forever stilled.
The Bodhisattva who first resolved his mind, the one who left home but was not a male, the three stupas, the six arhats, and Vaiśālī were all situated thereafter.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"While traveling through Vaiśālī, from this day forward I shall no longer see Vaiśālī; nor shall any other of the three Buddhas come to Vaiśālī again."
For what reason does the Venerable One say this?
Or why does he say:
"I shall no longer undergo rebirth in a womb"?

Furthermore, it was at that time when the Tathāgata, through his knowledge of equality, had extinguished the traces of death; when he wished to resolve the doubts of the beings in the city of Vaiśālī who delighted in the Dharma—this is what is meant by "at that time.
For what reason did the Blessed One invite Mahākāśyapa to share half of his seat?

Some say: At that time, the bhikṣus treated Kāśyapa with contempt and gave rise to defiled thoughts, not realizing that Kāśyapa had entered the essential principles of the Great Dharma. For this reason, the World-Honored One offered him half of his seat, desiring to open their minds and resolve their doubts, fearing they might incur unwholesome retribution.
Some say: "That venerable one possesses manifold virtues and was previously converted by the World-Honored One; we fear that the bhikṣus might commit offenses against the prohibitions and precepts.
Others say: [as before].
The Venerable Aniruddha was the foremost in respect; the World-Honored One went to visit him and used his robe as a seat, then further invited Mahākāśyapa to share half of his seat.
Some say this was because the World-Honored One wished to entrust the Vinaya to him, so that future sentient beings would believe and accept his words.
Furthermore, it has never occurred that [the Buddha] shared half of his seat with a disciple.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One wished to manifest his great virtue.
Moreover, the World-Honored One said:
"O monks, if śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas perceive night as day and day as night, their minds are inverted.
Monks, as I perceive day as day and night as night, my mind is free from inversion."
When these words were spoken, what was their meaning?
Some explain it thus:
He arouses the divine eye, eliminates perceptions of external forms, and cultivates the perception of luminosity, observing the day as he observes the night without distinction.
They may not be distinct; they may at times perceive night during the day, or perceive day during the night;
yet the Blessed One is not thus. Or it is said:
Those śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, while asleep at night, perceive it as day, and while awake during the day, perceive it as night; this is their perversion.

Furthermore, when dwelling in seclusion, they lie down on their right side and enter meditative absorption by contemplating such forms; yet the World-Honored One, whether walking or sitting, remains constantly as if in a single state of concentration.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"In this regard, a bhikṣu has three Tathāgatas; in this very life, he truly possesses them without doubt, having attained wisdom for himself and also teaching others to enter into wisdom."
What is meant by "attaining wisdom for oneself"? Some say:
since that [wisdom] cannot be attained and is empty and without reality, how much less could one attain the real?
Furthermore, this is the speech by which the Blessed One exhorted and instructed.
He spoke these words:
"I have awakened to this."
Or it may be said:

if one who is attached to form and whose mind dwells upon dharmas, out of pride in their own precepts, relies on them as a theft, taking what is real to be unreal—the World-Honored One observes such a person’s adherence to views (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*).
Furthermore, that false view holds that the self truly dwells within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The Buddha’s teaching is likewise: there are no other aggregates that can be spoken of as the locus of the self.
For what reason?
It refers to those non-Buddhists who, having exhausted their desire and love, attain realization by leaping over stages (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), and who possess the qualities of non-retrogression.
Or it is said as follows:
He extinguishes the fetters (saṃyojana) by means of two paths: either by the mundane path (laukikamārga) or by the supramundane path (anāsravamārga).

Some say: "If one attains realization by skipping stages (vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti) based on the dhyānas and so forth, the path arises for him upon observing the dhyāna; he does not [further] abandon what is to be abandoned through the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-heya), and therefore he does not fall back."
Furthermore, when they realize the stages in successive order, their cultivation of patience and wisdom gains the immediate benefit of the power and momentum of equal skillful means.
Even if that power and momentum were not beneficial, they would not regress from within that power and momentum; therefore, they are non-regressive.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"There are four pairs and eight classes [of noble ones].
How many of these have attained the fruits [of the path], and how many have not attained the fruits?
Some say: there are five accomplishments of fruition—namely, those of the *srotāpanna*, *sakṛdāgāmin*, *anāgāmin*, one who is proceeding toward arhatship, and the arhat;
and one non-fruition accomplishment—namely, one who is proceeding toward the realization of the fruit of *srotāpanna*.

These two individuals may either achieve the fruit or not achieve the fruit, as they proceed toward the realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* or proceed toward the realization of the fruit of *anāgāmin*.

Regarding those who proceed toward the realization of the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin*, if they employ skillful means while their desire for sense-pleasures (*kāmarāga*) is not yet exhausted and they attain realization by skipping stages, it should be said that they have not achieved the fruit.
If one has attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and seeks to realize the realization of *sakṛdāgāmin*, it should be said that they have accomplished that fruit.

If, having attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) fruit of *srotāpanna*, they proceed toward the realization of the fruit of *anāgāmin*—whether by exhausting sensual desire or by transcending stages to attain realization—it should be said that they have not accomplished [a specific] fruit.
Furthermore, when one has attained the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* and seeks to proceed toward the fruit of *anāgāmin*, it should be said that the latter fruit is being accomplished.
Since the fruit of *sakṛdāgāmin* is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), while that [subsequent] fruit is conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), it should be said that the faculties of the former have undergone decay.
This is called knowing the eight persons.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"There are four śramaṇas; there are not five."
When these words were spoken, what was their meaning?
The answer is:
With the wisdom of the Path as the fruit realized by the Tathāgata’s own attainment, he turns the wheel of Dharma by preaching the unattached Path and the pure Dharma.
For that reason, he extensively expounds the life of the Way in order to cause others to study all forms of wisdom and sever the net of doubts.

He fully perceives those who slander the Way—those who lack ultimate practice, who lack the precepts and dignified deportment, and who violate the various prohibitions, even while wearing the robes of a śramaṇa.

That second ascetic should be said to include the *pratyekabuddhas*; the third ascetic should be said to include ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*); and the fourth ascetic should be said to include all those who wear the robes of false ascetics while being outsiders—those who conceive of a self, cling to the life-principle, and conceive of sentient beings; all such persons have regressed from the Path.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"Non-attachment is what is meant by precepts.
"Clad in the unstained kāṣāya, The kāṣāya is the primary garment one wears."
"The mind has already attained what it desired; the kāṣāya is not worn out of attachment.
When these words were spoken, what is their meaning?
The answer is:
There are three kinds of turbidity: the defilement of body, speech, and mind.
If one contemplates and calculates these, it is called wearing the saffron robe without defilement.
To boast falsely and to be deceitful and indolent is not what is studied by the immortals; such conduct is not appropriate for them.
This is called patience; it is also not shifting about, but responding in accordance with reality, with a mind always discerning and truthful.

If one does not attain such patience, responding to abuse with abuse and responding to blows with blows, this is not the Dharma of a śramaṇa, much less should one act in such a manner. Therefore, one should not wear the kāṣāya; thus, that kāṣāya is without attachment.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"If that which has already arisen is cut off and no longer sown.
When these words were spoken, what is their meaning?
Answer:

When consciousness encounters the arising of sensation, it gives rise to the causal conditions for the impurities of formations within the abodes of the four dhyānas; thus, the meaning of what is produced is cut off, and there is no further encounter, nor is there the arising of further sensation.

Furthermore, he does not give rise to selective grasping regarding the abodes of the four dhyānas; even if he encounters the conditions for the causal basis of the four divine abidings (*brahmavihāra*), he does not accept them.

Having already cast off craving and exhausted all grasping, this second person runs forth; one should say that he is a non-learner (aśaikṣa) who lacks conventional decorum, yet does not contemplate the unexcelled wisdom, nirvāṇa, or cessation, having attained the state of a seer—this is called a Great Seer (maharṣi).
At first Kāśyapa was asleep, but the Most Victorious One, free from desire, had already spoken of the four kaṣāyas; they are extinguished and shall not arise again.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"From the knowledge of practice to the knowledge of non-arising, having subdued [the mind] and made it firm,
with outflows exhausted without remainder— this is called a brahmin.
What is the meaning of these words?
This is what is taught in the *Āyuṣmān Mahākāśyapa Sūtra*.

A monk who upholds the Dharma and practices the knowledge of wisdom is a learner; even if fellow practitioners of the holy life who abide in their respective tasks obtain the requisites for maintaining life through the Dharma, these too constitute the meaning of the Dharma and the Vinaya, and are therefore called "the wise."
Having known that one does not abide in the interval, one practices so that the mind attains the illumination of contemplative awareness and abides in the two liberations.

Having reflected upon the exhaustion of ignorance and craving, and wishing to declare this as the dharma of the śramaṇa regarding the faculty of the eye, it is said: "With the exhaustion of outflows and the absence of desire, one is called a brahmin."
The World-Honored One is indeed a great brahmin, whose mental defilements have been exhausted.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"The bhikṣu is free from desire; those with desire see great fear."
"Not retreating from desire—this is called Nirvana.
What is the meaning of these words?
The answer is:
One who delights in the tranquility associated with wisdom and is free from sorrow is called a bhikṣu without desire.

Those who are without affairs are pure and dwell in stillness; those who possess desire are subject to suffering and affliction. Only one who perceives the Dharma can realize this: such a person with desire beholds great terror.
To be non-retrogressive regarding desire, to cast off all defilements, and to be well and gradually increased in accordance with the [noble] qualities—this is called samādhi.
The exhaustion of all fetters and the realization of the noble path—this is called nirvāṇa.
For what reason is one who has entered the samādhi of loving-kindness (*maitrī-samādhi*) incapable of being harmed?
Some say it is because the devas attend to and protect their body.
Some say: That samādhi is secluded and free from affairs; harm does not touch the body, nor does the body undergo destruction.
Furthermore, one receives a body composed of the four great elements of the form realm.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"Deer return to the wild; birds return to the void; dharmas return to conceptualization;
and Arhats return to extinction."
"What is it that distinguishes persons?
The answer is:
"The learner is what is distinguished."
One is able to discern form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness; one discerns all the paths of the noble ones.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"There is thought within non-thought, and thought wherein there is no thought."
"Such are the transformations of form; their number corresponds to the objects of thought.
As for those who undergo these transformations of form, some explain it thus:
Regarding those born in the formless realm who are non-returners (anāgāmin), it should be said that they transform the perception of form; thus, their perception of form is transformed.
Furthermore, among them, the arhats also transform the perception [of that state].
An Arhat undergoes no transformation or change regarding the five aggregates and has reached the ultimate consummation of practice.
For what reason did the World-Honored One call Devadatta "the son who eats spittle"?

Some say: At that time, Devadatta employed skillful means with the intent to cause schism in the Saṃgha; for this reason, the World-Honored One rebuked him, fearing that the minds of the bhikṣus might be swayed.
Some say: A person of pure evil, instructed with tainted teachings, repeatedly dwells in the pursuit of destroying the Holy One’s person.
At that time, the World-Honored One, contrary to his intent, instructed him with beneficial words.
Some say: Because Devadatta desired to cause [the Buddha] to enter his own [mouth] when he obtained offerings from the Buddha, he was called "the son who eats spittle.

Furthermore, Devadatta originally possessed great supernormal powers; he transformed himself into the form of a small child, with a golden thread girdle around his waist, and stayed upon the lap of Prince Ajātaśatru, rolling about and playing with laughter.

At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru would take Devadatta onto his lap, play with him, kiss him, and give him saliva to suck; at that time, Devadatta likewise consumed the saliva, and the prince also recognized this venerable Devadatta as such.
At that time, the World-Honored One, with a mind of tranquility like that of a śramaṇa, rebuked him, saying: "O son of spittle!
How is it that Devadatta has first severed his roots of goodness, while you have destroyed the assembly and disrupted the Saṃgha, O virtuous one, and subsequently severed your own roots of goodness?"
Some say: Devadatta first severed his own roots of goodness and subsequently caused a schism in the Saṃgha; he also told the people that there is no retribution for good or evil.
Because of this vow, he resolved to bring about a schism in the Saṃgha.
Question:
It is not because one currently causes a schism in the Saṃgha that one has the perception of what is contrary to the Dharma.
Or, it is said as follows:

Devadatta first caused the schism in the Saṃgha and subsequently severed his roots of goodness; it was not because he severed his roots of goodness that he caused the schism in the Saṃgha, for there is a fixed number of kalpas during which he must repay his karmic debt.
Even if he were to proclaim:
"There is no retribution for good or evil," [the consequence would remain].
One does not, however, destroy the characteristics of the Dharma by destroying [the Sangha].
Question:
If one destroys the Sangha, will it cause one's own roots of goodness to perish and lead one toward the evil realms?
The World-Honored One also said:
"I do not see even a hair’s breadth of goodness in Devadatta.
This is explained at length in the sūtra passage.
Furthermore, since Devadatta first caused a schism in the Saṃgha, his roots of goodness have been severed ever since.
As it was said when he declared:
"I shall split the Saṃgha of the Śramaṇa Gautama and halt the turning of the Wheel of Dharma," whereupon he leaped for joy.
One should say that their roots of goodness have been severed.
From this point forward, they commit various evil deeds without any sense of remorse or regret; therefore, the roots of goodness of the Sangha are destroyed and immediately cut off.
What is meant by "severing the roots of goodness and yet attaining the roots of goodness"?
Some explain it thus:
even if one is born in the hells, one knows that one is undergoing the suffering and pain of hell.
"I have committed this transgression and now receive this retribution.
This should be said to mean that one has attained the root of goodness. Or, it may be stated thus:

Thus, while undergoing the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of hell, one may then possess the contemplation of the mind that bears such fruit; it should be said that one has attained the root of virtue (*kuśalamūla*).

Furthermore, within the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma*), there may be those who attain it: if one encounters a virtuous friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) therein, one gives rise to a mind of remorse, and they gradually teach one until reaching the Path.
Regarding "deer-calf calves," what is its meaning?
Because the thighs taper gradually, it is called "deer-calf calves.
Regarding "the seven cavities being full and overflowing," what is its meaning?

The flesh and veins are level and even; the seven points of the chain-like bones are fully developed, level, and stable, with their color neither changing nor shifting—this is called the "seven places being full and complete.
What is the meaning of "lion’s chest"?
The body has no unevenness and neither advances nor retreats; this is called the "lion’s chest.
As for the meaning of "knowing each taste":
being able to fully perceive all that is light, soft, and subtle is called "clearly understanding each taste."
Not nurturing the worthy leads to fear; compassion extends to all states of existence.
Whether in the state of non-perception or perception, what was their appearance in the past?
For what reason were birds and animals able to speak in former times, yet cannot speak now?
Some say: At that time, having passed away from among humans to be born among animals, they are able to speak because of what they previously practiced.
Question:
Now, those who have passed away from among humans and been reborn as animals are likewise able to speak. Some say:
"That which we consume is no different from that of humans; it is only because we currently lack such food, and our four great elements have undergone transformation, that we are unable to speak."
Question:
If one were now given exquisite food to eat, would they be able to speak?
Or might someone say this:

In ancient times, people were free from strife and litigation, and harbored no intent to kill; at that time, even animals did not fear humans when they saw them. They lived together with them and, by hearing their voices, were able to understand their speech.
Question:
Just as animals born in this life have no fear, can they also speak?
Or is it said thus:
Now they are also able to speak, yet their speech cannot be understood; if one possesses the eloquence of vocal resonance, one can then understand their language.
It is like the speech of barbarians: though their words cannot be understood, if one understands both languages, then one will be able to know them.
Question:
Did people of former times possess the eloquence of resonance such that they could understand [the meaning] immediately?
Furthermore, one does not see among animals those who know written characters.
As for those who hear the sounds of desire, parrots and mandarin ducks can understand them well enough.
Yet the World-Honored One’s metaphors are without error; what the wise say is intended to bring understanding to others.
This is not so. How does one who is diligent know for themselves that they will not fall into the evil destinies?
Or, it is said as follows:
One who knows there is no liberation does not fall into the evil destinies.
I have no such intention to transgress the precepts; therefore, I do not fall into the evil destinies.
Or it is said thus:
Having attained the power of merit,
just as one’s wholesome intention remains unchanged whether awake or asleep, he then thinks:
"At the time of my death, even if there were unwholesome retribution, I would not fall into the evil destinies."
Some might say:
"Even if unwholesome thoughts cause one to fall into the evil realms, I shall not give rise to evil intentions.
There are beings there who are fiercely tormented; I will not fall into those evil realms."
Some may say:
"He does not possess the skillful means to awaken to this by himself.
The World-Honored One has also said:
One who exerts such diligence perceives this and also knows their own destination: "I shall be born in that realm.
Just as I know the destination of such diligence, so too do they know it—even if they were to harm themselves with a blade or drink poison.
Question:
Although one knows through diligence, it is not yet as ultimate as that of the Buddha.

Furthermore, if there is one who teaches and precepts, they do not rely on those precepts, thinking, "I shall not be born in the evil realms, nor shall I attain the fourth dhyāna. While their mind gives rise to the thought of nirvāṇa, they still fall into the three evil destinies.
The same is also stated regarding the avoidance of the seven locations.
In the Mahāsaṃnipāta-vibhaṅga-sūtra, it is said that because the mind is defiled, sentient beings go to the evil realms.
The World-Honored One has also said:
Suppose one were to observe the complete precepts for a hundred years, yet because the precepts are weak and not fully relinquished, could one thereby uproot the miserable realms?
To cause the six heretical teachers to oppress the masses and lead the Koliyans into the evil paths—this is what is called "evil."
If he has attained the first stage of diligence and is also one who has faith in the World-Honored One, yet still possesses the conditions for rebirth in the evil realms, his wisdom is sovereign.
As for those who are fixed in the wrong, are they all accomplished in false views?
If one who possesses false view (mithyādṛṣṭi) is established, does that person necessarily possess all false resolve (mithyāsamādhi)? Or it is said:
All those who possess false resolve necessarily possess false view.
If one achieves wrong view, they all achieve wrong concentration; the five heinous crimes constitute the achievement of wrong view and wrong concentration.
Or it is said:
all those who achieve wrong view, they all achieve wrong concentration.
Is there one who possesses wrong concentration (*mithyāsamādhi*) but does not possess wrong view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*)?
One who has severed the roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) and does not commit the five heinous crimes (*ānantarya*).
Furthermore, all those whose concentration is wrong necessarily possess wrong view.
Is it possible that one who possesses wrong view is not one who is fixed in the wrong course? [Answer:
One who possesses wrong view possesses the intention and the mental state.
Regarding those who possess right view among the various states of meditative concentration, do they all possess right view?
If one has attained right view, is all of that necessarily right view? Or it may be said:
all that is right view is necessarily attained right view.
If one achieves right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*), all such persons certainly possess right view;
the noble path (*āryamārga*) is right view, and they certainly achieve right view.
Furthermore, all those who possess settled right view certainly achieve right view.
Is it possible to possess right view (*samyagdṛṣṭi*) without possessing meditative concentration (*samādhi*)?
One who possesses right thought (*samyaksaṃkalpa*) and right intention (*samyakcitta*) necessarily possesses right view.
All those who are "stream-enterers going upward" (*ūrdhvasrotas*) go to the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
If one establishes the Abhāsvara (or Akaniṣṭha) realm, are all those therein "Upstreamers" (Urdhvasrotas)?
Answer: There may be those who are Upstreamers but do not belong to the Akaniṣṭha realm.
There may be those who dwell in Akaniṣṭha but are not "those who go upstream";
there may be those who are both "those who go upstream" and [dwell in] Akaniṣṭha;
and there may be those who are neither "those who go upstream" nor [dwell in] Akaniṣṭha.
What is meant by "one who goes upstream but does not reach the Akaniṣṭha realm"?
It refers to one who, having been reborn in the form realm as an Anāgāmin, nevertheless recollects higher matters and thus does not necessarily reach the Akaniṣṭha realm.

If one born in the desire realm who is an Anāgāmin is reborn in the formless realm yet remembers the matters of the higher realms, or if one born in the desire realm [remembers] those of the upper realms, this is called "Upstreamer" (Urdhvasrotas) who does not reach the Akaniṣṭha heaven.
The initial Akaniṣṭha station is called "Akaniṣṭha who is not an Upstreamer.
If an Anāgāmin is born within the Form Realm (rūpadhātu) but recollects the higher matters and is certain to abide in Akaniṣṭha, this is called "Upstreamer and Akaniṣṭha."
What is meant by "neither an upstreamer nor one who reaches Akaniṣṭha"?
Answer: It refers to the meaning of excluding all those aforementioned cases.
For what reason do the Anāgāmins and Arhats remain unmoved throughout the kalpas?
Some explain it thus:
those who dwell through the kalpas are not turned back by the world.

Furthermore, having attained equal liberation, one who possesses soft and inferior faculties transcends them to abide in the superior state; therefore, equal liberation neither increases nor decreases, and is thus said to abide immovably.
However, regarding the Anāgāmin, it should be said that he has already attained his vow while remaining [in this life].
As for ordinary persons (pṛthagjana), should it be said that they die with a wholesome mind, or that they die with an unwholesome mind, or that they die with a neutral mind?
Some may say: "It should be said that this is an unwholesome mental state; it is not by means of a wholesome mind that one has a place of abiding.
Question:
As the Blessed One said:
"At the time of death, one attains a wholesome mind; what was previously contemplated returns to equal vision.
This is called a contradiction within the Sūtras.
Some say this:
if one is born among the evil destinies, it is because one passed away with an unwholesome mind;
if one is born in the heavens, it is because one passed away with a wholesome mind.
Just as it is with the final moment of consciousness, so too is it for one abiding in the process of rebirth. Or it may be said:

one should say that death occurs with an indeterminate mind (*avyākṛta-citta*), because with an indeterminate mind one dwells within the body while awaiting the end of the remaining karmic retribution.

Furthermore, if one does not cultivate the wholesome, does not cultivate wholesome dharmas, and neither abides in a subsequent mind nor brings it to cessation, for this reason it should be said that one passes away with an indeterminate mind.
If one were to say this, death would be certain beyond doubt; at that time, one should say that at the end of life there is a place of refuge.
For what reason does an Arhat not attain the final wholesome mind?
Some say: One abides in the mind that experiences retribution until the end; however, at that time there is no wholesome state, and therefore one does not attain the wholesome.
Furthermore, if one were to cultivate the wholesome, one would likewise not abide [in it] at the time of death.
Furthermore, that mind is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), and its fundamental activities have ceased.
Moreover, the Blessed One said:
"One may know [the state of another] by living together with them; yet there are cases where one does not know it, even when their facial expression is serene."
What is the meaning of this?
The answer is:

If one hears others’ slanders or praises, and being flighty and credulous, delights in accepting the words of others; though the facial expression is pleasant, one believes, delights in, and endures them for as long as a finger-snap; possessing outward decorum and etiquette, one finds pleasure in physical stillness and attains joy, yet while appearing outwardly not secretive, one harbors deceit and hypocrisy within.
Furthermore, when preaching the Dharma, if one lacks the eloquence of meaning and the eloquence of the Dharma, and thus does not accord with reality, this is called delusion.
Moreover, there are two types [of giving]: the giving of faith and so forth, and the giving of morality, learning, and wisdom.
When these two are present before one, which yields the greatest fruit:
that in which both are pure, or that in which only one is pure?
Or it may be said as follows:
Second is the purity of both parts.
The World-Honored One has also said:
"In the case of a bhikṣu who visits the household of a donor, both parts are pure; this is called the foremost virtue of a donor's kinship."
Question:
What are the two intentions such that, in one case, it constitutes a great fruit, while in the other, it does not? Answer:
If the field is excellent, it is like excellent grain seeds;
just as when the field is excellent, those grain seeds are good.
Question:
It is like a field or a grain seed; however, because it does not conform to the proper season, it is difficult to bring to uniformity. Some say:
"Both parts are pure."
Having attained purity, one performs such giving; through the causal conditions inherent in the mind, one obtains the reality of all retributions.
Question:
If giving to a superior person means that no gift is equal [to it], then one should speak of "equal giving."
Furthermore, when one contemplates the equality of the two fruits of the measure, that gift is pure in both respects and possesses its full fruit.
Question:
As the Blessed One previously stated, regarding those bhikṣus for whom both parts are pure, the donor’s almsgiving is the foremost gift.
If this were so, there would be a discrepancy.
He replied:
"For the most part, both parts are pure; what the mind intends and practices is also pure. When the mind and its intentions are equal, the fruit is likewise equal."
How can the insects that commit slaughter give rise to pure dharmas?
Or it may be said:
the customs of the state and the times cause one’s relatives, friends, and associates to dwell upon such thoughts in their minds.
Furthermore, regarding the analogy of the waves on water and the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*):
there may be a practitioner of purity who, due to the retribution of their past actions, experiences a state of cessation.
Yet, if that practitioner falls into acts of killing, they will suffer the calamity of that consequence through the causal conditions of the intermediate actions performed during that birth.
One who approaches a virtuous friend to hear and receive the Dharma, contemplates foul impurities, and thus commits such acts of killing—how could such a person be considered pure?
How could black dharmas arise within them?
Or it may be said:
it is the custom of neighboring countries that causes your relatives, friends, and associates to think as they do.
Furthermore, it is like the movement of waves upon water.

Regarding those unwholesome states and so forth, for one who practices purity, the retribution of their conduct may be obstructed; once the unwholesome conduct has been purified, they experience the retribution of that conduct while still in the intermediate state.
He associates with unwholesome friends, listens to unwholesome teachings, and does not contemplate the practice of foulness; thus, within such purity, dark dharmas arise.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"One accomplishes two dharmas: either one does not possess goodness and is not diligent oneself, or another is diligent, firm, and unshakable.
What is meant by 'another being diligent, firm, and unshakable'?"
Some say this: One should inwardly examine oneself by means of the five dharmas and teach others to be diligent, firm, and unshakable.
If one acts in contradiction to all these and fails to correspond with them, then ruin and failure will follow.

Furthermore, others may learn what is non-Dharma and act contrary to the Dharma, thereby committing transgressions; yet there has never been one who acts thus against the Dharma that accords with the meaning.
For what reason did the World-Honored One say that the Śrāvakas are the foremost?
Some say: "He manifests the subtle and wondrous Dharma. Others say:
[He manifests the subtle and wondrous Dharma].
They manifest the deportment of śrāvakas,
or they speak thus:
"It is for the sake of protecting the Dharma."
Some explain it thus:
[the Buddha] inspires a courageous resolve in the bhikṣus and brings their practice to fulfillment.

Furthermore, for two reasons, the World-Honored One declares him the foremost disciple among the śrāvakas: because he presently bestows the meaning of the prediction (vyākaraṇa), and because he manifests transformations within that liberation.
One who speaks the language of animals yet exerts diligence, one who flows upward and dwells without wavering,
one who is an ordinary person yet remains steadfast, one who is honored for their generosity,
and one who is neither black nor white and lacks precepts— such a disciple is the foremost.
The sixth *Khandha* (Chapter) of the Sūtras Compiled by the Venerable Vasumitra Bodhisattva is completed.
The fifth volume of the *Vasumitra-śāstra*;
the sixth volume of the *Vasumitra-bodhisattva-saṃgīta-śāstra*.
Composed by Venerable Vasumitra;
translated by the Kasmirian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti and others during the Fu Qin dynasty.
Section 7: The Chapter on Contact (Sparśa-vastu). Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
There are two kinds of pleasure that those who have gone forth should not cultivate: the pleasure of attachment to sensual desires and the pleasure of worldly leisure in the present life.
What is meant by being attached to the pleasure of sensual desires?
What is the pleasure of the present that is without objective basis? Some say:
"The pleasure arising from recollecting past desires is what is called the pleasure of one who is stained by and attached to desires."
To recollect the various pleasures produced by present sensual desires is called the pleasure of present non-substantiality.
Alternatively, it is said to be the pleasure produced by the characteristics of the fetters and sensual desires.
This is called being stained by and attached to sensual pleasures within desire;
it is the pleasure produced by the characteristics of desire.
This is called the pleasure of the present that is devoid of substance.
Some say: the pleasure produced by the characteristics of sensual desire is called attachment to sensual pleasure within the realm of desire.
The joy of mental perception, the pleasure of sleep, and the pleasure of obtaining gain—these are called present sensual pleasures.

Furthermore, there is the habitual attachment directed toward sensual desires; having already obtained the pleasure produced by body and mind that was previously sufficient, this is called being stained by and attached to sensual pleasure within the realm of desire.
Having already obtained the various pleasures produced by equanimity of mind arising from body and mind, this is called the pleasure of non-action in the present.
Furthermore, the Venerable Śāriputra said:
"O worthy ones!
By the gathering of these twelve modes of practice, one attains the Dharma of the noble ones."
When these words were spoken, what was their meaning?
The answer is:
"Abiding in various places means dwelling in the place of creation."
Abiding in the sphere of wisdom and abiding in the sphere of appropriateness—this is called the deportment of one's own person.

If one bestows a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa) selectively, one is attached to a single matter; if one analyzes principles and meanings, one expounds upon their distinctions; if one addresses those who pose doubts, one expounds upon those doubts; if one settles those who debate, one discusses what they find secure—this is called the deportment of that person.
Some may observe that being free from guile and deception, and possessing a nature of simplicity, is called one's own deportment;
discerning the meaning of the faculties is the deportment of others.

Having already attained a human body born in a central land and obtained the physical form of a worthy sage, their faculties of eye, ear, and mind are all pure, manifesting the reality of things as they truly are. Their minds are not stained by defiled conduct or the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); through wisdom, they follow in accordance with the truth without fault. They encounter the appearance of a World-Honored One endowed with the Ten Powers and attain the three joys, entering the fundamental non-arising, the blissful, profound, and wondrous Dharma of the Tathāgata.

The disciples of the Tathāgata who have achieved excellence do not experience confusion or delusion regarding that intention; they attain the dharmas of the noble ones and distribute them widely; embraced by wisdom, they preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma without hesitation; and they reverently uphold, recite, and chant it, never departing from it.
The commentators on all dharmas transmit them from one to another; within the realm of equal dharmas, they bestow the food of the Dharma upon others.

By means of causes and conditions, they bestow their own dignified deportment upon those people, practicing the various holy conducts (*brahmacarya*), so that there may be manifest and enduring benefit in the four bases of power (*ṛddhipāda*).

Having become a noble person, born in that auspicious realm, they manifest the five ways in which nothing is empty and cause them all to be far removed; with their faculties complete, they manifest the six ways in which nothing is empty and cause them all to be far removed.
That which has never been practiced before, he manifests as the seven non-empty states and causes all to be far removed from them.
Regarding the six abodes, he manifests the eight non-abodes and causes all to be far removed from them.
Furthermore, by means of the causes and conditions through which a person’s noble and holy faculties arise, he manifests benevolence, goodness, righteousness, and the majestic deportment of others.
The Buddha has appeared in the world to preach the subtle and wondrous Dharma by means of causes and conditions;

therefore, those who possess the strength of a great man and are established in majestic deportment find joy in the various sense-bases (*āyatana*). Having manifested the turning of the wheel and the teaching of all dharmas, he now dwells therein and seeks to expound them further.
With all faculties complete, he manifests the meritorious deeds performed in the past.
Furthermore, the Venerable Mahāpajjota said:
"One who possesses faith, joy, and mindfulness does not fail to pervade the Buddha’s realm."
"The place where the Most Excellent One has gone—therein the mind is constantly linked with joy.
What is the meaning of these words?
The answer is as follows:

Having achieved wisdom, one’s faith is firm; delighting in the Buddha-dharma, one’s resolve is undisturbed; upholding the dharmas of wisdom, the mind is always focused and diligent. Since these various dharmas are without discrepancy, one follows the teachings of the Dharma and enters meditative concentration therein; therefore, this is called "faithful joy and mindfulness."
"Gautama, from the very beginning you have never lacked followers; wherever you go, your mind is constantly preoccupied with returning to subtle and profound meanings.
Do not hold such a view, for this is not the sublime Dharma."
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"Faith is the foremost wealth.
When he spoke these words, what was their meaning?
Answer: Because it is that which is employed by the wise, it is said that faith is the foremost wealth.
Among the pursuits of wealth, the wealth of the noble ones (ārya) is the true wealth.
Regarding that which is not the wealth of the noble ones, once it has been obtained and the mind does not lose it, one should think:
"That is not the wealth of the noble ones.

A vessel made of *maṇi* jewels spontaneously produces objects, with various other miscellaneous gems interspersed among them; furthermore, there are extraordinary treasures such as *śukti*, *musāragalva*, and *aśmagarbha* which people covet, which must always be guarded and protected, for which one can never have enough, and which cannot be hidden away.
The riches of the noble ones each have seven aspects, such as the wealth of faith up to the wealth of wisdom.
Within these, each person finds delight and their heart leaps with joy; yet, they do not remain diligently established in equanimity.
Clinging to the wealth of others with an unstable mind, one acts upon whatever desires arise and fails to guard one's wisdom.
By eliminating greedy desire, one becomes replete with wisdom and, through that wisdom, triumphs over them.
Furthermore, that which is not the wealth of the noble ones is associated with wrong intention and action;
however, the wealth of the noble ones and so forth is associated with right intention and action. Therefore, it is said that the wealth of faith is foremost.

Furthermore, as for the meaning of "faith": it is to have faith in external wealth, to have no distraction of mind, to fulfill the laws of the household, to know contentment well, and to be skillful in fields and undertakings and in wholesome mental enjoyments.

Just as here the Dharma of the śramaṇas has renunciation as its joy—the joy of resting in secluded places and the joy of the site of enlightenment—it is therefore said that "the discernment of dharmas is a sublime joy."
Having first partaken of the nectar of immortality (*amṛta*), his words are free from falsehood; being most auspicious and perfected in merit, it is therefore called "Auspicious in Every Taste.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, one knows that wisdom is clarity; being devoid of deluded intent and not associated with perversity, it is therefore called "Supremely Clear."
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"For example, Ānanda Bhikṣu has already abandoned the six bases of contact without remainder and caused them all to be extinguished.

He no longer possesses a body that experiences the arising of suffering or pleasure as retribution; he has no mind, no physical form, and no sense-bases. He no longer performs actions that give rise to suffering or pleasure as retribution, nor does he have any state of vacancy. This is the end of suffering."
When these words were spoken, what was their meaning?
The answer is:

regarding these six contacts (*ṣaḍ-sparśāyatana*), the six internal contacts are forever exhausted without remainder; having abandoned all attachments to desires, one no longer practices them; desire is exhausted, the underlying tendencies of craving (*tṛṣṇā-anuśaya*) are forever removed, and the fetters of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*) are extinguished so that they do not arise again.
Again, it is said:
one contemplates the foulness of impurities with a mind free from desire, and having exhausted all desires, practices śamatha and vipaśyanā.
Again, it is said:
Being without desire, one attains the gate of liberation through wishlessness and fully accomplishes the gate of liberation through emptiness.

That [state] has no body and no reaching-knowledge; it has no speech and no such mind; it has no wisdom and no such essence; and as for the external sense-bases (*āyatana*), they do not exist if they have not been exhausted.
There are the sense-bases (*āyatana*), yet there are no internal bases, nor are there any others that remain unexhausted; they have no basis of support, nor are they ever utterly extinguished.
Furthermore, it is said:
"He has no body, having removed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*); in this way, all such things—his body and the characteristics of a body—are non-existent."

In this way, all those things are without body, and there are no bodily actions, vocal actions, or mental actions; nor is there any substance, and the movement of objects and the retribution thereof do not revolve.
Those sense-bases (āyatana) are also free from wrong views, and thus the internal sense-bases are fully perfected.
Based on that, there is no retribution of suffering or pleasure arising from disputes.
The Venerable Dharmatara spoke thus:
When one is in contact with the six types of sensory pleasure, there are the six subtle contacts; regarding those subtle contacts, there is accumulation.

Since he has nothing remaining and is fully possessed of freedom from desire, yet his craving and attachment are not yet exhausted, when he encounters their inherent nature, he perceives it as the root of suffering.
Thus, being without remainder and without desire, one who is thus associated with the departure from craving abides in the state of desirelessness.
Just as that nature is associated with suffering, one abides in the notion of non-self and manifests wisdom; in this way, one exhaustively practices the cessation of all things without remainder.

Having practiced in this way, one departs from delusion and abides in wisdom; with the cessation of ignorance and craving, the perception of clear knowledge arises, and thus it is said that one abides in the remainderless extinction.

He possesses no body, nor does he obtain a body composed of the four great elements; like one dwelling in a place of confinement, his own mind is free from suffering and pleasure, and there is no evil transmigration within the four bases of divine abiding (brahmavihāra).

Regarding those who enter into birth and enter into disputes—whether they are attached to themselves or unattached to themselves—in whatever place they dwell, even at the abodes of the four devas where the mind turns and seeks an opening for escape, all of this is ablaze.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"The eye has the longing and desire to see forms; yet there are unwholesome forms that the eye does not delight in.
How is it that the eye has the longing and desire to see forms, yet there are unwholesome forms that the eye does not delight in?"
Some say: "Aspiration arises through the gateway of the eye, whereby craving and aversion manifest their source.
Furthermore, what is aspiration regarding the eye?
It is not comprised within the sphere of objects.
Furthermore, when associated with the mind, it illuminates and brings about benefit.
As the Venerable Śāriputra said:
Having personally observed and known that all forms perceived as "mine" and so forth are devoid of the conceptualization of limbs and members,
how does one know that form abides without movement and thereby relinquish the perception of limbs and members?
The answer is:
In this way, there is the accumulation of contact and sensation, and that [contact] returns to its respective object; some may be "it," while others may not be "it.
For example, the Brahmin Dīrghanakha spoke these words:
"Gautama!
I cannot endure any 'self' whatsoever.
When this scriptural passage was spoken, what is its meaning?
Or some might say:
seeing the Venerable Śāriputra go forth into homelessness, they immediately gave rise to this thought:
"I cannot endure anything at all."
"Both of those two have gone forth as monastics; everything has occurred exactly as I wished. Therefore, I said to the World-Honored One:
'Do you not find this sight unbearable?
And I further said:"
"All contemplations involve doubt.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these words:
"Do you have doubt regarding your doubt?"
Again he spoke these words:
"Manifesting all as non-contemplation, contemplating all as non-existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One again spoke these words:
Furthermore, this is not your own view.
Moreover, the Blessed One said:

"Dwelling in seclusion and delighting in tranquility, one constantly finds joy; one draws near to and contemplates the purity and bliss of meditative reflection, such that reflection is associated with reflection."
What is the difference between delighting in stillness through secluded dwelling and delighting in stillness through contemplation?
Some say: delighting in stillness through secluded dwelling serves to rest the mind, while delighting in stillness through contemplation has already attained *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*.

Some say: "To those who dwell in seclusion and delight in tranquility, he manifests the rest of nirvāṇa; to those who contemplate and delight in tranquility, he manifests the path as the essential means of deliverance. Others say:

Those who dwell in seclusion and delight in tranquility manifest the first and second mental abandonments (*prahāṇa*); those who contemplate and delight in tranquility [manifest] the third and fourth mental abandonments.

Furthermore, there are two perceptions: the severing of all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the uprooting of all defiled attachments; to find joy therein without departing from that initial state is what is called "dwelling in seclusion and delighting in tranquility."

One should contemplate that there are three modes of reflection which serve as the dwelling place for wholesome dharmas, namely: dwelling in association; being beneficial through the association of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, which is called "recreation"; and this constitutes the joy of reflecting on tranquility.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"In this regard, a bhikṣu should contemplate the body as the body; he should not give rise to the perception of a self, nor should he form a conceptualization.
When these words were spoken, what is their meaning?
Some say: "Contemplate the impurity of the body and do not relish it; do not give rise to the notion of purity regarding the body.
Others say: [the same].

One should contemplate that the body is impermanent, empty, and non-self; one must not give rise to the notion that the body is permanent, the notion that it is pleasant, or the notion that it is a self—this is how one should contemplate.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Contemplate the body as the body, and do not calculate the origin of the body."

Furthermore, in the stage of purifying conduct, one contemplates and discerns great matters; through the skillful means of calculating impurities and reflecting upon them, having fully understood them so that they no longer arise, one thoroughly comprehends all that is distinguished by the illumination of the eye of wisdom.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"There are four dharma-phrases: the phrase of non-violence, the phrase of non-confusion, the phrase of equanimity of mindfulness, and the phrase of equanimity of concentration."
What is the meaning of "dharma-pada"? Some say:
because all dharmas sever [delusion], they are called dharma-padas.
The roots of goodness that cannot be destroyed, the roots of goodness free from ill-will, and the roots of goodness of equanimity, concentration, and non-delusion.
Alternatively, it is said:
because one practices all dharmas, they are called "Dharma-words" (dharmapada).

One does not give rise to sensual desire, and thus sensual desire is exhausted and non-existent; one is without ill will, and thus ill will is exhausted; one is equanimous toward sloth-and-torpor, and thus equanimity exhausts restlessness-and-worry and doubt.

Furthermore, the Dharma-verses of the śramaṇa are indestructible: there is the precept of being without ill will, the deportment of seeking concentration through equanimity, and the deportment of seeking wisdom through equanimity in concentration.
As the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā said:
"Pleasurable feeling is a portion of painful feeling.
What is the meaning of the term "portion" (aṃśa)?
Answer: Where there is opposition, there is division.

Within that pleasant sensation, there is an inherent opposition consisting of painful sensation; within painful sensation, there is an inherent division consisting of pleasant sensation; and within both painful and pleasant sensations, there is a division consisting of neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation.
Setting aside the neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation, there is the portion of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Ignorance associated with clarity (*vidyā*) is the portion of clarity; these are mutually exhausting causes.

Clarity is the portion of volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); the defilement of volitional formations is the portion of ignorance. To practice such volitional formations that lead to cessation is the portion of *nirvāṇa*.
Having extinguished all conditioned phenomena within the realm of nirvana without remainder, one attains this nirvana that is indivisible.
At that time, the World-Honored One praised it, calling it the supreme precept and holy life.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"The Venerable Māluṅkyaputta declares: 'This life is this body; the realization of the truths is what I have cultivated through the holy life.
How is it that the body is one thing and the life is another?"
"In this regard, when a bhikṣu has seen the truths and says, 'I have not practiced the holy life,' what is the meaning of these words?
He replied:
Although one [type of] view is specifically identified, the others are not.
The Venerable Dharmatrāta stated:
"If one holds that 'this very life is the self,' such a bhikṣu has seen the truths but does not practice the holy life."

Regarding the destination of knowledge and vision and its underlying basis: if one perceives and proceeds toward that which is not the basis, both will entail affliction; thus has the Most Victorious One spoken.
There are twelve aggregates of phenomena; there is the body and the view of self.
All patience and reflection constitute the life of a Dharma-verse bhikṣu.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"O Māra, son of the Great One, when you say that a young brahmin of handsome appearance should act in such a manner—
when these words are spoken, what is their meaning?"
Some say: The Venerable Mahā-Moggallāna, being inclined toward the ten perceptions, spoke thus;
furthermore, it was because the World-Honored One wished to uproot all fetters and latent tendencies.
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"In this way, that person desires to bring about the complete extinction of the fetters and underlying tendencies of sensual desire; the Venerable One has spoken thus.
This is just as the phrasing of the Sūtra states.

When debating with the heterodox brahmins regarding the accumulation of fetters arising from conceptual thought, you, Māra’s son, though so upright and yet so very young, lie there embracing disgrace; since you possess no sensual desire, how much less could your mind be bound by attachment through craving?
Regarding the fetter of the underlying tendency toward sensual desire (*kāmarāgānuśaya*), how does the Blessed One observe the transgressions of various faults?
Just as one knows the strength or weakness of the underlying tendency toward sensual desire, one is sustained by the training and the precepts.
If they possess the capacity, their words will not be contradicted.
If those who are attached to the lower or middle [realms] are not transformed, then the five higher fetters (pañca ūrdhvabhāgīyāḥ saṃyojanāni) do not exist.
One should thus examine this matter; it is no different [from what has been said], and for this reason the World-Honored One knows it.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"In this regard, the bhikṣu Bhadrapāli possesses complete practice; yet his precepts are not fully perfected. He dwells in a secluded and quiet place, sitting in meditation upon a steep cliff."

Dwelling thus in seclusion and quietude, sitting in meditation upon a steep crag, the World-Honored One gave this instruction; the devas likewise instructed him, the wise practitioners of the holy life likewise exhorted him, and he also exhorted himself.
What is the meaning of "instruction" (*anuśāsana*)? Some say:
the person who is rebuked receives the most excellent teaching; it is an instruction for the devas, an instruction for the wise in the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and it is also self-instruction.
Some say: It should be said that they are to be censured.
The World-Honored One also censures them, saying, "These are not my disciples."
The devas also reproached him, saying, "This śramaṇa is not a son of the Śākya.
Wise practitioners of the holy life also reproached him, saying, "This is not the Dharma of equanimity.
Furthermore, he reproached and admonished himself, saying, "I am not a śramaṇa."
Furthermore, because he thus praised the Blessed One’s impartial teaching and discipline, the Blessed One rebuked him in this manner.
As the Blessed One said:

"One who accomplishes five qualities—dwelling in a secluded and quiet place, sitting in meditation on steep mountain crags; being content with tattered and worn-out robes; and being content with alms-food and medicinal requisites for illness—yet conceives a desire for sensual pleasure."

At that time, the World-Honored One reprimanded and instructed him with reasoned principles; the devas likewise provided instruction, as did those of superior worldly wisdom and those who practice the holy life, each instructing according to what has been taught regarding the supremacy of the world, the supremacy of the Dharma, and the supremacy of the self.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"This is called suffering; this is called the origin of suffering; this is called the first contemplation. This is called the cessation of suffering;
this is called the path leading to the cessation of suffering; this is called the second contemplation."
When these words were spoken, what was their meaning? Some explained it thus:
"This is called suffering;
this is called the origin of suffering"—this is the contemplation of the actual fruit of causes and conditions.
This is called the exhaustion of suffering; this is called the essential path leading out of the exhaustion of suffering. One contemplates the fruit of dependent origination. Some say:
the first contemplation is of the fetters (*saṃyojana*), and the second is of purity.
Again, it is said:
first, contemplate what was originally created; second, contemplate one's own faults.
Again, it is said:

because of the faculties of others, when speaking of the name of virtuous conduct or when discussing unvirtuous conduct, one also offers praise and instruction.

Someone might say this: [and so forth].
"Just like that Blessed One, just like that Blessed One.
Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana seek out the community of monks, yet I never gather them.
Or he might say this:
Emerging from the meditative concentration of loving-kindness, Devadatta sought [him].
Emerging from that samādhi, the Venerable Ānanda asked this question.
Furthermore, the present reliance on the exhaustion of the self is based on the previous formulaic phrase.
"I shall protect my disciples by means of two phrases;
it is not for my own sake, but out of compassion for them.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
There are these ten kinds of craving for existence, which moisten the heart with compassionate concern, causing the world to tremble with fear.
For what reason does one take delight in the joy of seeing the love and compassion for precepts, extensive learning, and the holy life?
Some say: "It produces its own virtuous fruit.
Furthermore, it produces manifold perceptions.
Furthermore, the Blessed One said:
"The brahmin householder Nāgapiṇḍa, having seen forms with his eyes, thus takes delight.
What is the meaning of these words?
Some speak thus: "Such is their form;
they have no singing or dancing, yet the price of the perfumes for their bodies is exceedingly high.
Others speak these words:
It is because of these things—prostitution, music, play, and laughter—that this was said.
Furthermore, these words were spoken on account of desire for women.

It is not possible to act within the sphere of non-seclusion; for the thorns of sensual craving—gain, loss, dispraise, and praise—arise there. Therefore, one should dwell in the mountains and marshes for the sake of avoiding such gain and support.
As the bhikṣuṇī Dharmadinnā said:
"Pleasurable feeling is driven by sensual desire; painful feeling is driven by aversion; neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is driven by ignorance."
Regarding these words, what is their meaning?
Some say: These are the words of the Tathāgata’s instruction and admonition.
Again, he spoke these words:
"Is this teaching of the Tathāgata’s exhortation and admonition something that can be spoken of,
or is it something that cannot be spoken of?"
Or one might say:
it should be said that it can be spoken of. Why is this?
As the Blessed One said:
"I shall teach the Dharma, which possesses both meaning and flavor.
Since the flavor can be expounded, its meaning may likewise be explained."
If meaning cannot be expressed, then the teaching of the Dharma would be devoid of meaning.
Question:
When expressing meaning, does one express the flavor (*rasa*) or both?
When explaining the meaning and flavor, there is both meaning and flavor.
If that which is spoken were intended to make the meaning and flavor different from the Dharma,
and if the principles were indeed different from the Dharma, then it would not accord with the text of the sūtra.
Some say: "The meaning can be expressed by names;
names are that which convey meaning from one to another. Regarding the meaning itself, it should be said that it is inexpressible.
Furthermore, speech is produced by conceptualization (*saṃjñā*), whereas meaning is not produced by conceptualization; therefore, meaning is inexpressible.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"I shall preach the Dharma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
Within this transformation of the Dharma, what constitutes the beginning, what constitutes the middle, and what constitutes the end?
Some say: "Precepts are the beginning, contemplation of impurity is the middle, and Nirvana is the end.
They further say:
At the beginning, one studies the Great Precepts; in the middle, one studies the increase of the mind; at the end, one studies the increase of wisdom.

Furthermore, when the Dharma is preached, the initial conditions constitute the beginning; those who receive transformation and turn back toward it constitute the middle; and the subsequent stage constitutes the ultimate.

In this regard, it serves as the foundation for the beginning, the foundation for the middle, and the foundation for the end; therefore, it is said to be "good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:

"As it has been taught, one should recollect by means of three things without forgetting; having grasped the primary characteristics and taken them as objects, one does not lose their essential meaning at the outset."
Regarding what was said, what is its meaning?
The answer is:
In the past, the original objects were grasped, maintained, and guarded; because they were perceived and sustained as mental conceptions, they are called "original characteristics" (mūla-lakṣaṇa).
That which is encompassed turns back toward oneself spontaneously through causes and conditions.
"Spontaneously" means spontaneous through skillful means (*upāya*) and spontaneous through intimacy; therefore, it is called "spontaneous."
When one repeatedly subdues the mind within oneself, there arises a conscious guarding; thus it is said that one’s resolve is firm and memory is unforgetting.

As it has been taught, regarding these internal phenomena (*dharma*), their stability, their emptiness, and their suchness as conditions—these are the causal conditions; this is called dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Regarding the meaning of these words:
the answer is that "all phenomena therein" refers to those phenomena which are the objects of practice.
That which abides in the Dharma is without change.
That which is empty of dharmas is the fruit of causes and conditions.
Thus, one who knows that practice is not different from causes and conditions contemplates the actions performed.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
"Contact is one corner; the cultivation of contact is the second corner; and feeling is in the middle.
What is the meaning of these words?
Some say: "Contact (sparśa) constitutes one corner, and the conditioned activity (saṃskāra) constitutes the perception of accumulation (upacaya).
Contact and its accumulation constitute two corners; that which is situated in the midst of sensation (vedanā) is different."
Furthermore, regarding contact (*sparśa*): ignorance-contact has the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) as its condition; ignorance gives rise to contact, and sensation (*vedanā*) arises therein.
Moreover, the Blessed One said:
"Therefore, monks, you should train yourselves thus: 'We shall subdue our minds with the thought of renunciation.'"
Regarding these words, what is their meaning? Some may say:
These are the words of the World-Honored One’s exhortation; at that time, one should seek liberation and thus leave the household life to study the Way.
Furthermore, this statement was made because of the equality of their renunciation.
Moreover, the World-Honored One said:
"In this regard, what should the other bhikṣus do concerning the youth Māra?"
