"You are young in years, having left the household life not long ago and being but recently set upon the path; you have also not been long in entering this Dharma. How is it that you are now old and your form is matured?"
"Elder! You wish to quickly seek instruction and admonition from me.
What is the meaning of these words?"
Or someone might say:
"The young bhikṣus will further think:
'Even this person is only now wishing to study; we too shall study later, acting according to our own pleasure.'"
Again, he spoke these words:
"The young bhikṣu then thought:
'If even one as old as this has attained nothing, how much less shall we have any attainment? "
Lacking courageous resolve, he further spoke these words:
"That young bhikṣu should understand this: he seeks instruction; how much more so should he seek the Way?"
They further said:
"Many young bhikṣus have been seen and heard by us, let alone ourselves.
They seek instruction; how much more so should we, who are even younger bhikṣus, not seek it?"
Furthermore, these are the words of the World-Honored One’s entrustment: "Do not harbor thoughts of weariness.

For what reason? In the past, when the Tathāgatas, the Samyaksaṃbuddhas, dwelt in seclusion among mountains and marshes, sitting upon steep crags, they praised such matters yet did not dwell therein; however, while the World-Honored One praises their virtues, he also dwells within them.
Some say: "In former times, there were no secluded places, mountains, marshes, or forests; villages were so closely connected that chickens could fly from one to another.
Question:
If there is no present secluded dwelling, for what reason do you now praise it?
Answer: One praises the virtue of past secluded dwelling.
He further spoke these words:
"At that time, when the Buddha was transforming sentient beings, he did not employ seclusion as a means of transformation, fearing that they would not enter into his teachings and discipline."
He further spoke these words:

"At that time, sentient beings will value contemplative concentration and will not permit those who dwell in secluded and quiet places to do so; instead, within the villages, those sentient beings who are to be transformed should practice the contemplation of impurity."
He further spoke these words:
"At that time, the minds of the assembly were largely attached to pleasure; none permitted a secluded place, fearing that their minds would become weary and unable to endure solitude.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
Regarding these words—these words from the sūtra—who could possibly withstand them?
Whatever Devadatta may have argued in the presence of the World-Honored One, the World-Honored One did not dwell upon it.
Regarding those who praise the destruction of increase, the Blessed One would likewise do so.
That person has no basis for such a claim; nor does that person act in opposition, yet such a virtuous bhikṣu could not possibly utter such evil words in the presence of the Tathāgata.
Why is this? Because no one is able to know the Blessed One’s qualities as they truly correspond to reality.
Those who dwell in seclusion, however, come to know that person through their respectful service and attendance; for this reason, the Blessed One did not permit it.

For what reason does the Dharma abide from the time of the original World-Honored One, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, through to the realization and the disciples, and even after the long parinirvāṇa of the World-Honored One, does it continue to abide?
Some may say:
"Those sentient beings are emanations created by the Buddha; therefore, the śrāvakas are unable to transform them.
Others may further say:
At that time, sentient beings highly valued śamatha and vipaśyanā, and he preached the Dharma for them.
Furthermore, at that time, the Tathāgata’s lifespan was extremely long, just as it is now in Jambudvīpa.

Thereafter, while the World-Honored One dwelt within a short lifespan, for the sake of those sentient beings receiving transformation and those in other realms, I observed the teachings, admonitions, and verbal instructions he spoke to the śrāvakas as set forth in the sūtras of the past and future.
Having finished speaking, the World-Honored One addressed me and the assembly: "The experience of sensation is beyond description;
I have well explained the three dharmas and contact. This youth of handsome appearance praises his own origin."
The Seventh Chapter on Contact (*Sparśa-khaṇḍa*) from the *Ācārya-Vasumitra-bodhisattva-saṃgīti* is hereby completed.
The Sixth Fascicle of the *Vasumitra-śāstra*.
The Seventh Fascicle of the *Ācārya-Vasumitra-bodhisattva-saṃgīti-śāstra*.
Composed by the Venerable Vasumitra;
translated during the Fu Qin dynasty by the Kasmirian Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti and others. Chapter Eight:

The Section on Fetters and Latent Tendencies (Saṃyojana-varga). Regarding the defilements (mala): should they be said to follow from inversion (viparyāsa), or should they be said not to follow from inversion?
Some state as follows:
"Either they follow perversion, or they do not follow perversion.
The four perversions should be said to follow perversion; desire, conceit, hatred, and wrong view should be said not to follow perversion."
Question:
How is it that one is not defiled by what is not as-it-is?
It is also said that by observing it as-it-is, one comes to know it; therefore, one does not associate with it.
Answer: When gathered together, they can indeed be known, yet they do not possess intrinsic characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*).

If one were to perceive them through their intrinsic characteristics, there would always be a sense of weariness and aversion; there would be no sense of intrinsic characteristics that does not turn back.
Question:
As with a collection that can be known, such a collection possesses desire.

When one contemplates those inversions as one contemplates their own characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), one becomes defiled and attached; there is no lack of attachment, and because there is no characteristic of self, the mind does not turn back.
Or it may be said:
it should be described as being associated with delusion (*moha*) in accordance with perversion (*viparyāsa*).
Question:
Is ignorance not associated with ignorance? Would one wish for ignorance to follow after perversion?
Or it may be said:
it should be stated that it does not follow after perversion.
If one were to follow after inversion by means of inversion, then that [inversion] would not be extinguished; it is not by means of inversion that inversion is extinguished.
Question:
Just as wholesome and indeterminate minds and mental factors do not follow after inversion yet can be extinguished, so too is it with defilements.
Answer: Wholesome and neutral minds and mental factors continue as before, and the fetters can be made to cease forever; therefore, one should say that they are inverted.
Furthermore, one should say that they do not follow inversion.
When associated with wrong intention and its underlying tendencies, it does not accord with [right view], and thus it arises unaccomplished; that is, it is accomplished in impurity.

For what reason? It is said that the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is an inversion, impure, and incapable of being harmed; there is no real self, yet the view of a self-identity revolves [as if there were].
Or someone might say:
"The mind possesses pure characteristics and revolves toward the impure.
The answer is:
There is no pure characteristic; yet that which may be pure or impure is questioned:
if there were purity, there would be perversion, and one might say it is either "existent" or "permanent."
"Do you wish to prevent the characteristic of impermanence from being established?
He replied:
"The characteristic of impermanence is not established."

If the characteristics of permanence and impermanence are not established, they would nonetheless have to possess characteristics; yet, since they are not [true] characteristics, the characteristic of impermanence is not established.
Alternatively, it is said:
"The perception of inversion is associated with delusion (*moha*), whereas the perception of impurity is not an inversion and is associated with wisdom (*jñāna*)."
Question:
Ignorance does not associate with ignorance.
Do you wish to claim that ignorance is not a perversion?
Wisdom does not associate with wisdom.
Do you wish to cause wisdom to be inverted?
Or perhaps someone says this:
The view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is a defilement; since defilements accompany inversion, the view of a self is inverted and impure.
By the power of wisdom, wisdom does not follow non-wisdom or inversion; therefore, while it is impure, it is not inverted.
Question:
Since the mind and mental factors associated with defilements are not themselves defiled attachments,
do you intend for them to follow along with the inversions?
If the mind and mental factors associated with wisdom are themselves not wisdom, would you wish for them to follow after perversion?
Furthermore, just as one who possesses the characteristic of impurity does not become defiled by it, it is impossible for the aggregates to be defiled by their own intrinsic characteristics.
Just as the non-self of the aggregates is established, so too is their purity established according to their respective kinds.
Therefore, although the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) is a perversion, it is not itself impure.
Are all views subsumed within the sixty-two views, or do the sixty-two views subsume all views?
Some may say:
"Are all views subsumed within the sixty-two views?
Or do the sixty-two views subsume all views?"
Some say: "All views are subsumed within the sixty-two views, and the sixty-two views likewise subsume all views.
Question:
As it was said regarding the Brahmin Savi, who had thirty-six different types of views ranging from three up to thirty-six, how could these not be considered "views"?
The answer is:
this matter is thus; the same applies to the two and the sixty as well.
Some may say:
"All views are subsumed within the sixty-two views, but the sixty-two views do not subsume all views.
Which views are not subsumed?"
Regarding that nirvāṇa, it is said that there is no co-arising with nirvāṇa; from the five false views down to the single false view, none exist.
Furthermore, the views produced by the sixty-two views should be said to be subsumed within them.

As Sāṃbhiya has said: from three up to sixty, the śramaṇas, relying on wisdom, relying on the characteristics of wisdom, and relying on the conceptualization of syllables, have exhausted all defilements.
What are the sixty-three views? Some say:
"There are no sixty-three views; there are only these two views."
Some say: To claim that there is no nirvana is a false view;
this is called the sixty-third view. Others say:
To say that there is no path is wrong view; this is called the sixty-third view.
Furthermore, whatever is seen constitutes the sixty-three views.
Thus, there are five types of wrong views: views of self, views of uncertainty, wrong view, attachment to views, and attachment to precepts and rituals.
By what kind of view is the view of being produced without cause subsumed?
By what kind of view is the view of never relinquishing [one's position] until death subsumed?
Or, some say as follows:
The view that things arise without cause, yet claims they have a cause, is a false view (*mithyādṛṣṭi*) and is abandoned through the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).

Furthermore, there is the view that one does not abandon [wrong views] even unto death; to claim that there is "action" where there is no action is the "theft of precepts" (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*), and it is abandoned through the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
Furthermore, the view that things arise without cause is the view of non-existence regarding what exists, and is thus subsumed under [the category of] views.
As for those who do not abandon their views until death, they should be said to be subsumed under the possession of views.
By what view or underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) would an underlying tendency already exhausted within the mind arise again? Yet, there can be no such causal condition.
Or it may be said: when the causal conditions are present, the fetters and underlying tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*) are then exhausted.
When causes and conditions are not yet exhausted, there remains a residue; once they are exhausted, it no longer arises.
Question:

Regarding these truths as objects of untainted conditions (*anāsrava-ālambana*), among the fetters and underlying tendencies (*saṃyojana-anuśaya*), some are exhausted while others are not; what is the cause and condition for this exhaustion?
Answer: When conditions have been exhausted without remainder, this is called cessation (*nirodha*).
Question:

The conditions for these are different: while the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) have not yet been exhausted, the conditions themselves may already be exhausted; therefore, they are not the [sole] conditions, and thus the fetters and latent tendencies are exhausted.
Alternatively, it is said:
they are always associated and there is never a time when they are dissociated.
Question:
It is not a causal condition; furthermore, there may be instances where it does not serve as an object-condition.
Or, it is stated as follows:
When it is not yet exhausted, that itself serves as the condition;
yet by means of this very condition, it will no longer arise again.
Furthermore, once it is exhausted, it does not arise again.
Question: If,

when the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) that take contaminated objects as their condition are exhausted, those conditions no longer arise again repeatedly— being neither extinguished nor produced—
is it intended that the uncontaminated mind (*anāsrava-citta*) is the condition for them?
The fetters (saṃyojana) give rise to further fetters. Or it is said:

their association arises, abides, and ceases together, yet unlike their conditions, once exhausted they disperse individually and do not remain in one place; thus, those mental states possess latent tendencies (anuśaya), yet these do not follow their conditions.
Question:
When that mind has not yet been exhausted, do the associated latent tendencies (anuśaya) arise, abide, and cease together with it, or do they not follow its conditions?
Is it the case that the desire for these tendencies not to be severed constitutes their condition?
The fetters (saṃyojana) are not the conditions for the fetters. Or it is said:

the associated proclivities (anuśaya) that coexist with the mind do not do so in the same way as their conditions; therefore, although those associated proclivities have been exhausted, that mind still possesses proclivities, though not in the manner of their conditions.
This is also as previously explained. Or it is said:

the latent tendencies (anuśaya) associated with the mind do not defile it in the same manner as their objects; therefore, although the associated fetters have already been exhausted, that mind still possesses latent tendencies that do not correspond to their objects.
This is also as explained above.
Alternatively, it is said:

regarding the latent proclivities associated with the mind (*saṃprayukta-anuśaya*), that mind is defiled not by virtue of its object; therefore, although all associated latent proclivities have been exhausted, that mind still possesses latent proclivities not by virtue of its object.
This is also as explained above.

Furthermore, if it were the case that [the mind] conditions that [object], then that mind would possess latent dispositions (*anuśaya*); likewise, one would see that when an untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*) conditions a latent disposition, that [untainted mind] would also possess latent dispositions.

Furthermore, regarding the latent proclivities (*anuśaya*) associated with various [states], one should say that those minds possess latent proclivities, whether they have been exhausted or not; it is like the power of a sovereign king who arrives wherever he desires.
For what reason is it that wrong view associated with the desire realm regards the suffering of the form and formless realms [as non-existent], yet is not driven by those realms?
Some say: "That which is driven by its own realm does not interfere with other realms."
Question:
This too is my doubt: why do [defilements] not afflict other realms?
Furthermore, if one creates [defilements] of another realm within the desire realm, would one wish for those with outflows (sāsrava) to create defilements belonging to their own realm?
Because of wrong view, that realm is also driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Alternatively, some say:
because pride (*māna*) in that realm is slight and gradually departs, that realm is not driven by the underlying tendencies.
Question:

If that which is separated from [the fetters] were to be separated from them even while within its own realm, then its own realm would likewise be subject to being driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Or, it is said as follows:
It is not because there is doubt regarding that view, nor does it take that realm as its object.
Question:
How can there be this teaching in the absence of that?
The answer is:
There is. If he were to cause the speaker to speak by means of this statement, it would not be its true meaning and would offer no benefit.
Question:
One who is free from suffering and affliction does not entertain the thought that there is anything to be said;
nor does he say, "I know it, yet I say it is non-existent."
If one were to know [the truth] yet say it does not exist, would this not be the knowledge of suffering?
How then can one say there is no suffering?
If one does not know, how can one say that there is no such thing as "ignorance" which is to be exhausted? Therefore, [it is not by saying it does not exist that one exhausts ignorance].
There is no such thing.
Question:
Do you say it does not exist because you know it does not, or do you say it does not exist because you do not know it?
If one claims "there is no knowledge" while being ignorant of it, how can one say "there is none" if one does not know?
Therefore, it is non-existent.
Furthermore, it is that which is conditioned by and driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
Why is this? Because he is not driven by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).

Furthermore, he perceives that the realms (*dhātu*) have no fixed location; although all existence is suffering, he speaks of it as non-existent. He seeks to transcend the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) through successive stages, yet he considers that [transcendence] to be incomplete, and only thereafter does he become associated with the desire realm.
For what reason is it that, although one holds the false view regarding nirvāṇa by asserting "there is no nirvāṇa," one is not yet driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) toward that [view]?
Or it may be said: those [who hold such a view] do not possess these underlying tendencies.
Question:
Is there anyone capable of slandering him who would wish to cause slander regarding nirvāṇa?
Or is it said thus:
Slanderous speech is far removed from *nirvāṇa*; therefore, one is not driven by it.
Question:
Since tainted phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are likewise free from slander, should they not also be driven by the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
This is also as explained above.
To slander what has been taught is no different from the original [teaching]; such is slander.
Furthermore, if the conditions (pratyaya) do not function as the driven (paryavasthāna), then within the aggregates, elements, and bases (skandha-dhātu-āyatana), that view finds no place of arising.
Since that which has arisen already exists, why is it not driven by *nirvāṇa*?
For what reason is there no anger within *nirvāṇa*?
Or, some might say:
This is not the sphere of ill-will.
Question:
Regarding that sphere of slander, does one intend for the slander to have non-nirvāṇa as its object?
Some may say:
"Defiled phenomena are accompanied by ill-will, whereas Nirvana is not; therefore, there is no ill-will directed toward Nirvana.
Question:
Dharmas with outflows (sāsrava) involve anger and hatred; the outflow-free (anāsrava) is nirvāṇa. Would you then wish for anger and hatred to be conditions for non-nirvāṇa?
Or it may be said:
by abandoning sentient beings through skillful means (upāya), anger and hatred arise.
However, nirvāṇa is not a teaching for sentient beings; therefore, there is no anger toward the conditions of nirvāṇa.
Question:
Among the categories of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), there is the designation "arising."
Furthermore, the characteristic of non-creation quickly gives rise to anger; however, nirvana is a state beyond creation. Therefore, there is no anger within nirvana.
If one were to say:
"I shall certainly fall into hell; there is no need for nirvāṇa," with which fetters (saṃyojana) is that mind associated?
Or it is said:
It is associated with ill-will (*vyāpāda*).
Question:
Is there aversion toward *nirvāṇa*?
Some say: it is a form of ignorance associated with defilement; thus, one does not know *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, that mind should be said to be associated with craving.
Moreover, the Blessed One said:
"In this regard, monks, within the realm of desire there are devas who experience joy and pleasure," as is explained at length in the sūtra passage.
How does one, at the end of life, undergo rebirth in another form and immediately remember: "I was originally a Deva of Joy," and then think:
"I was originally a Deva of Joy"?
Or some may say:
regarding that regression, one further reflects:
"He does not give rise to the notion of a self within the desire realm."
Question:

When one is born within the desire realm and recollects what was previously experienced in past lives, thinking, "I was originally such-and-such a person," and thus gives rise to the notion of a self (*ātman*),
is it possible to cause that [notion] to regress?
Furthermore, regarding all those fetters associated with name-and-form that have the desire realm as their causal condition, they possess strong mindfulness and further form this thought:
"At the very moment of birth, there was indeed a solemn vow."
Furthermore, the perception of a self-view does not contemplate annihilation.
Again, one forms this thought:
"Because they are equal, ordinary persons are originally the devas of joy."
For what reason do ordinary persons not perceive suffering as suffering, yet regard the view of a self associated with the desire realm and the view of doubt as annihilationism?
Some say: "Impurity (aśubhā) eliminates lust;
it also uproots one kind of suffering in the present and is abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
Question:
Are those abandoned through the Four Truths not abandoned through reflection?
Are these two types of abandonment one and the same?
When that which is abandoned through the Four Truths is exhausted, if that which is abandoned through reflection is not yet exhausted, is it not relinquished?
Or it may be said:
various fetters have been exhausted, eternally exhausted, and gradually exhausted, yet regarding that view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), they are exhausted but not completely exhausted.
Question:
If the fetters are gradually exhausted, they shall never arise again.
It is also said that there are three kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (view of a self-identity):

the *satkāyadṛṣṛṣṭi* that binds rebirth, the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* that exhausts the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), and the *satkāyadṛṣṭi* that is the locus of phenomena. When one attains illumination regarding these, one practices the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) toward them; thus, the underlying tendency of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* arises.
Furthermore, when one has cultivated the ten perceptions of the nature of arising, one speaks thus:
"That which is abandoned by the mind cannot sever the fetters through the Noble Path in the interim."
Perverted views of impurity, the five views including the view of precepts and observances,
the two types [of craving and existence], and hatred— these are the roots of merit that lead to suffering in hell.
For what reason?
The view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*) associated with the desire realm are called neutral (*avyākṛta*);
yet, are they not unwholesome (*akuśala*)? Some say:
"They cannot be produced by the great activities of body, speech, and mind."
Question:
There are also other views that are fetters abandoned through the [noble] truths, which arise from body and speech.
Do you intend to say that these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)?
Some may say: "That body has degrees of excellence or inferiority.
Question:
How is it known that there is superiority or inferiority? Some say:
when those fetters increase and flourish, one is not reborn in the evil destinies.
Question:
It is not necessarily the case that those [actions] are unwholesome, leading even to rebirth in the evil destinies.
Or, some might say this:
The unwholesome has retribution, while the fetters have no retribution; therefore, these are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*).
Question:
Just as when one perceives the acquisition of a physical form, how can it be that there is no retribution?
Furthermore, even if one were to hold such a perverted view, it would have no basis; how could it not be unwholesome?
Such a person would then maintain that there is no retribution for those views, and for this reason, it is unwholesome.
How could there be defiled feeling that results in an unwholesome retribution?
Therefore, it is indeterminate; this matter is not so.
The Blessed One has also said:
In this way, monks, ignorance is itself an unwholesome root.
If one were to say that it is indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), that would not be correct. For what reason?
The latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the form and formless realms are called indeterminate; why then are they not unwholesome?
Some say: "He does not perform bodily or verbal formations.
Others say: [He does not perform mental formations.]
When they receive their physical forms, there is no distinction of superiority or inferiority.
Or, some say this:
they do not undergo karmic retribution.
Or it may be said:
"That has no retribution.
This is also as explained above.
Furthermore, as for those who are attached to sensual desires, is that not unwholesome?

They might think, "I shall not receive an evil retribution; I shall not undergo perversion; I shall not be subject to cyclic turning; I shall not be insecure. Yet this is not so; therefore, one should abandon them.
If the fetters (*saṃyojana*) are not non-virtuous, how can they now be unwholesome?
Furthermore, since the fetters also increase through volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), the claim that they are "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*) is incorrect.
Regarding that mind which is applied to slandering the four noble truths, how can that mind be said to have defiled objects?
Or, it may be argued:
it is not possible for a single mind to cause the four truths to possess diverse characteristics.
Furthermore, that mind arises from the convergence of causes and conditions.
Question:
If the Four Noble Truths are distinct and their causes and conditions are likewise distinct, then one does not misrepresent the Four Noble Truths.
If the causes and conditions for the Four Truths are identical, then the mind takes the Four Truths as its object.
This is also answered as above without difference; what has been said does not accord with reason.
Furthermore, it is not the mind that slanders, but rather it is through wrong view that one slanders.
The first step is the locus of the Truth of Suffering; without the Truth of Suffering, there can be no Truth of Cessation.
Since there is no Path without cessation, each must seek the locus of the Truth of Suffering for themselves—this is what is meant.

Since there is no principle from which such a conclusion could be derived, for what reason does a person free from defilement proceed to sever the fetters, such that the fetters and proclivities associated with the desire realm and those to be abandoned by cultivation are first exhausted, and only thereafter those associated with the form and formless realms?
Or some say:
this gradual arising of the noble path first distinguishes the matters of the desire realm, and subsequently those of the form and formless realms.
Question:

If one wishes to cause the Path of the Noble Ones (āryamārga) to arise, why first distinguish the matters of the desire realm (kāmadhātu), then those of the form realm (rūpadhātu), and finally those of the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu)?
Some explain it thus:

the fetters and proclivities (saṃyojana-anuśaya) of the desire realm are coarse, while those associated with the form realm are subtle; therefore, one first abandons the fetters associated with the desire realm, then those associated with the form realm, and finally those associated with the formless realm.
Some say: "That which corresponds to the desire realm is near; that which corresponds to the form realm is distant; and that which corresponds to the formless realm is even more distant. Others say:

Regarding the locus of resistance (*sapratigha*), it refers to the fetters that have previously ceased; first those associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) cease, followed by those associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Therefore, the fetters associated with the desire realm cease first, followed by those associated with the form realm, and finally those associated with the formless realm.
This is also as previously explained.
Furthermore, as that path gradually increases its counteraction (*sapratigha*), the [afflictions] are then extinguished; subsequently, this state occurs.
Why is it that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) to be abandoned through reflection (*cintāmayaprahātavya*) are not abandoned gradually?

One should contemplate in this way: the knowledge of the unknown contemplates the form and formless realms; therein, there is no fixed limit to its increase or benefit, yet there is also a successive upholding of faith and adherence to the Dharma.
Because they are known through the patience of non-knowledge (*anājñātam-ājñāsyāmīti-kṣānti*), there is no suffering for them; thus, they observe by means of skillful means (*upāya*).

For what reason do those factors associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) involve the contemplation of suffering and so forth, and are realized by transcending the sequence, yet those associated with the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) do not?
Or it may be said:
this gradual arising of the noble path first distinguishes the matters of the desire realm, and subsequently treats the form and formless realms in the same way.
Question:
When one wishes to contemplate the arising of the Path, one first distinguishes the phenomena of the desire realm and subsequently those of the form and formless realms;
this is also as explained above.
This suffering is coarse, for it constitutes bondage and attachment.
This is also as previously explained.

Furthermore, regarding this skillful means of exhortation, even those elders who are able to oppose it have abandoned all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) involved in such undertakings and have exhausted the root of suffering.

For what reason do those associated with the form realm practice the contemplation of suffering regarding suffering, yet they do not attain the fruit of non-returner or arhatship? Furthermore, why is this not the case for those associated with the desire realm or the form realm [in the same manner]?
This is also as explained above.
This suffering is coarse and one is closely attached to it in this world; by means of this, one is bound and fettered.
Furthermore, when one forms the notion of "no-self," that which was previously bound and fettered should be said to be entirely free from desire.
Do you wish to cause one who does not contemplate asceticism to instead contemplate other forms of suffering?
It is like abandoning one's own field while weeding the weeds and thorns from another’s; observe that this is exactly how it is.
Is there perhaps a case where, while all phenomena are extinguished within a single state of mind and one returns to wisdom, the body does not experience realization?
Or is there a case where the body experiences realization, yet one does not return to wisdom?
Is it that one who has returned to the body of wisdom also attains realization?
Or is it that one who has not returned to the body of wisdom also does not attain realization?
Or is it stated thus:

When one attains the patience regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayadharmanidhyānakṣānti*), the fetters associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the cultivation of the truths of exhaustion and the path are exhausted; at that time, wisdom returns, yet the body does not yet receive the realization.

When the fetters associated with the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and its origin are exhausted, at that time the body experiences the realization of the wisdom of non-returning.

When the fetters associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and its origin are exhausted, at that time the body also experiences the realization of the wisdom of returning.

The exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through the truth of cessation and the truth of the path associated with the form and formless realms, as well as the exhaustion of the fetters to be abandoned through cultivation, is neither attained through the wisdom of non-returning nor through bodily realization.
Question:

If the patience regarding the knowledge of exhaustion (*kṣayadharmanirvedhabhāgīya*) gives rise to the truth of exhaustion (*kṣayadharma*), and the fetters to be abandoned have not yet been exhausted, is it not also of that same category?
Answer: [It is].
That which arises ceases; once ceased, it does not arise again. If that which arises were not to cease, it would not be of its own kind.
Question:
One who wishes to contemplate the exhaustion of arising should contemplate that what has arisen is already exhausted.
Or it is said:

when the patience regarding the knowledge of the exhaustion of phenomena (kṣayadharmanirvedhabhāgīya-kṣānti) arises, the fetters associated with the desire realm and associated with the truth of the path (mārgasatya) that are to be abandoned are exhausted; yet, one does not yet receive the realization within the body of wisdom.

When the fetters associated with the realms of form and formlessness that are to be abandoned through the truths of suffering and its origin are exhausted, one realizes this with the body through the wisdom of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).

At that time, when the fetters associated with the desire realm that are to be abandoned through the truths of suffering, its origin, and cessation are exhausted, one also realizes this with the body through the wisdom of a non-returner.

The exhaustion of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) associated with the form and formless realms that are to be abandoned by the truth of cessation and the truth of the path is not yet realized through the body of wisdom of a non-returner (*anāgāmin*).
Furthermore, when the knowledge of the dharma regarding exhaustion (*kṣayadharman*) is attained, it is likewise no different: both parts are not yet exhausted.
Is there a case where a sensation (*vedanā*) is associated with the fetter of craving (*tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana*) but not associated with the fetter of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*)?
Some explain it thus:

When one has exhausted the excessive craving for the realm of desire (*kāmadhātu*) and so forth, attaining realization by skipping stages (*vyutkrāntaka-samāpatti*), and while the knowledge of destruction (*kṣaya-jñāna*) has already arisen but the knowledge of non-arising (*anutpāda-jñāna*) has not yet arisen, there are sensations associated with the higher, middle, and lower grades of views to be abandoned through the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*) and the Truth of the Path (*mārga-satya*) within the realm of desire; these are associated with the lower grade of the fetter of craving, but not associated with the fetter of views.
Question:
The Blessed One has also said:
"When a bhikṣu extinguishes craving for feeling, with the exhaustion of craving, feeling is exhausted."
How is it that with the exhaustion of craving, suffering is exhausted?
Some say: "The one who has seen the truths is equal to the worldly person."

Feeling associated with views (dṛṣṭi-saṃprayukta-vedanā) may be associated with the fetter of craving (tṛṣṇā-saṃyojana) but not associated with the fetter of views (dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana); yet, even when that fetter of views is exhausted, it is not the case that the fetter of views is [thereby] exhausted.

Furthermore, when the knowledge of cultivation (bhāvanā-jñāna) has arisen and craving for the formless realm (ārūpyadhātu-tṛṣṇā) is exhausted, feeling associated with views—whether mundane (laukika) or otherwise—is associated with the fetter of craving, but not associated with the fetter of views.
How does one follow after nirvana due to ignorance conditioned by nirvana?
Some say: "It is because they are entangled by lack of wisdom and delusion."
Question:
Does one who thinks thus consider lack of wisdom to be delusion?
Or does one state it thus:
There are two kinds of delusion that accompany [the notion of] nirvāṇa and are associated with wrong view:
ignorance which claims that nirvāṇa does not exist, and the ignorance associated with doubt, which is characterized by hesitation and indecision regarding a single dharma.
Question:
Are wrong view and ignorance not distinct from one another?
[Answer: Such as doubt and ignorance—these various dharmas are each distinct.
Furthermore, does ignorance follow along with nirvāṇa?
Furthermore, regarding these five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādāna-skandha*), one says "this is mine.
It is like closing both eyes; those who possess the eye of omniscience are few.

Just as the body, conditioned by outflows (*āsrava*), gives rise to various fetters (*saṃyojana*) and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*), are those fetters that arise conditioned by [the body] themselves outflows of that body?
Or is it said:
all outflows of the body are like those fetters that arise conditioned by them?
That body is not subject to outflows (*āsrava*), unlike those who possess various fetters (*saṃyojana*) when taking either cessation (*nirodha*) or the path (*mārga*) as their object.
Question:
Furthermore, the World-Honored One said:
In this regard, monks, whatever forms there are—past, future, or present—if desire arises toward them, then lust, anger, and delusion arise.
Furthermore, all other mental afflictions and fetters that are associated with the mind are called "the bubble of outflows."
This would contradict that sutra.
Alternatively, it might be said:
"All bodies are with outflows (sāsrava); conditioned by them, various fetters (saṃyojana) arise, just as fetters arise conditioned [by objects]."
That body possesses outflows (*āsrava*); it gives rise to the sense of being without outflows, the sense of having outflows, and the sense of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) having outflows.

Furthermore, if one does not give rise to views within that intermediate state of the body, then although that body possesses outflows, the various fetters do not arise in dependence upon those conditions as they would otherwise.
When he forms fetters, he becomes stained by attachment to the locus of the body.
Two types are said to be unwholesome: slander and abandonment.
The Arhat possesses a single patience; the dark outflows remain behind.
For what reason is frivolous play (*auddhatya*) abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*)?
Some say: because frivolous play exists even in those who have seen the truths (*dṛṣṭasatya*), it is said to be abandoned through cultivation.
Question:
Does one who has seen the truths (dṛṣṭisatya) also possess ignorance? Is that [ignorance] abandoned through seeing the truths or through cultivation?
Or is it said as follows:
Both types of frivolity (*auddhatya*) are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*darśana-prahātavya*) as well as through cultivation (*bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, this frivolity arising from the vision of the truths is abandoned through the vision of the truths.
Just as that frivolity is slight, what is spoken does not accord with it; thus, its function is not distinguished.
If one transgresses the boundaries, that is abandoned through contemplation (*cintāmayī-prahāṇa*).
If there is even a slight degree of discernment, pressure, obstruction, or maintenance, for this reason both are frivolous.
Or it is said as follows:
Ordinary persons have intense frivolity, while those who have seen the Truths have subtle frivolity; both types of frivolity are abandoned through the vision of the Truths.
Furthermore, why is it that having fearlessness yet possessing a defiled mind is not abandoned through the vision of the Truths?
If one sees a track, there may be those who follow it; that is severed by the contemplation of playful distraction.
Having passed away from the formless realm and been reborn in the desire realm, how could fetters associated with desire manifest?
As stated above in the Khandaka on Aggregates:

furthermore, if one forms the intention that the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the desire realm are permanently severed upon being born into the formless realm, yet the latent tendencies associated with the formless realm are not [severed].
Regarding these latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the desire realm: if they take that [object] as their condition, do they exist there?
They do not arise in the desire realm.
Even when arising, they do not arise in the interim; nor do the fetters and latent tendencies manifest before them, for there is no causal condition for their manifestation.
Furthermore, ordinary persons do not exhaust their fetters (*saṃyojana*) when they perform unwholesome actions; rather, it is said that their fetters associated with the desire realm are exhausted.
As the Blessed One said:
"In this regard, monks, if you do not reflect and do not apply skillful means, then by reason of those fetters, the consciousness will find its place of abiding."
He shall apply skillful means in this regard:
when one passes away from the formless realm and is reborn in the realm of form, how do the fetters and latent tendencies of the realm of form manifest?
The answer is:
Not uprooting the fetters (saṃyojana) is like a flame that exists by depending on a flame.
Thus, one who is enveloped by ignorance and performs unwholesome actions will undergo existence in the realm of form (rūpabhava).
This is also as explained above in the *Khandhavagga* (Chapter on Aggregates).
When one passes away from the Form Realm and is reborn in the Desire Realm, how do the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) associated with the Desire Realm manifest?
As explained in the *Khandaka* on Aggregates (*Khandhaka*) above:

furthermore, as sensual desire gradually increases in strength and power, it becomes the cause for the exhaustion of that [desire] and the occurrence of these three calamities: the calamity of wind, the calamity of water, and the calamity of fire.
Does this mean that these three calamities arise because of the defilements of sentient beings, or that sentient beings possess defilements because of these three calamities?
Some say: "These calamitous transformations exist because sentient beings are attached to their defilements, just as there is the 'sword-weapon kalpa' due to the sins of sentient beings."
Some say: "Due to calamities and transformations, sentient beings become defiled and attached, just as dogs and other animals engage in sexual union only at certain times.
Others say: [the same].
Due to defilement and attachment, calamities arise; for those various sentient beings who possess the fetters of the desire realm, various calamities emerge.
Just as there are various calamities, so too do the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) increase.

Furthermore, when sentient beings constantly cultivate and practice wholesome dharmas, they may travel to other lands; due to the intensification of those practices, there are cases where sentient beings lose what they have learned and the foundations of their training.
How is it that through conditions one is driven by latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
and how is one driven through association?
Some explain it as follows:
The latent tendency of sensual desire is that which causes intense attachment; this is what is meant by "that which is latent.
The latent tendency of ill will is that which causes non-attachment and non-adherence of the mind; this is what is meant by "that which is latent.
The latent tendency of craving for existence is that which causes intense attachment; this is what is meant by "that which is latent."
When the latent tendency of pride (*māna-anuśaya*) is blazing, intensely blazing, and the mind is courageous and fierce, this is called "that which is latent.
The latent tendency of views (*dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) consists of the five views.
Among these, the latent tendency of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi-anuśaya*) is that which is dependent upon itself as its latent object.
Those with views of doubt are driven by the notions of annihilationism and eternalism; this is what is meant by being "driven.
Those with false views are driven by the denial of causes and the repudiation of karmic action; this is what is meant by being "driven."

The latent tendency of views-holding (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa-anuśaya) is that which cannot be guarded or maintained, yet is extremely subtle, excellent, and supreme; this is what is meant by "that which is driven.

The latent tendency of adherence to precepts and vows (śīlavrataparāmarśa-anuśaya) is the pure liberation, the supreme transcendence, and the essential way out; this is what is meant by "that which is driven."
The latent tendency of ignorance (*avidyā-anuśaya*) refers to being blind, dark, deluded, and confused due to a lack of wisdom; this is what is meant by "that which is latent.

The latent tendency of doubt (*vicikitsā-anuśaya*) refers to longing and hesitation as to whether something is right or wrong, such that the mind does not ascertain the truth; this is what is meant by "that which is latent."
In this way, one is bound by the underlying tendencies (anuśaya) that take [the object] as their condition; it has never before been associated with those [tendencies] that bind.
Question:
Are the untainted (anāsrava) also objects of the underlying tendencies? If so, are they likewise bound by them?
Is it intended that those objects of perception (*ālambana*) are also the objects of the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*)?
Or is it said: "In whatever way there are various underlying tendencies, in that same way they have those as their objects"?
When those various latent tendencies (anuśaya) find their conditions, they each mutually draw one another along, and one becomes driven by these latent tendencies.
In this way and that way, being driven by the conditions of the latent tendencies, one is defiled and attached by them; thus one is driven by what is associated with the latent tendencies.
Question:
As for the untainted proclivities (*anāsrava-anuśaya*), they increase progressively according to their objects.
Are those untainted objects themselves proclivities?
What is it that is conditioned by these? Some say:
that which is associated with them cannot attain liberation; this is what is meant by "being conditioned by."
Question:
Are those with outflow-free objects (*anāsrava-ālambana*) also proclivities (*anuśaya*), and are those with objects also proclivities? There are no other objects that are made into proclivities.
Furthermore, although there are proclivities and those to whom they belong, it is only in the place where they revolve that those proclivities exist.
If that which is associated with the underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) is itself driven by them, then the others are likewise associated.
Furthermore, sentient beings are driven by the underlying tendencies; they are driven by causes and conditions.
Regarding the phenomena (*dharma*) that serve as the conditions for sensual desire (*kāmacchanda*), how many underlying tendencies drive them?
Some say: it refers to all outflowing objects associated with the desire realm.
Furthermore, when one falls away from the outflowing objects of the three realms, one is born in the desire realm and acquires the fetters of the three realms.
When these [afflictions] are attained within the three realms, they are driven by the outflows (*āsrava*) and their objects.
As for the meaning of the term "driving forces" (*anuśaya*),
some explain it as follows:
That which is successively driven by the proclivities (anuśaya) is itself both the object of those proclivities and the proclivity itself.
"Proclivity" has the meaning of attachment and also the meaning of arising; it has the meaning of maintaining and also the meaning of proclivity.

Furthermore, it shall now be explained that conventional knowledge (*samvṛtijñāna*) is that which is driven by those [defilements]. For when there are outflows (*sāsrava*) that drive it, it is sometimes employed and sometimes not.
What is the meaning of "impurity" (*mala*)?
Some say: Defilements adhere to the human body;
experiencing various cravings is also a defilement, and being conditioned by suffering is likewise a defilement.
Furthermore, there are two kinds of defilements: those associated with the mind (*citta-saṃprayukta-kleśa*) and those pertaining to sentient beings (*sattva-kleśa*).
That mind is defiled and attached, staining the mental faculty just as dirt stains a garment.
The defilements of sentient beings may sometimes follow others, like carrying a heavy burden.
Due to these causes and conditions, and through such deliberations, the defilements of the mind arise at that time.
The World-Honored One has also said:
"Deluded by the defilements of the mind, when the mind is pure, conduct is pure.
The World-Honored One spoke thus because sentient beings are formed through the coming together [of these factors].
What is the meaning of these "wholesome roots"?
To destroy unwholesome roots is the meaning of wholesome roots.
To give rise to various wholesome practices is the meaning of wholesome roots.
Furthermore, regarding the seeds of the self (ātman), that which is wholesome and follows its source to receive retribution is the meaning of "wholesome root" (kuśalamūla).
What is the meaning of "unwholesome root" (akuśalamūla)?

The indeterminate (avyākṛta) has the meaning of a grain seed; the indeterminate has the meaning of a root; the indeterminate has the meaning of a causal condition (hetupratyaya); the indeterminate is the root.
Furthermore, the fact that physical form, color, and indeterminate phenomena are compliantly maintained and upheld is what is meant by the meaning of "indeterminate" (*avyākṛta*).
For what reason is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) said to be abandoned through the Truth of Suffering?

Some say: "By knowing suffering in this way through its conditions, suffering is extinguished; once it is extinguished, its conditions are exhausted, and all fetters and latent tendencies are brought to an end.
Others say: [the same].
There is the notion of permanence and the notion of self; regarding the body as "mine," one forms the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) and conceives of it as impermanent.
Once the notion of self regarding suffering is exhausted, this is therefore said to be abandoned by the Truth of Suffering.

Furthermore, one observes the body; seeing that the body experiences suffering and affliction, one therefore speaks of the body as presently manifesting suffering and affliction; thus, one should contemplate it as being subject to cessation.
Mischief no longer arises; as if there were three fetters, the body and all fetters are severed by the three kinds of roots.

For what reason is it that when the knowledge of cultivation (*bhāvanājñāna*) arises regarding the path to the exhaustion [of outflows], the view of grasping at extremes (*antagrāhadṛṣṭi*) is said to be exhausted?
Some say: "At the very beginning, there is the view-grasping (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) that defiles and binds that view; when that [view] is extinguished, this [grasping] is also extinguished.
Question:
Since the fetters (saṃyojana) and outflows (āsrava) involve the view of grasping (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), they are therefore also abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).

Alternatively, because there is a contradiction with the view of grasping and doubt regarding the truth of suffering (duḥkha-satya), they are therefore abandoned through the four truths (catur-āryasatya-prahātavya).
Question:
Since the fetter of suffering (*duḥkha-saṃyojana*) is foremost, supreme, and sublime, how can it differ from [the fetter of] grasping (*parāmarśa*)?
Furthermore, how could one cross over the fetter of suffering before crossing over grasping?
If suffering cannot serve as a precursor, then the view of attachment to what is not the self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is abandoned through the abandonment of the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
As it has been said: "The truths have no abiding place; [yet] one says, 'This is mine.'"
For what reason is it called "wrong view"? Some say:
it is so called because of these causes and conditions; therefore, it is termed wrong view.
Or it may be said:
if this were truly a theft,
furthermore, that would not be conditioned by emptiness.
Furthermore, when there is the notion of "mine," this view arises.
What are the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*)?
Some explain it as follows:
The five lower fetters are: sensual desire, ill will, the view of a self-identity, attachment to rules and rituals, and doubt.
As long as these are not fully exhausted, there remains suffering in the desire realm.
Furthermore, when the three higher fetters are not fully exhausted, one undergoes the aggregates of the form and formless realms.
"Do you wish to say that this is a disease of the higher realms?
He replied:

"It is not because of this that there is disease; they have already exhausted [the defilements] of the *anāgāmin* and receive existence in the form and formless realms; therefore, they are without disease."
Question:
If those three fetters have been exhausted and they receive existence in the form and formless realms, for that reason they are not born in the desire realm.
Yet, even though the stainless person has exhausted them, they again receive existence through the three fetters.
Is it intended that one should not turn back from the realms of existence?
Or is it said thus:
"Two fetters belong to the lower portion: sensual desire and ill will"?
If they are not exhausted, one undergoes existence within the desire realm;
once they are exhausted, one no longer undergoes it again.
Question:
When all fetters (saṃyojana) of the desire realm have not yet been exhausted, one undergoes existence in the desire realm.
Are these proclivities (anuśaya) of the desire realm fetters that are exhausted, or are they higher-tier fetters (ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana)?
Some make this statement:
It should be said that all these are the higher fetters (*ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
If they are not completely exhausted, one undergoes existence in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Question:
As it has been said, the five higher fetters (pañca-ūrdhva-bhāgīya-saṃyojana) would then lack their designation. Or, as some say:
if two fetters are not yet exhausted—namely, sensual desire (kāmacchanda) and ill will (vyāpāda)—one does not transcend the realm of desire (kāmadhātu).
Because the three fetters are not yet exhausted, one returns again to the desire realm; therefore, the five higher fetters are also not yet exhausted.
Furthermore, as for the various fetters and proclivities, since their cessation occurs within the desire realm and not in any other place, they should be called "higher" (ūrdhvabhāgīya).
What are the five higher fetters? Some say they are the five higher fetters:
attachment to the realm of form, attachment to the formless realm, restlessness, conceit, and ignorance.
For what reason does this not come to an end? Because one experiences existence in the form and formless realms while the three fetters have not yet been exhausted;
at that time of practice, one undergoes existence in the form and formless realms.
Is it intended that these are the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*)?
The answer is:
they do not undergo existence in the form realm or the formless realm through grasping; therefore, they do not grasp that existence.
Question:
When the three fetters have been exhausted, does this stainless person still experience the desire realm?
Are these [experiences] caused by the five higher fetters?

Some say: if the fetters (saṃyojana) are not yet exhausted, one leaves the desire realm and undergoes existence in the form and formless realms; these are called the five higher fetters (pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni). Others say:
The second consists of the five higher fetters (*pañcordhvabhāgīya-saṃyojana*): attachment to the realm of form (*rūparāga*) and attachment to the formless realm (*ārūpyarāga*).
By practicing therein, one undergoes existence within the realms of form and the formless.
Or, it is said as follows:
All existence in the form and formless realms, as long as it is not yet exhausted, constitutes the experience of existence in the form and formless realms.
Furthermore, those fetters (*saṃyojana*) which can be brought to exhaustion regarding existence in the form and formless realms are the five higher fetters (*pañca ūrdhvabhāgīya-saṃyojanāni*).
What is the condition for ill-will? Some say:
it is neither excellent nor superior, and it is accompanied by sorrow, lamentation, and distress.
Some say: "Sorrow and anxiety gradually depart and become distant.
Others say: [the same].
It is because of sentient beings that there is anger.
Furthermore, it is to be abandoned forever, just as one removes weeds.
What is the difference between desire (*chanda*) and attention (*manasikāra*)?
Some say: "Desire is defiled attachment, whereas mindfulness is not defiled attachment. Others say:
Desire is unwholesome; mindfulness is wholesome or indeterminate.
Some say: desire leads to the acquisition of existence, whereas mindfulness does not lead to the acquisition of existence.
Or it may be said:
when desire and mindfulness are to be associated, there may be both desire and mindfulness.
For example, as when someone has the desire to attain final exhaustion [of suffering] and possesses mindfulness toward the Teacher.
Furthermore, desire arises through skillful means, while longing arises through mindfulness.
Therefore, desire is also a form of longing.
What is the difference between these two: ill-will (*vyāpāda*) and defilement (*saṃkleśa*)?
Some say: "Ill-will (*vyāpāda*) is a fetter (*saṃyojana*), whereas corruption (*kliṣṭa*) is not a fetter.
Furthermore, ill-will is unwholesome (*akuśala*), whereas corruption is wholesome (*kuśala*) or indeterminate (*avyākṛta*)."
Again, he spoke these words:
"One who harbors ill will experiences existence; one who is free from defilement does not experience existence.
Again, he spoke these words:

Is that which is ill-will (*vyāpāda*) also defilement (*saṃkleśa*), or is there that which is defilement but not ill-will? This refers, for example, to the practice of the meditation on impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*).
Furthermore, ill-will leads to the various states of existence (*bhava*), whereas defilement does not lead to existence; in that regard, ill-will likewise does not lead to existence.
What is the difference between indolence (*kausīdya*) and sleep (*middha*)? Some say:
indolence belongs to the body, while sleep pertains to the mind.
Some explain it thus:
the conventional meaning of *kausīdya* (indolence) is laziness, while the supramundane meaning is torpor (*middha*).
Furthermore, the former refers to indolence, while the latter refers to physical exhaustion.
What is the distinction between false liberation (*mithyā-vimukti*) and the four perversions (*viparyāsa*)? Some say:
those abandoned by the vision of the truths (*satya-darśana-prahātavya*) are the perversions, while those abandoned by both vision and cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*) are called false liberation.
Some may say: "To be able to expound [the Dharma] for others is perversion; to be unable to speak it for others is false liberation.
Or some may say:
Those who possess various inversions either have false liberation, or they have false liberation yet are not inverted.
[They are those] liberated from the fetters and latent tendencies.
Furthermore, regarding one with false liberation, should it be said that their mind is inverted?
Furthermore, is there not a distortion of the mind that does not depart from the four inversions?
What is the distinction between frivolous play and doubt?
Or, some say as follows:
Restlessness is abandoned through cultivation, while doubt is abandoned through the vision of the truths.
Furthermore, when the mind is defiled and accompanied by remorse, this is called restlessness; when the mind is not settled, being wavering and uncertain, this is called doubt.

For what reason, when an ordinary person falls away from their state, the fetters abandoned through seeing the truths (*dṛṣṭi-heya*) as well as those abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) increase;
yet, when a disciple of the World-Honored One falls away, only the fetters abandoned through cultivation increase, and not those abandoned through seeing the truths?
Some say: By means of a single path of cultivation, an ordinary person severs all fetters;
when that path of cultivation regresses, everything increases again.

However, among the disciples of the Blessed One, there are those who abandon [defilements] through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), rather than through the abandonment by seeing the truths (*satyadarśana*).
All of these are not subject to increase (*anuśaya*).
Others state: "Ordinary persons (*pṛthagjana*) extinguish the various fetters (*saṃyojana*) through wisdom; when that wisdom regresses, all [fetters] increase."

It is said that the disciples of the World-Honored One extinguish all fetters through patience and wisdom; yet they do not regress from that patience, nor do they increase [their defilements] significantly.
Or it is further stated:
when ordinary persons extinguish all fetters during the intermediate state, they experience an increase in all [defilements] at the time of their regression.

However, among the disciples of the Blessed One, there are some who have attained a partial cessation but not ultimate cessation; when they regress from that state, during that interval of regression, they experience an increase [in defilements].

Furthermore, ordinary persons have various latent tendencies (anuśaya) conditioned by their formations; these persist throughout their entire lives as obscurations, and because they are bound by those conditions of formation, they continue to increase.

However, when the disciples of the World-Honored One, through insight and so forth, transcend the stages and attain realization, all their fetters and afflictions are exhausted and they increase [in merit]; therefore, that increase is immovable.

When right view, perception, and mind are equalized and guarded by that [restraint], and even if one should occasionally regress from maintaining them, why are those fetters associated with the form and formless realms called "without retribution"?
Some say: "He does not augment his bodily, verbal, or mental conduct so as to provide any benefit.
Others say: [the same].
Although he possesses actions of body, speech, and mind, he does not possess any increase [of karma]. Or it is said:
there is no retribution for beauty or ugliness.
Some say: "The indeterminate (avyākṛta) has no retribution.
Furthermore, if the fetters (saṃyojana) were to have retribution, how could there be any contradiction?
Just as one who possesses such conditions, if they engage in slander, will not receive retribution in the realm of form or the formless realm;
so too, such conditions do not exist. Since they do not undergo existence, there are thus no fetters, nor are they even determinate; therefore, they are to be relinquished.
Neither crossing over nor being destroyed, with anger and the desire for anger, one plays with higher liberation; there is regression and no fruit.
If there is no defiled mind regarding both the five desires and the desire for existence, what is the difference between these two?
Or they speak thus:
"There is the underlying tendency of craving for the five sensual pleasures; one whose mind is not defiled by it does not undergo existence through that craving.
They further speak thus:
Among the five sensual desires, there is craving that is unwholesome; there is also a non-defiled mind that is wholesome.
Furthermore, it is said:
Among the five sensual desires, there is craving that leads to existence; for one whose mind is non-defiled, existence is not taken up.
Again, he spoke these words:
"Within the five desires there is craving and various wholesome perceptions; one who does not defile the mind does not sever the source of all suffering.
Furthermore, regarding those who have craving for the five desires, they say, 'I have a causal condition,' and thus they rejoice and leap for joy."

Regarding the undefiled mind: it is unmoving within the ultimate truth (paramārthasatya). By giving rise to the perception of sentient beings, one attains equalizing wisdom (samatājñāna); this is truly the undefiled mind, and that indeed shall exist.
How can those ordinary worldlings claim that their minds are not defiled when they take "I" and "mine" as objects?
Those who are not ordinary worldlings perform various deeds, and the various ṛṣis and sages, through skillful means regarding external phenomena, claim that their minds are undefiled.

If there is the view of grasping at extremes (*dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*) abandoned through the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), and that which is abandoned through the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), what is the distinction between these two? Some state:
that which is the view of grasping at extremes abandoned through the truth of suffering is itself abandoned through the truth of suffering.
As for the "thief of views" (dṛṣṭiparāmarśa), it is abandoned through the cultivation of the Truths.
Question:
Since both of these are "thieves of views," they pervade both Truths.
Some say: "If it is not associated with the truth of suffering (*duḥkhasatya*), then it is abandoned by the truth of suffering;
if it is not associated with the truth of origination (*samudayasatya*), then it is abandoned by the truth of origination."
Question:
When the fetter of suffering manifests, it is the most exquisite, the most supreme, and the foremost; yet it is said that "theft" is dissociated from the Truth of Suffering.

Furthermore, regarding the fetters and proclivities to be abandoned by the Truth of Suffering, one should cultivate this contemplation: because they are uprooted by means of the Truth of Suffering, they possess the notion of being exquisite.
What is the difference between this and *nirmāṇa* (transformation)?
The answer is:
when the mind is governed by internal deceit and guile, such that the external does not accord with the internal mind, there is much difference from *nirmāṇa*.
For what reason is the mind not the noble path?
Some say: This is the teaching spoken by the World-Honored One; when he speaks of this, he speaks of the mind as being no different [from the path], whereas that [path] is associated with the mind.
Question:
For what reason, when speaking of the mind, does one not fully speak of the mental factors (caitta) that are associated with it?
Or, as some say:
These are the words of the Tathāgata’s instruction; possessing such instruction, one possesses wisdom.
Just as when grinding incense powder, fragrance is the primary element, so it is with form, sound, smell, and taste.
Question:
Regarding the place of rebirth produced by the performance of a single act, the various associated mental factors (caitta-dharma) lack power and efficacy.
Or, it is said as follows:
The mind that is comprised of its own characteristics and the mind that is gathered together constitute the noble path; therefore, the [isolated] mind is not the noble path.
Alternatively, it is said:
the mind is also the noble path, for in the various samādhis, many minds share a single object of focus.
Regarding samādhi: when the mind undergoes increase or decrease, there is no distinct samādhi apart from it.
Furthermore, as the aspiration for the Way flourishes, that which is produced by the will and intention is what the mind speaks of.

Regarding the view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and doubt associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), excluding the ignorance (*avidyā*) associated with them and other factors, can they be said to be obscured (*nivṛta*)?
Or it may be said:
one can attain the mental liberation through the practice of mindfulness associated with those factors and other mental concomitants (*caitasika-dharma*).
For what reason is it said that for a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the impure is called "the cessation of purity"? Some say:
To perceive purity in the impure is an inversion (viparyāsa), and this has been exhausted by the stream-enterer.
Question:
If the perversions of a stream-enterer (srotāpanna) have been exhausted, he is no longer subject to defilement.
Yet, regarding the perception of suffering, the perception of non-self, and the perception of impurity, he would still be subject to defilement.

Furthermore, for a stream-enterer (srotāpanna), the perception of purity regarding what is impure has already been exhausted; one should know that among the views, wrong view has also been exhausted. Among the hindrances (nīvaraṇa), which fetter (saṃyojana) is doubt?
What is the fetter of doubt that is not among the hindrances?
Some explain it thus:
if it is associated with the desire realm, it is the doubt regarding the way of escape.
If it is associated with the form or formless realms, it is not the hindrance of doubt. Or it is said:
if one has entered into samādhi internally, that is the hindrance of doubt.
If it were a true fruit, it would not be the hindrance of doubt (*vicikitsā-nīvaraṇa*).
Furthermore, all frivolous play is a very great increase of the hindrance of doubt; that which is associated with the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) is not the hindrance of doubt.
If one conceives of a self, all such instances constitute the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Conversely, if something is the view of a self-identity, does it necessarily involve the conception of a self?
To this, some might say:
Whatever phenomena there may be that are reckoned as "self," all of them are the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
Is it possible for something to be the view of a self-identity while those phenomena are not reckoned as "self"?
Relying on the view of self,
some might say:
"Is there any phenomenon that one reckons as 'I' which is not the view of a self (satkāyadṛṣṭi)?"
Regarding the mental states associated with the view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) that one contemplates:
is it possible that there is a view of a personal identity (satkāyadṛṣṭi) which does not itself reckon "I" as a self,
yet relies upon the view of self?
Is there that which is the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and yet is not the conceit "I" or "mine"?
Yes. Is there that which is neither the view of a self-identity nor the reckoning of "I" or "mine"?
Yes; there is such a case, excluding the aforementioned instances.
Furthermore, if one reckons a self within those phenomena that exist, is that not the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*)?
Moreover, the World-Honored One said:
"I shall now speak; he who speaks of 'I' shall speak."
There may be those who possess the view of a self-body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), yet they do not personally reckon it as "I" or "mine.
Or there may be those who neither possess the view of a self-body nor personally reckon it as "I"; this refers to the meaning of excluding the aforementioned matters.
There are those who hold the view that birth is pleasant and that being free from illness is happiness.
How do they give rise to this view?
Some speak as follows:
By the power of samādhi, he personally recollects his past lives.
He fully recognizes and knows the bliss within the stages of the first, second, and third dhyānas; it is for this reason that he experiences such [bliss] and knows there is bliss therein.
Furthermore, regarding the contemplation of the body through the superior method of overcoming greed and envy, there is the contemplation of cold and heat as various forms of suffering.
Within this, one then forms the thought:
"I possess this pleasure, yet it leads to the realms of suffering."
Regarding the various views arising within the miserable realms, there is the biased view that one suffers only a single type of suffering and will die without illness.
How does such a view arise? Some might say:
By the power of this samādhi, they recognize their own past lives; even when fallen into the evil realms, they likewise recognize their own past lives.
Amidst the sorrows and sufferings therein, they then form this thought:
"I have already undergone extreme suffering."

Furthermore, regarding the self-conception of "I," one uses skillful means to contemplate its conditioned activities; just as with the perception of food, even the partial view that pleasure and pain are suffering is itself suffering.
Regarding all that arises as views, one reckons them as suffering, yet perceives pleasure and the notion of security;
what kind of fetter is this? Or it is said:

through the power of samādhi, one personally recollects past lives among humans and devas, and within the desire realm, one personally recollects suffering and pleasure in this very interval; therein, one then forms this thought:
"I have this suffering and pleasure.
Furthermore, conceiving of a self, one observes the means by which that suffering and pleasure are experienced, and therein forms this thought:
"Suffering and pleasure are mine."

In the state of security, one gives rise to the perception of death; regarding all that arises as views, one reckons for oneself that the state of security is neither painful nor pleasant, and forms such a conception.
How does this view arise?
Or they may say:

"This is the samādhi of self-recollection of past lives; within the stage of the fourth dhyāna, one fully understands and knows all that was experienced here as suffering or pleasure. Then, one forms this thought:
"There is no perception of suffering or pleasure."

Furthermore, one who conceives the notion of a self falls into the evil destinies and experiences suffering and pleasure; at times there may be no pleasure, yet such a person still maintains that notion.
They further think:
"There is neither suffering nor pleasure, and there is no view of a self," and they also form the perception of death.

Regarding all views that arise—namely, the view that "I am material form," or that "what is produced by the four great elements perishes at death"—such views as these incline toward those [other] views.
What kind of view is this?
Answer:
At times one may see their conduct and, through the divine eye, know that they will be reborn in the desire realm; yet they do not form such a contemplation, but instead think:
"I shall not fall into the evil destinies."
Regarding all those views that arise claiming there is a self: when one cuts off the sensations of the desire realm, undergoes decay, and reaches death, such a self is likewise utterly severed.
From what kind of view does this [notion] arise?
The answer is:
At times one may see formations through the divine eye, perceiving the forms of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). One does not form such a contemplation, but rather thinks:

"Whatever views arise among those born in the miserable destinies (*apāya*), claiming 'I am,' are severed, destroyed, and rendered non-existent in the formless sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*); yet they do not abandon them until death."
How can such views arise when these [factors] have been severed?
The answer is:

At times, one may observe their conduct and perceive that they possess a physical form within the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); yet, not examining other modes of behavior, they further conceive this thought:

"The 'self' that is seen among those born in the miserable destinies (*apāya*)—that which is formless and situated in the sphere of emptiness—is indestructible and cannot be brought to ruin; it is never abandoned until death."
This is called the severance of the view of self-identity.
How does this view arise?
The answer is:
Entering samādhi equally, one does not observe that which is produced; having formed such a thought, that [production] is severed and destroyed.
It is likewise for the sphere of infinite consciousness, the sphere of nothingness, and the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
As it has been said: "The life-principle is different from the body," and so on, up to "at death. For what reason does the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*) arise? Or, as some say:
because one conceives of a self that is permanent and possesses pure fruits, yet does not perceive those fruits, this view of non-existence arises.
Furthermore, regarding the dharmas contemplated by the mind, one might claim they are permanent; yet, due to those causes and conditions, one then slanders them by saying:
"In that [entity], there is no present existence.

For example, within an entity there is association with the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the present; within that entity there is association with the latent tendency of ignorance in the present, just as within an entity there is association with the latent tendency of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in the present.
Or it may be said:
just as there is the association with the present latent tendency of craving within that entity, so too is there the association with the present latent tendency of ignorance within that same entity.

Is there a person who is associated with the underlying tendency (*anuśaya*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) in the present, yet is not associated with the underlying tendency of craving (*tṛṣṇā*) in the present, and who furthermore has other fetters (*saṃyojana*) manifest?
Furthermore, although two fetters may coexist, they do not manifest simultaneously.
Why is this? Because when one contemplates the various fetters and proclivities (*anuśaya*), two do not arise together at once.
Regarding this contemplation of analogies, there are four inversions: should it be said that they take the Truths as their object, or should it be said that they do not?
The inversion regarding the five aggregates is their object; within the aggregates, there is neither permanence nor self.
If it were the case that one takes those [conditioned things] as an object, this would not be so.
The answer is:
