The accomplishment of wisdom regarding immeasurable realms is called immeasurable wisdom.
Immeasurable *nirvāṇa* is called immeasurable wisdom.

Furthermore, immeasurable wisdom is the accomplishment of immeasurable great wisdom; the World-Honored One’s removal of that which is the cognitive phrase of awakening-wisdom is called immeasurable wisdom.
Regarding "non-defiled": within this internal sphere there is the appropriation of existence (*upādāna*), while externally there are other things.
Furthermore, it is said:
within this internal sphere there is the appropriation of existence, while externally one goes to a favorable destination (*sugati*).
Again, it is said:
regarding this teaching on the love of dharma (dharmatṛṣṇā), those who are transformed do not give rise to external [attachments].
Regarding that teaching on the love of dharma, they do not give rise to any fetters (saṃyojana).
One should venerate and make offerings according to reality; one should make offerings in this manner.

Toward those who are attached or unattached, toward those who are proud or free from pride—one who understands suffering as their own field of action should venerate and make offerings according to reality.
Regarding attachment and non-attachment: all views are attachments.
If one perceives the exhaustion of views within the three realms, that is called the past.
Regarding pride and non-attachment to pride: there are three types of pride; while they are worldly attachments, one does not become attached to them.
To know that suffering arises from one's own field of action means to endure the various sense-bases external to that suffering.
Furthermore, it is said:
regarding attachment and non-attachment, having already transcended the attachment of pride is called non-attachment.

Regarding "not being attached to pride while not being one who possesses pride": among the seven types of pride, it refers to being free from attachment toward that which would otherwise cause defiled attachment.

Regarding "knowing the field of action for suffering itself": this refers to the field of action consisting of the dwelling places of the consciousness of suffering and the consciousness of feeling, wherein there is defiled attachment.
Furthermore, it is said:
regarding attachment and non-attachment, one sees for oneself the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths.
Regarding conceit and non-conceit, one sees for oneself the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation.
To know the field and the karma of suffering: the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*) are the field, and the formations (*saṃskāra*) are the karma;
these constitute the fetters (*saṃyojana*). Furthermore, all forms of attachment and clinging—transcending them all—is called non-attachment (*asaṅga*).
Regarding "not being attached to pride while not being one who possesses pride": it means being stained by attachment to various forms of pride, yet not being stained by those various forms of pride.
To know suffering as one's own field of activity is to know the Truth of Suffering; to know that [field] is to know the Truth of the Path.
That which is the work of the farmer is the root of the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
The exhaustion of all fetters (*saṃyojana*) is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Not relying on expectations, one contemplates with revulsion; yet, through mutual assistance, various views arise.
Since causes and conditions have no inherent existence, one should pay respectful homage according to reality.

Regarding those who do not rely on hope or aversion in their contemplation: they should not rely on the hope for gain or the hope for life. These consist of two types: those characterized by craving and those characterized by views. Those characterized by craving support the craving for life;
those characterized by views support the contemplation of aversion. There are two kinds of paths: the path itself and the fruit of the path.
One gives rise to the views of others and the contemplation of others' revulsion; there are two types of views of annihilationism, and there is the view of permanence by which one transcends them.
Regarding "the absence of causal conditions," there are two causal conditions: craving and views; these are extinguished.
Furthermore, it is said:
For one who does not rely on expectation, there is craving and view.
For one who relies on the contemplation of weariness with expectation, the essential [truth] manifests before them, yet they give rise to various other views.
Among all views, he also knows the way out for others and has already transcended them.
Regarding the absence of causal conditions, consciousness dwells in the sphere of infinite consciousness until its exhaustion.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One who does not rely on expectation manifests the exhaustion of the fetter of craving; one who gives rise to other views manifests the exhaustion of all fetters.
Regarding 'the absence of causal conditions': if the fetter of craving and the fetter of conditions are exhausted, that is the absence of an object of focus."
Furthermore, by not relying on the contemplation of expectation or weariness, one contemplates the fetters to be abandoned through reflection; thus, the arising of other various views is exhausted.
When the arising of other various views is exhausted, the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truths are exhausted.
That which has no causal conditions is that which has already transcended all fetters.
Through contemplation, one sees that the fetters to be abandoned through the vision of the truths have been exhausted; thus, there is nothing for them to take as an object.
One is able to extinguish the mind regarding one's own household and remains unstained by attachment to the households of others.
Without giving rise to the afflictions of "this" or "that," one should pay respect and make offerings according to reality.
Regarding the ability to extinguish the mind within the household, there are three types of attachment and views;
"extinguishing the mind" refers to the mind that relies upon these households.
If, having rejoiced, one relies upon those two, one then relies upon mental association.
This path of abandonment, being associated with the mind, is without attachment regarding the abandoning of other families.
There are two kinds of "other families": the family of craving and the family of views. One is not defiled by or attached to them.
Regarding the statement "one does not give rise to the affliction of 'this' or 'that,'" this is because that which arises from craving is due to views.
When all these cravings and views are exhausted, there is nothing that arises for them.
Furthermore, it is said:
one who does not give rise to this or that affliction is no different from those who have attained [the state] as described above.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One who can extinguish the mind regarding the household extinguishes all fetters;
one who does not become defiled by or attached to other households is not defiled by or attached to wives, children, or grandchildren."
If craving and views do not arise, their cessation is manifested within the arising of the four types of sensation.
Furthermore, it is said:
that which can extinguish the mind regarding the household is the fetter of desire.
Regarding "the mind being unstained by other families": it does not arise; it is without craving.
That which does not arise does not arise within desire; thus, craving for desire is exhausted.
Furthermore, it is said:
The "home" is the truth of the origin; the "mind" is the truth of the path; being unstained by other homes is the truth of suffering; and non-arising is the truth of cessation.
Furthermore, it is said:
"One who can extinguish the mind regarding one's own home is seen to have severed the fetters;
one who is not stained by attachment to another's home is seen to have exhausted the fetter of craving."
One who does not arise has exhausted all fetters of craving and fetters of views, and thus performs no further karmic action.
Furthermore, one who is unstained by attachment to the household life has, through direct vision, exhausted those fetters to be abandoned by the truths.
One who is without attachment to the families of others has exhausted the fetters abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).
One who does not give rise [to such thoughts] has exhausted all fetters abandoned through vision (*darśana-heya*) and cultivation; he performs no further karmic action.
"Many hopes and oral words, / Cast aside and extinguished until non-existent;
/ Awakening to all liberation, / One should pay respectful offerings according to reality.
Regarding "many hopes and oral words": "many hopes" refers to the cultivation of hope, and "oral words" likewise refers to cultivation.
It is said thus:
"Much expectation" refers to craving;
"words and letters" refers to what is expressed by the mouth.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Much expectation" refers to the various views (*dṛṣṭi*), and "letters" refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
Moreover, "much expectation" is abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*), while "letters" are abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-heya*).
That which has been relinquished is already extinguished.
That which is without attachment is called the "unarisen dharma.
As for the one who is able to awaken: to be aware of all dharmas is called awakening; to be aware of the three types of sensation is called awakening.
To penetrate all forms of knowledge and achieve complete perfection therein is called awakening.
Regarding "liberation from all things," this refers to liberation from the three realms.
Regarding "liberation from the three fetters," these are the fetter of craving, the fetter of defilement, and the fetter of views.
Delusion finds no opportunity; all phenomena are illuminated.
Supported by the body, one attains the most supreme awakening—this is the speech of the most pure ghost.
Delusion finds no opportunity; "delusion" here refers to ignorance (*avidyā*). Taking internal ignorance as its condition, it is associated with delusion within the intermediate state.
Furthermore, it is said:
delusion is ignorance, and it is associated with delusion within the intermediate state of all views.
Furthermore, it is said:
Ignorance (*avidyā*) is delusion; between the fetters of delusion, it is associated with delusion.
Moreover, ignorance is delusion; conditioned by ignorance are volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); between these, delusion is associated with delusion.

There is no such exhaustion; regarding all phenomena, he manifests various forms of knowledge, manifests their causes and conditions, manifests their skillful means, and manifests the tracks of the path.
Those who are sustained by this body dwell in the realm of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, and through this patience, they realize that there is no time of awakening.
The ten powers, omniscience, and the four fearlessnesses.
The supreme transcendence is the place of rest and peace.
This is the speech of the pure spirits and yakṣas; this is the most wondrous purity of the spirits; this is the gateway of those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
The verse says one should not eat, for one should contemplate those dharmas equally;
the verse says that all Buddhas rejoice, for all dharmas are originally the Brahmin.
Regarding the statement in the verse that one should not eat, it is said as follows:
The World-Honored One did not go there for the sake of food;
rather, he stayed there because he wished to convert the brahmin.
Later, when he spoke thus, some did not accept his words.
Furthermore, fearing that the brahmin might think,
"The śramaṇa Gautama preaches the Dharma for the sake of food," he spoke again as follows:
Because he wished to manifest his supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*), he did not accept the food.

That brahmin was one who should be transformed by the Buddha; when observing his Dharma, for this reason, the observation, as well as the śrāvakas and the Great Man (*mahāpuruṣa*), constitute his majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).
That which is said to bring joy to all Buddhas is the cessation of grasping through eradication.
All phenomena are fundamentally brahminical; within them lies the Dharma of the noble śramaṇas—such is the teaching of the noble ones.
All other great seers, having exhausted their outflows and observing shame and remorse, were offered sweet delicacies;
they are the supreme fields of merit for planting virtue.
"All others" refers to those who, amidst various impure foods and drinks, currently accept invitations and offerings.
The Great Divine Sage (mahārṣi) refers to returning to the Great Dharma; this is called the Great Divine Sage.
One who has exhausted the outflows (kṣīṇāsrava) refers to one who has completely eliminated all ignorance and craving within the body; this is called one who has exhausted the outflows.
When shame and remorse have ceased, and if the grasping at precepts has been exhausted, then that shame and remorse have ceased.
What is meant by "offering sweet delicacies, planting merit, and this field of blessings"?

The field of virtue is the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); by focusing one’s mind with single-minded devotion upon it, the sprouts of the body grow ever more, and thus it is called the field of merit.
Some offer this explanation, for which there is a verse composed on this subject.
That great seer has exhausted all taints, possesses a sense of shame, and has attained rest.
By making offerings of sweet delicacies, one plants merit in this field of blessings.
Or, it may be said:

When that brahmin had spoken these verses, all the other great seers—those who had exhausted their outflows, were possessed of shame and modesty, and had attained rest—honored him with sweet delicacies; he was a field of merit for those who plant virtue.
He transforms those submerged in suffering, transcending birth, old age, sickness, and death.
The Muni, fully endowed with the outflows-free states, has all his vows universally fulfilled.
As for "transforming those submerged," he causes them to abandon the various views and fetters in which they are submerged.
"Transcending birth, old age, sickness, and death" means crossing over and transcending birth, old age, sickness, and death.
"The Capable One" refers to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) who has severed all fetters and latent tendencies (*anuśaya*).
"Endowed with the exhaustion of outflows" means being fully accomplished in the possession of all wisdom and the exhaustion of outflows; this is called liberation.
Having accomplished infinite wisdom, he is called the Able One (Śākyamuni) who has accomplished the exhaustion of outflows (āsrava-kṣaya).
Regarding those whose various vows have all reached universal fulfillment: they possess such merit as this, transcending birth, old age, sickness, and death, and surpassing all fruits and vows.
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"All submerged fetters and latent tendencies, he is able to abandon and leave behind; having crossed over birth, old age, sickness, and death, this is called Nirvana.
This too he fully understands, which is what is meant by crossing over birth, old age, sickness, and death.
He speaks thus:
"I teach and transform those who are submerged, seeing that they are defiled by attachments.
I deliver those subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death, manifesting the exhaustion of the fetters of craving."
Furthermore, if he teaches and transforms those who are submerged [in ignorance], he manifests the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths (*satyadarśana-prahātavya*).
To deliver those subject to birth, old age, sickness, and death, he manifests the exhaustion of the fetters abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prahātavya*).
The remainder is also like this.
The Sage practices celibacy; he is not entangled by vigor.
He is liberated from the body of desire; that Sage is firm and steadfast.
Regarding the Tathāgata’s practice of celibacy, it was extensively explained in the prophecy granted to the Venerable Mahākāśyapa.
As for the "Tathāgata," this refers to one who is beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
"Practice" means approaching [the goal]; practicing without sexual desire, one departs from and abandons non-celibate conduct.
One who is not entangled by vigor is, even when young and strong, free from craving for sensual desires, let alone when they have grown old and infirm.
One who has attained liberation from pride does not form intentions toward or crave the four types of pride; therefore, one should remain far removed from them.
That which is firm means: "Alas! Abandon all unwholesome dharmas; achieve firm wisdom"—this is called being firm.
The Capable One (Śāstṛ) is one beyond training (aśaikṣa), who fully awakens to what is to be done.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The Able One (Śākyamuni), practicing celibacy, manifests the state of peace and security.
Not being entangled by vigor, he manifests that youth and vigor shall come to an end."
For one who seeks eternal liberation from desire, present karma shall be exhausted;
the remainder is likewise so.
One does not cross to the further shore by doubling, nor does one reach the end by halving.
The meanings of words, high and low, are what is transmitted by the śramaṇas.
Those who have not yet doubled and leaped over the shore, being caught in the net of various doubts, do not cross over the shore of immeasurable birth and death.
If the net of doubt is not yet exhausted, one cannot transcend birth and death.
"Twofold" refers to deceit, falsehood, and delusive confusion.
Furthermore, it is said:
Regarding those who possess the "twofold," they are unable to transcend and do not transcend.
Those with the twofold are accomplished in the defilements of conduct, while the singlefold perish at the end.

As for the meaning of the phrases "high" and "low": the "high" refers to one who realizes the path of deliverance in the present life; the "not high" refers to one who practices for the path of deliverance in the present life.
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"The 'high' refers to rebirth in the heavens; the 'not high' refers to falling into the evil realms.
This is what has been transmitted by the śramaṇas and expounded by the World-Honored One."
Some do not wear lower garments, nor do they delight in ornamentation;
some possess the fragrance of precepts, their speech straightforward and free from abruptness.
Some who are free from abruptness do not wear clothes, yet they violate various prohibitions and restrictions.
Furthermore, they do not delight in ornamentation; they do not form the intention to adorn their body or speech, nor do they listen to music and song.
There may be those who possess the fragrance of precepts, or scholars who travel through the four quarters, extolling their names with a mind that is never weary.
Or those who practice the holy life, whose precepts are never found to be deficient.
I take refuge in the Buddha, the most supreme; all are liberated.
This Honored One is most courageous, having traveled to abide within the unconditioned.
"Buddha" means one who has awakened to and realized all phenomena (*dharmas*).
"Most Victorious One" means being fully endowed with the powers (*bala*).
"Taking refuge" has the meaning of reverence.
"All are liberated" means they are liberated from the three realms, and liberated from the two bonds: the bond of craving and the bond of views.
Furthermore, there are three bonds: the bonds of desire, anger, and delusion.
This Honored One, the most courageous, receives the Dharma teachings spoken by the Honored One.
Having entered into the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), he neither possesses diligence nor manifests diligence; yet it is not that he lacks diligence.
The Non-returners have all attained the fulfillment of their present tasks; it is not that they lack the intent of diligence.
One should maintain such protection, just as those who do not regress abide in the dharma of non-regression.
The Venerable Vaṇavāsa dwelt in the deep mountains and spoke these verses to himself in the presence of Udraka Rāmaputra:

"Grasping the nose, grasping the tip of the nose, the people of Tiṅtiṇi do not understand; repeatedly [practicing] the Kṛṣṇala-miśra, my mind is free from attachment, and my heart is always clearly awakened."
*Chik-bi-chwa-bi-na-ti-te* is the sound of flying birds.
*Pi-pi-ke-lai-lu-to-mi-che* is the sound of deer and fawns.
When my mind is free from defiled attachment, I neither regress nor give rise to various desires.
When the mind is constantly and radiantly awakened, one delights in the joys of the paths and in nirvāṇa.
This is called *bibi-kai-lai* (比比罽賴).
The five shrines of pleasure, whose branches and leaves do not decay,
from which various sprouts are seen to grow— these the Muni severed with wisdom.
"The five shrines of pleasure" refers to existence within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
The branches and leaves that do not decay are the branches of craving, which give rise to birth within the three realms;
the branches of various views are impermanence and suffering.
That the Benevolent One cuts them off with wisdom means that the practitioner’s knowledge abides in severance.
Furthermore, it is said:

"The five pleasant abodes of shrines and temples are the Truth of Suffering; that their branches and leaves are not destroyed is the Truth of Origination; that one perceives the arising of those branches is the Truth of the Path; and that the Able One cuts them off with wisdom is Cessation."
Furthermore, it is said:
"The branches and leaves of the five pleasure-places of the stūpas do not decay; this is called defiled attachment.
Seeing that these various branches arise, the Muni cuts them off with wisdom, eliminating the fetters and purifying the signs."
The Venerable Vaṇavaśa dwelt in the deep mountains; when the heavens sent down rain, his heart was filled with joy, and he spoke this verse:
"Upon steep cliffs, lush and flourishing, With flowing streams where one may bathe the body— Dwelling in seclusion, free from desire, The wise man’s goodness redoubles."
"Those who dwell in precipitous cliffs and lush thickets" refers to those who live among mountains, marshes, and beneath trees.
"Those who bathe their bodies in flowing springs" refers to those who bathe their bodies with rainwater.

"Those who dwell in seclusion, free from desire" refers to those who reside in remote places, delighting in quietude and solitude, giving rise to various forms of non-greed, and not dwelling among the crowds.
The wise person, generating even more goodness, gives rise to various joys and increases in virtue, dwelling in the awakening-factor of joy.
The fool creates birth and death, entering the womb again and again;
therefore, the wise person does not create [such karma], and would rather have his head split than sleep [in negligence].
The fool creates birth and death; lacking wisdom, he accomplishes ignorance.
One who creates birth and death performs all tainted actions that accomplish craving and desire.
Repeatedly entering the womb means dwelling within the mother’s womb.
Therefore, because wisdom is perfected, the wise do not perform actions that lead to outflows or undergo further existence; nor do they act within such states.
"Even if their heads were split, they would not sleep"—this refers to such a person.
Some may say:

"The fool's creation of birth and death is the Truth of Origination; his repeated entry into the womb is the Truth of Suffering; therefore, the wise person's non-creation of these is the Truth of the Path; and his not sleeping even when his head is split open is the Truth of Cessation—just like such a person."

The first chapter of the *Gāthā-varga* compiled by the Bodhisattva Vasumitra concludes here. [The verses] concerning the equality of numbers, looking toward existence, the meaning of the verse on ignorance, the womb, non-crossing, the mind, the constant, the Buddha, grasping the nose, grasping the *pāyaya*, the multitude, and the five delusions of ignorance—these are not clear.
[End of the First Chapter of the Gāthā-varga.]
The Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Nine;
The Abhidharmamahāvibhāṣā-śāstra, Volume Ten;
composed by Venerable Vasumitra.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Saṃghabhūti of Kaśmīra and others during the Fu Qin dynasty.

In the "Chapter on Verses Collected by Bodhisattvas," the Venerable Upāsikā first traveled by waterway and then proceeded on foot, moving like a caterpillar inching forward until she entered the *saṃjñā-samādhi*. Thereupon, she no longer perceived objects of perception or their causal conditions; the states of both perception and non-perception were extinguished.
He asked the World-Honored One:
"I drift alone across the measureless [ocean]; lacking a support, I cannot cross over.
Tell me its conditions, that which serves as the support for crossing to the other shore."
Regarding "I alone flow through the immeasurable": "alone" means non-dual.
Without an object, the flow of birth and death cannot be crossed.
Furthermore, it is said:
One cannot cross over this realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Furthermore, it is said:
first, one cannot attain crossing over the flow of ignorance.

Regarding my explanation of its conditions: the Universal Eye pervades those conditions; where there is no eye, one crosses the stream of birth and death. This is called crossing the stream of ignorance through neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Contemplating the concentration of non-perception, one crosses the flood by relying upon it;
how does one sever sensual craving?
By contemplating that, craving is exhausted.

Regarding the contemplation of the signless concentration (*ānimitta-samādhi*): one gives rise to the untainted signless concentration, contemplating it as impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self.
One who forms such a contemplation focuses their spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*) upon the place of abiding; this is called "resting."
Furthermore, it is said:

When contemplating the sphere of nothingness, one contemplates the cessation of Nirvana; in this way, you cross the stream and extinguish craving therein, just as that craving was previously exhausted.
Question:
All cravings within the three realms are stained attachments to desire.
Yet, it is further stated:
One should cause craving to be exhausted and likewise cause seeking to be exhausted.
Furthermore, it is said:
"While that craving is not yet exhausted, various fetters and attachments persist; these are not extinguished by means of non-Buddhist paths."
Having abandoned non-discourse and listened to excellent discourse, their attachment repeatedly causes them to regress.
For this reason, the World-Honored One instructed them to abandon non-discourse and bring about the exhaustion of attachment.
As for those who contemplate this, they form the notion that they have fallen into nirvana, and thus they maintain that state for themselves.
Thereupon the World-Honored One spoke of non-nirvāṇa and non-resting:
"All desires are without craving; relying on the stillness of the base of nothingness, the liberation through perception is supreme; abiding therein, one does not arise."
One who is free from craving for all desires has exhausted the desires of the three realms; the fetters of the desire realm are forever extinguished through the Noble Path that exhausts craving.

One who relies on the concentration of non-perception (*asaṃjñi-samādhi*) does not rely on the samādhi of non-perception, nor on the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), nor on the other three [formless attainments].
If one relies on the perception of nirvāṇa as the supreme liberation, that liberation from perception pertains to both the realm of perception and the realm beyond perception.
If one dwells in the rest of nirvāṇa, that dwelling does not arise, nor does one fall back from it, nor is there anything further to arise.
The World-Honored One spoke thus:
"He abides without arising; for countless eons his pure eye has remained so.
Regarding those two liberations, he knows through his vow what is transmitted."
Regarding the statement, "He dwells there without arising for incalculable eons, possessing the pure eye," the answer is:
He shall likewise dwell for a long time in those two liberations and attain parinirvāṇa therein.
I recognize the vow and that which is transmitted; I shall not give rise to regression therein, nor shall I enter into birth by means of entering it.
Like fire fanned by the wind, its extinction is beyond counting;
you, O Benevolent One, are able to escape from name-and-form, and your extinction is likewise beyond counting.
"Just as fire blown out by the wind cannot be counted [as it vanishes], so too that fire does not extinguish within the air, nor can it be reckoned as having gone to the east or the west."
The Sage who has attained liberation from name-and-form refers to the four formless aggregates and the physical body as "name-and-form. They together constitute name-and-form.
One who sinks into darkness will inevitably return to light;
if one were to sink into non-existence as it is now, yet conceive the thought that it is permanent existence, please explain this to me, O One with Pure Eyes.
"Those who have entered the darkness will surely return to the light. Question:
What is meant by "light"? Answer:
It is like the illumination of the sun's light.
If that which has perished is now non-existent, then whether it be eternalism or annihilationism, one would still enter the pure assembly.
O One with Pure Eyes, explain this to me; reveal it to me, for there is nothing you do not know, O Venerable One.
"Extinction beyond counting—please explain that which is non-existent:
the dispersal and separation from all craving, and likewise the dispersal of all conceptual objects.
'Extinction beyond counting' means that those things which are finite phenomena do not exist therein."
I pray that you explain that which does not exist: for one whose cravings have been exhausted, there is no limit to those cravings; for such a person, these aggregates of craving do not exist.
As for the limit of the aggregates produced by formations (*saṃskāra*), those aggregates do not exist for them.
He who has dispersed and abandoned all craving has also dispersed all conceptual objects; his craving for the three realms is exhausted.
[The Buddha] answered the two questions of the Śākyan son:
"The Pure-Eyed One did not grant me a prediction, nor did the Three Great Sages; I wish to hear the prediction you now bestow."
Second, regarding the question concerning why the Śākyaputra Viśuddhacakṣus was not granted a prediction: at that time, he asked two questions:
"How does one contemplate the world so as to neither see birth nor death?"
The World-Honored One did not grant him a prediction of enlightenment.
Why was this? It was because he wished to instruct and discipline him.
He too received the prediction after hearing the three words, and among them he spoke thus: "I wish to hear the predictions granted by the three great seers.
Neither in this world nor in future lives, nor among the gods of the Brahma heavens, has anyone been seen who possesses such realization as that of Gautama."
The present world refers to the human realm; the future world refers to the evil destinies.
The Brahma Heaven refers to the Brahmakāyika devas; "the various heavens" refers to the devas of the desire realm.
"Even in seeing, there is nothing known. How so?
Gautama, you who have attained universal virtue, the World-Honored One whose fame resounds in the four quarters—thus, in accordance with worldly truth, you possess all-knowledge;
like the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, you proclaim the teachings for the śrāvakas and even unto the Brahmā heavens.
If one wishes to see in this way— the ultimate destination of all treatises—
how can one observe the world and yet not perceive birth and death?
If one wishes to see in this way, having thus accomplished sublime wisdom, the world, including the gods and the Brahmās, will neither know nor see it.
The ultimate aim of the treatises on meaning is the desire to hear and receive the definitive prediction of enlightenment.
How does one contemplate the world without seeing birth and death? How does one contemplate the six sense bases so as not to give rise to other realms?
Observing that all worlds are entirely empty, the foolish king likewise focused his mind;
by being able to uproot the view of self, he thus transcended the places of rebirth.
Observing that all worlds are entirely empty, he also saw the foolish king himself.

At that time, the World-Honored One taught him emptiness: "Those who are constantly focused and do not shift their thoughts do not contemplate perverse matters, but allow their minds to dwell within the foundations of mindfulness.
What is called 'the view of self' is the foolish view of a body."
And by extinguishing it, one thus transcends the realm of death and is not reborn within the sphere of Jambudvīpa.
When the Venerable Vasula spoke these words—
claiming that he had heard of the annihilation of what is permanent— the World-Honored One did not grant him a prediction of enlightenment.
He also heard the third sentence of the track and received his prediction, wherein it was said:
"The two questions concern the Śākyaputrīyas.
'This world and the next world' refers to the gods of the desire realm; 'Brahmā' refers to the Brahmakāyika gods; and 'the gods' refers to the other gods of the form realm."
"Even those who see do not know" means that while abiding within the tracks of the middle way, they do not know.
Thus, transcending what is seen, one accomplishes such sublime wisdom that neither the world nor the gods can understand or know it.
In this regard, there is also the annihilation of permanence; one contemplates the annihilation and permanence of the world and yet does not perceive death and birth.
How does one eliminate annihilation and permanence, abide in the middle path, and cross beyond the shore of birth and death?
When one contemplates that all things are entirely empty, one returns to what is personally realized.
Whether it be annihilation or permanence, those who contemplate them as entirely empty abide at the limit [of reality].
Contemplating the six sense bases in this way, one is able to cross beyond the shore of birth and death.
Surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens, he also associates with malevolent spirits;
that garden is named "Delusion," so how can one find peace there?
Surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens, that practitioner hears the sounds of the Heaven of the Thirty-three.
Surrounded by hosts of celestial maidens, he is also attended by celestial music and yakṣas.
At the head of the streets of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, there are gateways on both sides, with gardens, fruit trees, and bathing pools.
The Four Heavenly Kings have various female spirits whose complexions are hideous and whose voices are coarse and harsh; they delight in terrifying people.
Their garden is named "Delusion," where the various fruits are exceedingly delightful and beyond measure.
The five celestial pleasures delight themselves, and the gardens can delude men; how, then, can one obtain a place of peace?
How can one attain liberation?
That path is called "Equanimity," and that direction is called "Fearlessness."
Phenomena are also called "soundless," and awakening to phenomena is called "complete.
That path is named "equality," for it is neither obscured nor crooked.
That direction is named "fearless"; Nirvana is called a "direction," for therein there is no fear of birth, sickness, aging, or death.

Regarding the statement that "the matter is also called 'soundless'": *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* are what is termed "matter"; because they are free from fetters and attachments, they are called "soundless.
If a noble one (*ārya*) is fully endowed with the factors for awakening through untainted (*anāsrava*) samādhi, their awakening to the essential way out is in perfect correspondence with it.
Shame likewise has no external object; mindfulness follows the person, wisdom is able to drive the chariot, and equal vision leads the way from before.

"Shame likewise has no external object" means that shame regards all fetters, defilements, and evils as being like a boat or a chariot; thus, by relying on shame, one gives rise to the mind of the Path and no longer engages in discursive thought.

One who harbors thoughts of malice toward others is like a carriage covered with tiger skin or wound about with leopard skin; one should not approach such a person, for fear that they will find an opportunity to cause harm, just as enemies or thieves might find an opening.
Reflecting thus, one will not be able to draw near to unwholesome actions.
Wisdom is like a driver who can control a chariot, like a charioteer, and like a fine carriage.

Such is the supreme wisdom of the Path; this Path is like a charioteer who knows both the path and the non-path, just as a charioteer attending to his chariot proceeds, advancing when it is time to advance.
When such wisdom is about to decline, one should arouse a courageous mind;
if that mind becomes overly intense, one should cause it to rest.
Just as a charioteer knows when to advance and advances accordingly, so too is the skillful means of contemplating wisdom.
"Preceded by right view" means that one practices the path with right view preceding and leading the way.
The World-Honored One has also said:
"Right view gives rise to right intention."
Furthermore, it is said:
Just as those noble ones [possess] the eightfold path, this is also called "shame" (*hrī*) because it is taught as its fundamental basis.
It is also that which, through the practice of conditions, increases the training in higher morality; "mindfulness" (*smṛti*) refers to one who follows after others.
Training in the higher mind is said to be the chariot of wisdom, with right view as the precursor leading the way.
Furthermore, it is said:
"That chariot is its basis; the various practices, together with a sense of shame, are its conditions," and these conditions are of three kinds.
The "path" refers to right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
"Mindfulness" refers to right mindfulness and right concentration.
"Wisdom that can drive the chariot" refers to right intention and right effort.
"That which is preceded by right view" refers to right view itself. Furthermore,
it is stated that "all śamatha and vipaśyanā are its nutriment," as explained in the *Mūla-śrāvaka-bhūmi*.
Shame also has its conditions; precepts are its nutriment.
Mindfulness that follows after others has cessation as its nutriment.
Wisdom that can drive the chariot has contemplation as its nutriment.
All those beings, whether men or women, who possess such a vehicle— riding upon such a chariot— they proceed to the realm of non-abiding.
All those beings, whether men or women, who possess such a vehicle, have already practiced the Path and, by means of that vehicle, proceed to the realm of non-abiding.
Having already practiced the Path, he causes one who has not yet reached Nirvāṇa to reach it.
Having abandoned the five and extinguished the five, practicing the five higher [virtues], the bhikṣu transcends the five categories;
this is called "one who has crossed the flood."
The "five abandonments" refer to the five hindrances (*pañca-nīvaraṇa*).
The "five already extinguished" refer to the five lower fetters (*pañcāvara-bhāgīya-saṃyojana*).
The "cultivation of the five superior" refers to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*).
Regarding "a bhikkhu who has transcended the fivefold enumeration": he has already transcended the five higher fetters (*pañca uddhambhāgiyā saṃyojanā*).
This is called "one who has crossed the stream," meaning he has already crossed the stream of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, it is said:
The five abandonments refer to the five wrong views.
The five that have already been extinguished are the five bodily fetters (*kāyagrantha*).
The five superior practices refer to the five types of dhyāna.
Regarding "the five classes of beings who have crossed over": they have already crossed over those categories of desire.
As it has been said, being attached to desire is what is called the "category of desire.
This is called "one who has crossed the flood," meaning one who has already crossed the flood of desire.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The five abandonments" refers to the fetters within the five destinies;
"having already extinguished the five" refers to these five paths.
The "five superior practices" refer to the five modes of liberation (*pañca-vimokṣa-dhātavaḥ*).
The "monk who transcends the five counts" is one who has gone beyond those five destinies (*pañca-gati*).
This is called "crossing the stream," meaning crossing the stream of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"The five abandonments" refers to the five fetters of the mind;
"having extinguished the five" refers to the five defilements of the mind.
The "five superior practices" refer to the fetters of the five mindfulnesses.
The "five monks who have passed beyond" refers to those who have already transcended the five bonds of the mind.
This is called "crossing the stream," meaning crossing the stream of birth and death.
The five awakenings and the sleep; The five sleeps and the awakening.
There are five that receive the defilements of dust, And five that constitute pure conduct.
Regarding "the five awakenings and the sleep": the sleep of the five wrong views and the arising or sleeping of the five faculties.
Regarding "the five who sleep and wake": the five faculties are the sleep, and the five wrong views are the waking from that slumber.
Regarding "there are five who possess the defilement of sensory objects": these are the five views.
Regarding "these five practitioners of purity": these are the five faculties.

Thus, regarding the five fetters of the body, the power of the fetters, and the foundations of mindfulness: among the lower fetters, there are those who attain the dhyānas; among the higher fetters, there are those who attain liberation—namely, ordinary persons who have entered the stage of anāgāmin.
"Rushing about, not finding joy within; Nourishing the new, one is bound by attachments.
It is like rushing toward a lamp in the darkness, Seeing and hearing what is produced in a single place.

Regarding "rushing about, not finding joy within": having already severed [the cycle] and attained liberation, one no longer rushes toward the permanence of existence (*bhava*), nor does one delight in annihilation (*uccheda*).
Furthermore, they are free from the views of annihilationism and eternalism, yet they do not delight in eternalism.
To "nurture ever-new fetters and attachments" means that the views one has produced increase all forms of bondage.

"Like moths rushing toward a dark lamp" means that just as the *pāṭhīna* insect or a moth, perceiving the oil lamp as a place of rest rather than as something to be abandoned, falls into it; so too, those with such wrong views perceive it as a place of rest and fall into it by perceiving it as abandonment.
Regarding "seeing and hearing that which is produced by a single cause": seeing purity has pure conditions, and hearing purity has pure conditions; such is the case for all views.
Furthermore, it is said:
"running about and not finding joy within" means not finding joy among the five desires, nor even finding joy in a single desire.
Those who nourish ever-new attachments fall under the bondage of sensual craving.
Those who act solely based on what they have seen and heard dwell within the five desires.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Running about and not finding joy within" means not finding joy in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), but running about within the form and formless realms (*rūpa- and ārūpyadhātu*).
The rest is also like this; it is according to where one runs toward, as is now being realized.
Or it is said:
This matter, too, is not one for rushing toward bondage; rather, one should run toward the firmness of liberation, toward the firmness of new liberation.
Old age covers the world, and one is surrounded by death.
Sentient beings suffer from the disease of craving, yet the Dharma abides in the world.
That which covers the world with old age cannot be escaped once covered;
those surrounded by death likewise find no way to flee.
As it is said:
"Neither in the sky nor in the midst of the ocean, nor by entering into the crevices of mountain rocks,
is there any place on earth where one can dwell and escape death."
Sentient beings who suffer from the disease of craving are bound by the fetters of craving and are unable to cross beyond the triple world.
As for those who abide in the world, they dwell amidst the eight worldly dharmas; their ten paths of wholesome action may be either wholesome or unwholesome.
Furthermore, they say:
"Abiding in the twelve links of dependent origination. Or they say:
It is to cause those who are afflicted by suffering to abide in the Path.
Alternatively, it is said that one abides in the seven factors.
Or someone might say:
"What is the nature of its abiding in the world?
The verse is the object-condition, and the letters are the sweet flavor."
Based on names there are verses; the composer is the body of the verse.
Taking the verses as the causal condition for the matter, one intends to compose verses to expound and recite them.
Regarding "letters as the sweet flavor": this refers to the division of letters into sequential parts, arranged in lines and columns.
Regarding "verses existing based on names": these are constructed based on names, such as a verse consisting of ten phrases.
The creator is the body of verse; the composition of verses is primary.
By means of the six, the world arises; by the six, karma is accomplished;
by the six, worldly dharmas are created; and there are six through which one undergoes suffering.
That which gives rise to the world through six factors refers to the six bases of craving (*ṣaḍ-tṛṣṇā-kāya*).
That which has already accomplished the six factors refers to the six bases of disease (*ṣaḍ-roga-kāya*).
That which constructs the phenomena of the world refers to the construction of the six internal sense-bases (*ṣaḍ-ādhyātmika-āyatana*).
There are six that undergo suffering and affliction; these are the six external sense bases (*ṣaḍ bāhyāyatanāni*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"That which causes the world to arise is the six groups of craving (*ṣaḍ tṛṣṇākāyāḥ*)."
The six already-accomplished activities refer to the six external sense bases (*ṣaḍ bāhyāyatanāni*).
The six factors that create the world refer to the creation of the six objects (*ṣaḍ viṣayāḥ*).
There are six ways of experiencing suffering and affliction, which refer to the six painful sensations of the body (*ṣaḍ vedanākāyāḥ*).
The four directions are not four directions; the supreme realm above and below is neither heard nor perceived.
It is the preaching of the Dharma that causes me to awaken.
Regarding "the four directions are not four directions; the supreme realm above and below," one should say it is like the sound of an echo.
"Not hearing, not perceiving, and not knowing" refers to the characteristic of accumulation; therefore, it is said that there is nothing that is not known.
"The teaching of the Dharma awakens me" means that it explains the path of thorough discernment and the practice of the essential way of deliverance.
The World-Honored One knows the faculties of beings and the meaning of the Dharma, so that I may attain awakening at this time:
"When what is old is exhausted and nothing new is created, one has no attachment to existence or non-existence;
when the seeds are exhausted, phenomena do not arise—nirvana is like the extinguishing of a lamp."
"To exhaust the old and not create the new" means that past craving has been exhausted.
"Not creating the new again" means that future craving will be exhausted.
"To have no attachment to existence or non-existence" means that present craving has been exhausted.
The exhaustion of seeds refers to the exhaustion of the seed of consciousness and the seed of existence produced therefrom.
The non-arising of phenomena means that those states of consciousness do not arise, having removed the defilements of formative activity (*saṃskāra*).
Regarding "Nirvana is like the extinguishing of a lamp": it is Nirvana by not arising.
Just as the extinguishing of a lamp cannot be measured—whether it remains toward the east or subsequently toward the south—in the same way, the Parinirvāṇa of an Arhat cannot be measured.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The exhaustion of the fundamental" refers to the cessation of past fetters;
"not creating the new" refers to the exhaustion of future defilements.
For one who is free from attachment to existence and non-existence, the defilements of the present are exhausted.
That which exhausts the seeds is the exhaustion of these defilements.
For one in whom the seeds are exhausted and for whom things are no longer subject to arising, there is no further taking up of existence.
Nirvana is a state of radiant purity, free from defilement.
It is like the extinguishing of a lamp, which is not bound by anything created.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Exhausting the fundamental" means that the past karma which was to be experienced as retribution has been exhausted.
"Not creating the new" means that new defilements are not produced.
"Having no attachment to existence or non-existence" means that there is no further activity of becoming.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The exhaustion of the fundamental" refers to the exhaustion of causes.
"Not creating the new" means that for those causes, no fruit exists.
Regarding those who are without craving and attachment, there remains something further.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The fundamental exhaustion" refers to the exhaustion of the six sense bases and the emptiness of fundamental formations.
"Not creating new" means not performing new actions;
the rest is likewise.
This king’s chariot is decayed, and the body is likewise decayed.
The True Dharma is imperishable; it remains impartial toward oneself.
As for this king’s chariot that has decayed—it is King Pasenadi’s chariot; because it is deeply decayed, it lacks luster and color.
"The body is likewise subject to decay": such a body, even when in a secluded place, is oppressed by old age and illness and lacks a radiant countenance.
"The True Dharma is not subject to decay or ruin," and it is likewise never weakened.
Why is this? Because it is impartial toward oneself.
What is this principle of impartiality?
The Truth of the Path is this.
The Dharma taught by all Buddhas is the impartial Dharma.
The Path consists of the eightfold noble excellence; the Noble Truths comprise four propositions.
The dharma of desirelessness is supreme; it serves as the eye for bipeds.
Regarding the Eightfold Path as the most excellent among all paths: among all paths, the Noble Eightfold Path is supreme.
Regarding the four phrases of the Noble Truths: among all truths, the truth of the noble ones is supreme; among all phenomena, the cessation of nirvana is most wondrous.
As for "acting as eyes for those with two feet": among all sentient beings, the Buddha is the most noble, for he knows everything.
Question:
Just as there truly exists the path to nirvāṇa, for what reason are these two matters presented together when speaking of the venerable Indramāla Śramaṇa:
that seeking constitutes the path, and emergence is the essential means to nirvāṇa, which is the meaning of the truth that is not empty?
Viśākha spoke thus:
"Just as wisdom revolves toward its objects, so too does the Path.
Just as wisdom has objects, so too do the Truths; Nirvana is like the severing of fetters."
Just as wisdom has its objects, so too is the truth.

One perceives the coarse and perceives the subtle; yet that which is feared by those whose minds are filled with pride is not what wisdom perceives, for the mind may otherwise rush toward the various realms of existence.
To perceive the coarse is unwholesome.
To perceive the subtle wholesome with outflows is to undergo various states of existence.
Furthermore, it is said:
That which is perceived as coarse is abandoned through the vision of the truths;
that which is perceived as subtle is abandoned through cultivation.
Furthermore, it is said:
Coarse awakening is associated with the desire realm;
subtle awakening is associated with the form realm.
Furthermore, it is said:
To perceive the coarse is to perceive desire.
To perceive the subtle is to perceive wisdom.
That which is feared by one whose mind is filled with arrogance arises from one's own mind; it is the mind that rushes about, and the corresponding awareness of that rushing about.
Thus, for one who possesses the wisdom of non-arising, there is awakening.
Each [sense] runs its course, and as they successively perceive, the mind is constantly disturbed.
Thus, when the mind awakens to this, it maintains undisturbed dignity and mindfulness.
When the mind is intensely active, all other Buddhas have passed into extinction.
One who thus awakens through the mind should abide equally in that awakening and gradually apply skillful means.
Regarding "one who possesses mindfulness of untroubled deportment":
as for deportment, one does not even perceive it; as for mindfulness, [it is likewise].
To focus one's mindfulness so that the mind does not waver and remains settled is to be no different from mindfulness itself.
That which is blazing is extinguished without remainder;
the Buddha can extinguish it forever.
Question:
"Is he who has no doubt regarding what is doubtful and whose body is free from the fetters of desire also a Buddha?
The answer is:
"The Buddhas are the Dharma; one approaches the Buddhas through this sūtra."
Furthermore, the various realms are extinguished by the Buddhas; the Śrāvakas cannot extinguish these realms.
It is further stated:
"The realm of all Buddhas is extinguished without remainder."
The heavens are distant and the earth is boundless; the great ocean likewise has no limit.
Where the sun and moon descend their light, and where they set—these real and unreal phenomena are called the four ultimate distances.
Regarding "the heavens are distant and the earth is boundless," this is explained at length in the verse.
Up to the place of cessation, both distance and simultaneity are transcended.
As for "dharmas that are real and unreal," these four are extremely distant by their very nature; this is the path of dharmas, wherein unreal dharmas are defilements.
Furthermore, he says this:
"The ten wholesome dharmas are real dharmas; the ten unwholesome dharmas are not real dharmas.
Furthermore, he says this:
Substantial dharmas are nirvana; insubstantial dharmas are birth-and-death.
Furthermore, it is said:
substantial dharmas are the truths; insubstantial dharmas are the various views.
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"The real dharmas are these seven dharmas; the unreal dharmas are these seven non-dharmas.
He further spoke thus:

The true Dharma is the essential core of all Buddhas; they expound the teachings of the Dharma, elucidating every dharma through the teaching of the Seal of the Dharma (Dharmamudrā), which is the natural principle that will manifest before long.
King Upānanda, having awakened, fled;
the verses on the cessation of worldly existence show that birth and old age are far removed from the Path.
The second chapter of the Geyyavagga is concluded.
Throughout one's entire life, though one remains ignorant, if one associates with those who possess wisdom, one will not understand the Dharma;
it is like a ladle that cannot distinguish flavors.
To be ignorant throughout one's entire life is what is meant by being "foolish"; such a person lacks the power and capacity to understand the meaning of well-spoken words and ill-spoken words.
Even if one associates with spiritual friends for as long as one lives, one may still fail to understand the Dharma.
Wisdom lies in a single moment; by associating with those who possess wisdom, one is able to recognize and understand the Dharma, just as a tongue distinguishes all flavors.
Wisdom arises in an instant for one who draws near to those who possess wisdom; "wisdom" refers to the skillful maintenance, skillful entry, and skillful mastery of the aggregates (*skandhas*).
Furthermore, this power and efficacy accomplish the various vessels of the teachings.
The foolish are said to lack this power and capacity, and thus cannot understand the twelve links of dependent origination;
the wise are said to possess this power and capacity, and thus they expound the twelve links of dependent origination.

The foolish are not vessels for the Noble Truths; the wise call them "reckonings," as the Truths are expounded in four sets of four. Therefore it is said: "Wisdom lies in a mere moment; draw near to those who possess wisdom."
Regarding death and non-death, he neither abides nor does not abide;
even in his extremity, he delights in giving—this Dharma is not without purpose.
As for "regarding death and non-death," among those who are envious, he dies by the envy of others; as for "delighting in giving," he does not die through attachment to envy.
One lives by the life-force of wisdom; even one who dwells [in the world] does not truly dwell.
It is like merchants on a journey who lose their way and are harmed by wild beasts and bandits;
whereas those who do not lose the path of the Dharma are not harmed by wild beasts or bandits.
This is the supreme gift.
One who is able to give to the poor takes pity on the orphaned and the destitute; this is the eternal law from time immemorial.
Or, it is said as follows:
Regarding those who die and do not die therein: the stingy and envious die within the evil realms, while those fond of giving are born in the heavens with provisions already before them.
It is just as a merchant who, when his provisions are scant, encounters hardship and distress.
Regarding those who are able to give even a little, this dharma is for the solitary and destitute; it is the dharma for the solitary and destitute.
Originally delighting in the preservation of life, these disciples of Gautama, while protecting their lives, know their own brevity; they seek that which is to be given amidst impermanence.
The sitting mat is also impermanent; one should realize that the world is impermanent.
Life is easily satisfied with contentment, which is the fundamental exhaustion of the root of suffering.
For those who originally delight in preserving their lives, at that time the devas spoke these words of the Buddha to the weary bhikṣus:
It is fundamentally joyful to preserve one's life.
Contentment makes one easy to satisfy and easy to support; one dwells happily in the bliss of dhyāna and samādhi.
Seeking what can be bestowed upon others through impermanence, one leaves nothing behind, making begging for alms one’s very livelihood.
Regarding the impermanence of the sitting mat: dwelling beneath trees in open spaces, one plays therein with the mind not fixed upon a single point.

Regarding the knowledge of the world’s impermanence: it is to exhaust the root of suffering at its source and, knowing the impermanence of the six sense bases, to cross over the flow of birth and death.
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"Those who originally delighted in preserving their lives—these disciples of Gautama—originally took wisdom as their life; they sought what was bestowed through impermanence."
Regarding the fact that even the sitting mat is impermanent: one begs for alms with the perception of impermanence, and likewise uses that sitting mat with the perception of impermanence.

One who realizes that the world is impermanent and understands that this is the fundamental exhaustion of suffering practices the liberation of wishlessness; realizing there is nothing to be created, they enter parinirvāṇa.
By what wisdom does one know that there will certainly be no obstacles to wisdom?
By what wisdom does one know this—that it is called "wisdom"? What is this wisdom?
"Just as perception has no difference, by what wisdom does one know this? This is called being wise. By what kind of wisdom does one know?
"Knowing that which is already known": if phenomena have no difficulty and all phenomena are without dualistic perception, by what wisdom within this does one know?
This is what is called wisdom.
All phenomena are without dualistic perception and without dualistic arising;
by what wisdom is this known? This is what is called wisdom.
This wisdom-knowledge has already known; this is precisely what constitutes knowing. What kind of knowledge is this?
It is like the knowledge that all things are impermanent—the knowledge itself is also impermanent;
it is like the knowledge that all things are non-self—the knowledge itself is also non-self.
Just as there is one who possesses all-knowledge and yet has specific cognitions;
just as there are those who are few and those who are born; just as there are cows that go out and cows that come in, and there are also cows that grow large;
and just as when there is desire, the heavens send down rain.

There is the barren cow and the one that has given birth; these are the origins from which the *dāni* proceeds. The barren cow does not give birth to a heifer; it is the memory [of the past] that guides her forward, while the one who drives the cow follows behind.

As for the owner of the cows, there is no great bull, no barren cow, and no one who has given birth; there is likewise no one who brings the cows out or leads them in, nor is there any growth of the cows.
When one desires, the heavens rain down; there is no lack.
The World-Honored One has said this:
"All things are non-manifest and without anything to be grasped."
Furthermore, it is said:

among the fetters of the form and formless realms, there are none that are not exhausted; there are none that do not arise. Among the fetters of the desire realm, there are likewise none that are not exhausted.
"Recalling the ox" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).

"Entering" refers to the mental states and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) associated with it, as well as the formations dissociated from mind (*citta-viprayukta-saṃskāra*) that revolve along with it.
"The ox growing large" refers to the exhaustion of pride (*māna*) therein and the completion of what was to be done.
"Free from anger, having removed impurities, staying one night by the side of flowing water, with my hut as a vast canopy of open space—if you so desire, the heavens shall rain.
Regarding "free from anger, having removed impurities, staying one night by the side of flowing water": this manifests freedom from anger.
"The one who removes defilement" refers to manifesting the exhaustion of anger and the complete removal of great impurities.
"Staying one night by the side of a flowing stream" means traveling along a path and staying overnight there.

"Wishing to transform the cowherd" means that all manner of deceptions—both physical misconduct and the roots of impure views—are eliminated; such misconduct is the deceptive nature of consciousness, and that too is exhausted.
I have extinguished the fire; the three fires have been stilled.
I have seen the chamber and shall no longer give rise to craving or attachment.
You have completely crushed the rafters and beams; the house is utterly ruined.
"I have seen the house" refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) as the abode of the various realms of existence (*bhava*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"The house is the conceit (*māna*) of this world."
Furthermore, it is said:
"Dwellings are conditioned phenomena subject to outflows.
It is further said:
Regarding the "dwelling," one who gives rise to the various consciousnesses but no longer gives rise to craving and attachment will not again undergo existence.
You, having exhausted, restrained, and crushed [the defilements], have already brought craving and desire to an end.
Furthermore, it is said:
"As for 'the side-restraint,' therein those phenomena associated with conceit are forever exhausted.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Flank" refers to the arising of all conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) and their exhaustion.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Flank" refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and its exhaustion.
"The dilapidated house" refers to the five aggregates of clinging (*pañca-upādānaskandha*); these are exhausted without remainder.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The house is entirely dilapidated" refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); this is exhausted without remainder.
Furthermore, he spoke thus:
"The house is ignorance; it is exhausted without remainder.
He further spoke thus:
The dwelling is the abode of consciousness;
when that is exhausted without remainder, one can sleep well.
One should also guard against what causes anxiety, always delighting the mind in meditative concentration, desiring to destroy worldly pleasures.
Regarding those who can sleep well, this is explained in detail within the *Āṭānāṭiya-vatthu* (The Discourse on the Āṭānāṭiya Protection).
Therein, the Āṭānāṭiya says:
"They do not give rise to sorrow, such as the sorrow I have."
The World-Honored One said:
"He does not grieve as I grieve;
he is no longer a bhikṣu for those who beg from him."
One who accepts a dwelling in this manner is not a bhikṣu;
according to the bhikṣu sūtras, he is not a bhikṣu, for he does not perform the practices of a bhikṣu.
The "householder's dharma" consists of receiving and taking up dwellings and engaging in the activities of building various houses; it is not by means of begging for alms that one is a bhikṣu.
If one possesses merit or evil, yet removes them to cultivate the holy life (brahmacarya), refining and extinguishing them so that sensations do not arise—him they call a bhikṣu.

Regarding those who possess merit and those who possess evil: "merit" refers to the aggregate of conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra-skandha) that is wholesome and with outflows (sāsrava); "evil" refers to that which is unwholesome.
"Elimination" means that they have already been severed.
The practitioner of the holy life cultivates that path.
One who refines and extinguishes so as not to give rise [to afflictions] subdues all hosts of Māras and subdues all fetters.
"Practice" (*cāra*) refers to "abiding. This means that a bhikṣu is one who has accomplished the dharmas of bhikṣu practice.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Merit" (*puṇya*) is the practice of the baseless concentration (*asaṃjñisamāpatti*), while "evil" (*apuṇya*) is the absence of meritorious practice.
Having already eradicated those [defilements] and practicing the holy life, one enters the two pairs of samādhis and the two pairs of conjunctions.
As for "refining and eradicating so that they do not arise," this refers to turning away from various paths and establishing mindfulness; such a person is called a bhikṣu who has severed all fetters.
Blue numbers covered by white, / A single-spoked wheel moves along;
/ One cannot behold this limit, / Having severed all floods, fetters, and bonds.
/ The detailed exposition is as in the *Saṃyukta Āgama*.
Twenty-nine years I have been a practitioner of *brahmacarya*; I went forth from home to practice the Way.
Fifty years have now passed since I came to know this, and within them I have cultivated *brahmacarya*.
In the practice of the arts of precept and concentration, in solitary walking meditation and mindfulness,
and in the exposition of the wisdom of the Dharma— therein lies no true śramaṇa.
As for "precept," it is the purity of bodily discipline and verbal conduct.
Samādhi refers to all wholesome states of mind.
Walking alone refers to its practice.
The art refers to wisdom.
Walking alone, he contemplates the samādhi of mental reflection and expounds the wisdom of the Dharma.
Regarding those for whom there is no śramaṇa, the wisdom of the Dharma is the Path; they enter into the state where there is no śramaṇa within or without.
Question:
What are the distinctions among the various types of ethical conduct? Answer:
Precepts are with outflows (sāsrava), while practice is without outflows (anāsrava).
Furthermore, it is said:
precepts are training (śaikṣa), while practice is beyond training (aśaikṣa).
What is the difference between samādhi and the mind dwelling in solitude?
The answer is:
samādhi is with outflows (sāsrava), whereas the mind dwelling in solitude is without outflows (anāsrava).
Samādhi is training; dwelling alone with a single mind is beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Furthermore, it is said:
morality is higher morality (adhiśīla); samādhi is the practice of higher mind (adhicitta); and higher wisdom is called the path of seeing the truths (darśanamārga).
To contemplate the path with a single-minded focus—this is called the path of seeing the truths and the path of contemplation.
This profound Dharma is entered by only a few; there are no outsiders among śramaṇas.
Furthermore, it is said:
The practice of precepts is the training in higher virtue; one who trains in the art of higher mind through solitary concentration trains in higher wisdom.
This is the Dharma of knowledge; as little as one enters into it, there is no ascetic outside of it.
Furthermore, it is said:
Precepts and samādhi are as previously described.
Regarding precepts, this is practice, namely, training in the higher trainings.
To practice the arts is to cultivate higher wisdom; this is called training in higher wisdom.
To dwell alone and contemplate with the mind is called training in higher consciousness.
This is called knowing the Dharma with little penetration; externally, there is no śramaṇa.
Through the accumulation of the measurable and the immeasurable, the Muni has abandoned all formations;
by personally exercising restraint over his inner mind, the egg of ignorance is spontaneously destroyed.

Regarding the accumulation of the finite and the infinite: "the finite" refers to existence born of the retribution of formations (*saṃskāra*); "those who perform formations" refers to those who relinquish the life-formations (*āyuḥ-saṃskāra*); "the Capable One" (*Śakya*) refers to one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); and "the internal bliss of the Capable One" refers to the bliss of dhyāna, liberation, and samādhi.
Within samādhi, one is naturally cautious, taking emptiness as the foremost; through these three forms of natural caution, one achieves perfection.
As for the spontaneous destruction of the egg of ignorance, it is like the breaking of an eggshell.
No longer observing the "egg-born" [conditioned states], the World-Honored One thus relinquishes his life-span, no longer observing the formations of life.
Some say: "The 'measured' refers to this person, while the 'immeasurable' refers to other formations."
The practitioner undergoes the various conditioned formations of existence (*saṃskāra*).
"Delighting within oneself" means delighting in the various paths.
The rest is also like this.
If craving has no place of abiding, the mind gradually attains liberation;
that craving is removed by the Sage, who knows neither gods nor humans.
Regarding "if craving has no place of abiding": when the emotions run wild in heedlessness, there are two kinds of such craving.
Craving and views.
There is no abiding place, whether by means of craving or by means of views.
There are two kinds of mental intention:
"Intentional affection" refers to views (*dṛṣṭi*).
"Gradually" means that one transcends two or three [fetters] together until craving is exhausted.
That which the Tathāgata practices is unknown to devas and humans; that which the Tathāgata practices cannot be known by devas and humans.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If craving has no abiding place, then craving refers to sensual craving;
the abiding place refers to various views."
Regarding "the mind gradually attains liberation": "mind" refers to craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and "gradually" refers to ignorance (*avidyā*).
When these two types of craving are exhausted—something that neither gods nor humans can know—the various views and ignorance are also exhausted.
If one is free from anger within, and possesses the seeds of grain, they will have no fear or affliction; even the gods do not go to see them.
To be free from anger within means to personally rejoice in being without malice.
There are those who cultivate the seeds of millet; among them, there are those who are called "existent," for they exist within this world.
They are free from fear and affliction because they have skillfully cultivated emptiness and clearly understood the twelve links of dependent origination.
As for "joy," it is the accomplishment of the four essential joys of renunciation.
As for "being without affliction," it means there is nothing remaining.
Even if there were a remainder of anxiety regarding wealth and possessions, one would feel no sorrow or distress whether one gains or loses within those possessions.
As for the devas who do not go to see [the Buddha], they have already attained *nirvāṇa* and thus do not perceive the five destinies (*pañcagati*).
Furthermore, it is said:
"If there is no anger within, manifest anger is exhausted."
There is one who obtains the seed of millet, manifesting the exhaustion of desire.
He who is without fear or affliction is virtuous and free from sorrow, manifesting the exhaustion of delusion.
As for the gods who do not go to see him, they are without desire, without hatred, and without delusion; having attained their own nirvāṇa, they do not perceive it as "nirvāṇa."
The Supreme Perfectly Awakened One among humans, Trains himself with a single-minded resolve;
Wandering within the traces of the Brahma-path, He ever delights in the cessation and stilling of the mind.
"Among humans" means being born among humans.
The Samyaksaṃbuddha fully awakens to and knows all phenomena.
The Self-Trained One is naturally endowed [with these qualities].
The One Whose Resolve Is Solely Right attains the three samādhis.
Those who wander upon the traces of Brahmā revere the Dharma within their hearts.
Those who always delight in cessation find rest in their minds through various *samādhis*; having eliminated the fetters, their minds find rest, and they take joy therein.
Venerated by all people, Transcending all phenomena,
Even the devas take refuge in them— This is called "hearing without attachment.
"Venerated by all people" means they are served and taken as refuge by everyone.
"To completely transcend all dharmas" means to go beyond all wholesome dharmas, just as one transcends various verses and stanzas, and likewise to cross over all unwholesome dharmas.
"The devas also take refuge" means that the devas also serve and take refuge [in him].
This is called one who has heard and is unattached; he has heard from the Blessed One, the Buddha who is honored by gods and humans.
All fetters are past; having transcended the garden, he has attained the fruit of transcending the garden.
He finds the joy of the escape from desire, like refined, pure gold.
Regarding "all fetters have passed away": transcending nine fetters is called "all fetters have passed away.
Furthermore, it is said:
"transcending the three fetters has passed away."

Regarding "crossing over the garden by transcending the fruits of the garden": the five sensual pleasures constitute the garden; therein, through the exhaustion of craving, one transcends all afflictions of craving, transcends all fetters, and transcends the pleasure of existence.
Regarding "the escape from sensual desire": it is the liberation from sensual desire, which is the joy of the first dhyāna.
Furthermore, regarding the joy of renunciation from sensual desires and the joy of the state of purity, he finds equal joy therein; this is called the joy of renunciation from sensual desires.

Just as a refiner of pure gold, when gold has been refined, is free from impurities and is most exquisite, so too the Tathāgata has transcended sensual desires and is entirely free from all taints (*āsrava*).
The names of the three Buddhas are spread abroad, Like the sun dispelling the darkness;
The Most Honored One in the world Is also like Mount Sumeru. Regarding "the names of the three Buddhas are spread abroad":
the sound of their merit and fame reaches the World-Honored Ones in the four directions and above and below, even as far as the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, where all hear their voices.
"Just as the sun dispels darkness" means that when the sun rises, it illuminates the entire world; all darkness becomes light, and there is none that does not receive its grace.
In this same way, the World-Honored One, having attained perfect enlightenment, universally illumines the three realms with his radiance.
Regarding the Most Honorable One in the World, he is so called because he brings illumination to all things.
He is like Mount Anavatapta; just as Sumeru, the King of Mountains, is the highest and greatest among all mountains.
The World-Honored One is likewise; among all sentient beings, he provides guidance through verses.
I shall now explain their meaning: without harboring any expectations, all who are called "dragons" are in truth named "Tathāgatas."
When I say "I shall explain its meaning," it refers to the merit of the dragon.
Furthermore, the Venerable Indramāṇava stated that such a claim is meaningless speech.
The Venerable Maheśvara spoke thus:
"One does not perform any conditioned activities. Or he spoke thus:
One does not create enmity.
As it has been taught, one also acts without harboring anger.
Furthermore, it is said:
Nor do they commit unwholesome deeds.
All who are called "nāgas" are in truth named Tathāgatas.
Among all those known as nāgas, the Tathāgata is the most sublime nāga.
One who is able to endure and not envy others, like a dragon with two feet, diligently cultivates the holy life;
such is the conduct that leaves behind the traces of a dragon.

Regarding "one who is able to endure and not envy others, like a dragon with two feet": just as a dragon-elephant first withdraws its forefeet and only then can its body turn around, so too does the Tathāgata, by means of his firm Dharma-body, achieve the turning [of the wheel].

Regarding "diligently practicing the holy life and following the tracks left by the dragon": it is just as a great elephant follows the tracks of its own hind feet so that its body may turn around; the Tathāgata is also like this.
The noble and holy dharma-robes of the Tathāgatas of the past have already attained the firm Dharma-body and achieved mastery over it.
Faith is the great nāga-elephant; heedfulness is its pair of white tusks;
mindfulness is its neck and wisdom its head; majestic deportment is its application of the contemplation of the Dharma.
Regarding faith as the great dragon-elephant: just as a dragon-elephant receives and takes up things entirely by means of its trunk, so it is with the Tathāgata;
through faith, he abandons unwholesome dharmas and gathers wholesome dharmas, just as the trunk is the most essential part of a dragon-elephant.

The Venerable Dharmatrāta has committed this error, which is a grave fault for one who composes verses on the sūtras; he must not say that the Tathāgata’s faith possesses its own independent causes and conditions.
Among all forms of calculation, the elephant is considered the great dragon.
Just as a noble elephant receives things through its trunk, so too is the Tathāgata.
