He approaches the various categories of phenomena and likewise discerns and contemplates the existence of the physical body. The pure conduct protected by the Tathāgata is also like this: the Noble Eightfold Path is pure and free from dust and defilement.
Furthermore, it is said:
Just as the tusks of a dragon elephant cannot be moved, so too is the Tathāgata; within the four immeasurables, he receives all flavors and attains mastery over them.
The Tathāgata’s tooth is likewise; it is courageous and possesses various marks.
The Tathāgata is also like this: among those who come from the six directions, he shall possess the various marks and the qualities of a Great Man.
Regarding the mindfulness of the neck: it is like the neck of a dragon-elephant, which takes in all flavors.
The Tathāgata’s supernormal power (*ṛddhi*) is likewise; all dharmas are universally and completely possessed therein.
Furthermore, it is said:
Just as a noble elephant supports its head with its neck, so too is the Tathāgata; mindfulness is his supreme head and he is the wise one.
Just as a dragon-elephant regards its head as its life, so too does the Tathāgata regard wisdom as his life.
Furthermore, it is said:
just as among the physical body of a dragon-elephant the head is supreme, so too is the Samyaksaṃbuddha supreme within the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the application of the contemplation of deportment (*īryāpatha*), some say:
"This matter is likewise; the two eyes are applied through the contemplation of deportment.
Just as a dragon-elephant has two shoulders on its left and right, so too does the Tathāgata have two kinds [of application]."
He practices the path of transcendence with his own body and exhausts the path of transcendence with his own body; having reached cessation, he does not arise again.
Furthermore, it is said:
Just as a noble elephant perceives all phenomena through its observation with swift cognition, so too is the Tathāgata; he knows sentient beings through various marks of perception.
Some say: Just as the mind of a dragon-elephant possesses various characteristics and knows them all—whether it be walking or moving about—the Tathāgata is likewise.
Just as the head is the most supreme among the physical body, so too is the Tathāgata; among the dharmakāya of anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, he is the most supreme.
Or it is said: this too is that matter;
there is the entry into the contemplation of dharmas.
Just as a dragon-elephant has two shoulders on its left and right, so too is the Tathāgata thus, having two kinds:
The renunciation of the body through the equal cultivation [of its nature], and the renunciation of the body through the equal exhaustion [of its nature].
Furthermore, it is said:
"Just as one who observes the various characteristics of a dragon-elephant according to the Dharma knows those characteristics by riding the elephant."
The Tathāgata is also like this; he knows their characteristics and understands sentient beings.
Some say it is like a dragon-elephant:
whatever the mind intends, it can accomplish entirely, whether walking or standing, it knows them all.
The Tathāgata of Original Non-arising is likewise thus; he knows the fundamental nature of sentient beings.
Or it may be said:
just as a noble elephant knows whatever is conceived by its mind, whether it is walking or standing still, [the Tathāgata] knows all things completely.
The Tathāgata of primordial non-existence is also like this, knowing the characteristics of the faculties of sentient beings.
Or he may speak thus:
"One knows the faculties of sentient beings in this manner."
Some say: Just as a noble elephant knows whatever its mind intends, whether it is standing still or walking, so too is the Tathāgata;

he knows the characteristics of all faculties and their various modes of activity, and among sentient beings he expounds the Dharma, remaining silent to receive and practice it, with each successive stage in harmonious correspondence.
The treasury of Dharma is fully complete; illuminating and sweeping away [defilements], one delights in the breath of dhyāna, inwardly maintaining self-restraint and vigilance.

Regarding "the treasury of Dharma is fully complete": it is like a dragon-elephant whose belly can hold various kinds of food and relies upon them all; the Tathāgata is likewise, for the various treasuries of the Dharma rely upon the food of the Dharma.

"Shining light to sweep away" means that just as a dragon-elephant uses its tail to brush away mosquitoes, gadflies, flies, and gnats, all of which it can thus remove, so too does the Tathāgata expound the teachings from within his own body.

Delighting in dhyāna, he is inwardly well-restrained regarding inhalation and exhalation; just as a dragon-elephant nourishes its body through inhalation and exhalation and always takes this as its pleasure, so too is the Tathāgata:
he constantly nourishes his body through the four dhyānas, being fully endowed with internal skillful means.
When the dragon walks, he seeks lush grass; when the dragon stands, his majestic deportment is full;
when the dragon lies down, his majestic deportment is complete; even when seated, his majestic deportment is perfected.
All these majestic accomplishments of the dragon are what is called "the dragon’s majestic deportment."

When a dragon goes about seeking lush grass, this is what is called the "dragon's majestic deportment. In all modes of deportment, the World-Honored One is accomplished in both ethical discipline (*śīla*) and meditative concentration (*samādhi*), and he has attained and perfected meditative concentration as well.
If one is accomplished in dignified deportment, one does not eat in impure places even when eating by mental intention (*manomaya-āhāra*).
Even when a nāga eats according to the measure of its belly, it does not harbor greed.
Regarding "not eating in impure places even when eating by mental intention," what constitutes an impure place? What is it that is eaten in such impure places?
When a mind accompanied by craving arises together with wrong livelihood, that is a state of defilement.
A state free from defilement is the opposite of this.
That Tathāgata eliminates defiled food and selects undefiled food, ensuring that his faculties are fully nourished and free from all ailments.
It is like applying ointment to a wound, or like greasing a cart.
Taking various medicinal herbs without any craving or attachment is called "non-greed.
One takes food to eliminate hunger, yet does not hoard or accumulate leftovers.
Receiving the food offered by the faithful, one must refrain from taking what is not given.
Having obtained food to eliminate hunger, one may take grass for food and leaves for clothing.
One should not hoard leftovers; one must not accumulate possessions nor expose the body, receiving only as much food as is necessary to sustain the physical form.
Regarding the acceptance of food offered in faith and the elimination of taking what is not given, one seeks it through the Dharma.
Furthermore, I shall now explain its essential points.

If one receives surplus provisions, one might store them away as family property; however, the Tathāgata fully knows this and eliminates such improper conduct. Therefore, he is called the one who has severed all hunger and thirst.
Having severed all fetters and likewise severed all bonds and attachments,
wherever he may go, he shall have no sorrow, fear, or affliction.
"Severing all fetters" means the extinction of the seven fetters.
"Furthermore, severing all fetters and attachments" means the extinction of the three bonds (*bandhana*).

Moreover, since the Tathāgata fundamentally lacks the roots of fetters (*saṃyojana-mūla*), he causes those roots to be forever exhausted so that there is no longer any fettering or attachment; he gives rise to various illuminations, and therefore it is said that "he severs all fetters whatsoever."
The Tathāgata beholds all defiled minds without being stained or attached; therefore it is said that his conduct is present everywhere.

There are two counts regarding the death of the fool: there is the one who has no anger toward family affairs, and the two bhikṣus who sleep well—[like] grass covering their clothes, they are driven by every impulse.
The third chapter of the Gāthā-varga is completed.
Seeing forms, one finds no delight; being free from desire and all greed, how much less would one allow this leather bag filled with excrement to cause the five faculties to waver?
"Seeing forms, there is no delight; as for those who find delight, why is this so?
The World-Honored One has spoken thus.
How much more so for one who is like a leather bag filled with excrement," or someone might say this:
He manifested the exhaustion of his craving; even the celestial music and goddesses were constantly free from desire for him, let alone this leather bag filled with excrement.
Furthermore, he wished to sever the bonds of the brahmin Mahātyāgī and did not wish for him to come to the Buddha’s presence again.
The brahmin carries a full burden of pride; the smoke of anger turns him to ash.
His mouth is pure, yet his heart is like fire; the mind is a hidden pit of flames.
Regarding "the brahmin carries a full burden of pride": just as one carrying a heavy load does not fear others, so too one bound by pride has no fear.
Regarding "wrathful smoke": it is just as fire only ignites after smoke has first appeared.
Likewise, instruction only occurs after wrath has first arisen.
Just as smoke confuses all forms, so too does wrath confuse all phenomena.
That which is harmed becomes like ashes; just as ashes have no utility for things, so too does such harm have no utility for things.
As for purity of speech, it is like casting pure [substances] into fire; thus, the lengthening of the tongue benefits all dharmas.
The mind is a fire-pit; the storehouse is like a place for sacrificial fires, for in this way the mind is ignited by the fire of wisdom.
It moves spontaneously among men as the light; it is like the foremost of fires.
Faith is the seed laid bare; wisdom serves as the plow;
the mind is bound by a sense of shame, and the hands hold the staff.
"Faith is the seed laid bare" means that just as there must first be a sprout, so too must faith precede the practice of the Path.
"Exposure" means dwelling in seclusion; it is like a sprout that receives the nourishment of rain, for in this way one nurtures the growth of wholesome merits through such exposure.
"Wisdom as the plow" means it is like gathering and tilling the soil; in this way, faith accomplishes various wholesome merits, and likewise, wisdom accomplishes various wholesome merits.
The plowman’s fetters are like the yoke and plow-handle; thus, one who possesses shame and remorse abides in wisdom.
The bonds of the mind are the three samādhis; the bonds of the intellect are like the spokes of a wheel; thus, these samādhis are like something that does not move.
One who holds a staff is like one using a plow-handle to drive oxen across a field; likewise, through mindfulness, one gains skillful control over the fetters.
With body composed and speech composed, one goes as if seeking food;
truly practicing the selection [of what is wholesome], one receives the teachings and attains liberation.
"Integrity of body" refers to bodily restraint (*kāya-saṃvara*).
"Integrity of speech" refers to verbal restraint (*vāk-saṃvara*).
It is like one who goes out seeking food; it is the purity of livelihood (*ājīva-śuddhi*).
One who truly practices the removal of impurities plows away all defilements with the plow of wisdom and truth.
One who accepts the teachings and attains liberation is like a farmer who, once the work is accomplished, abandons the plow.
Thus, by being in accord with these [teachings], one abandons such practices; once they have been extinguished, there arises a courageous mind.
With this courage, joined with the two yokes, one attains a state of peace through skillful means;
having gone forth, one does not return, reaching a place where there is no sorrow or fear.
Regarding "courageous and sharing the same yoke": just as an ox possesses great strength and does not abandon its yoke, so too the power of courage does not abandon its yoke.

Regarding "attaining a state of peace through skillful means," there are four skillful means by which one has reached the end; this is called nirvana, and it is also a state of security characterized by courageous resolve.
As for "having gone there, one does not return," it means that once one possesses such power and momentum, one does not return.
Wherever one goes, there is no sorrow or fear; having already reached nirvāṇa, all sorrows, fears, and afflictions are forever exhausted without remainder.
Thus is the work of plowing the field; that is called the fruit of ambrosia.
One who can endure such labor is liberated from all suffering.
In this way, those who work the field cultivate the path in such a manner.
That which is called the fruit of the nectar is nirvāṇa as its fruit.
One who is able to endure such labor cultivates this path.
"One who is liberated from all suffering" is one who has attained liberation from the suffering of the three realms.
Or it is said: "The Way-teaching causes wisdom to sever all fetters (saṃyojana) therein; thus the body is disciplined and the speech is also disciplined."
"Just as one who goes out seeking food" refers to right speech, right action, and right livelihood.
"Vigor together with the two yokes" refers to right effort.
"Mindfulness as a staff" refers to right mindfulness.
The "bond of the mind" (*manoyoga*) refers to the samādhis.
Having already explained the five faculties (*indriya*), that which is the seed of faith is the faculty of faith (*śraddhendriya*).
Vigor, together with the two yokes (*yuga*), is the faculty of vigor (*vīryendriya*).
"Mindfulness as a staff" refers to the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*).
"The mind is bound" refers to the faculty of concentration (*samādhīndriya*).
"Wisdom as the guide" refers to the faculty of wisdom (*prajñendriya*).
"Single-mindedly mindful and seeking with skillful means, / Nor does one take pleasure in the household life;
/ Like a flock of geese flying toward a pond, / They all flow forth, having removed their anger.
Regarding "single-mindedly mindful and seeking with skillful means": this refers to leaving the household life to study the Path.
"One who is single-mindedly mindful" means one whose mindfulness is fixed and does not waver.
"Nor does one delight in the household life" means one does not take pleasure in dwelling amidst the affection and attachments of the home.
"A flock of geese rushes toward a pond and completely sweeps away the flow of anger" is like a flock of geese leaving a great mountain forest without any lingering attachment or longing.
In this way, he extinguishes his attachment to the five desires; the path by which he extinguishes the five desires is as it has been taught:
"If even that which is in accordance with the Dharma is eliminated, how much more so that which is contrary to the Dharma?"
Furthermore, it is said:
Those who single-mindedly seek skillful means always delight in dwelling in seclusion and practicing seated meditation.
They also do not delight in the household life, nor do they delight in the sentient beings of the triple world.
When the flock of geese fled toward the pond, those who were entirely full of anger had their flow become ignorance; the path by which that ignorance is removed also removes that [anger].
Furthermore, it is said:
"One who seeks with focused mindfulness and skillful means practices the path while dwelling with a mind like that of one roaming in the mountains."
Furthermore, one who does not delight in the household life remains far removed from craving and attachment.
As it has been said: "Among all forms of suffering, craving is the primary cause; this is what is meant by 'craving.
Having already been able to relinquish that, one likewise does not delight in craving or attachment.
Regarding the phrase "the flock of geese rushes toward the pond and flows with anger," the "flow" refers to the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*).
As it has been said: "Householder, the eye is the source of the flow of consciousness; he is able to extinguish it through the path that serves as the means for dealing with the six sense bases."
When the six sense bases are extinguished, that path is also extinguished.
Those who cross the rivers and seas build bridges to reach the other shore;
those bound by "I" seek to cross, but the wise have already reached the shore.

Regarding those who cross the river, as it has been said: when the World-Honored One Gautama, because he was a seeker of other teachings, went to receive water from the Ganges, the deity of the water spoke this verse.
Regarding that river Hiraṇyavatī, people frequently build various bridges across it; yet none possess the power of supernatural flight (*ṛddhi*).
Some say this:
"Those who undergo frequent disturbances are bound by rebirth (*saṃsāra*); death is *hiraṇyavatī*."
As it has been said: because of the *sāra* (essence/substance), there is this pond.
Building various bridges is the practice of the Path.
"Leaving the mountain" means extinguishing the five desires.
"Those bound who seek deliverance" refers to non-Buddhists seeking the Way.
"The wise who have first reached the shore" refers to those who preach crossing over to the far shore of birth and death.
Furthermore, he says this:
The various crossings (tīrtha) refer to the cessation of the fetters abandoned through the vision of the truths (satyadarśana-prahātavya).
The fords (sāra) refer to the cessation of the fetters abandoned through cultivation (bhāvanā-prahātavya).
Building bridges refers to the arising of the Path (mārga).
One who abandons the mountain extinguishes all hindrances;
one who uproots the bonds practices and studies the Path.
The wise person first reaches the shore, while the Arhat crosses over the shore of birth and death.
One does not perceive vigor as "mine," nor is it my boundary;
it cannot be removed by practice, nor is it stained by worldly entanglements.
Regarding "one who does not perceive vigor": this refers to one who has achieved vigor through equalizing wisdom (*samatājñāna*).
Regarding that view of impurity, one does not hear of vigor; for one who lacks vigor cannot purify its limits.
He likewise desires to purify his zeal for sensual desire, yet he does not even hear of the realm into which he shall go.
Why is this? One who is not defiled by the burdens of household life does not follow such views.
If the pillar of the forest is firm, it withstands all the words of others.
If one possesses the roots of goodness that are free from desire, the Sage’s wisdom shall likewise be firm.
Regarding the firmness of the forest pillar, the Venerable Anuruddha explained this in detail within his prophecy.
Just as a pillar in a forest cannot be moved, so too that venerable one cannot be moved whether by revilement or by praise.
Regarding "exhausting his speech toward others": the speech remains within him, whether it be revilement or further praise.
One who is good and free from desire has exhausted all fetters and proclivities (*anuśaya*).
A "root of goodness" refers to the root of these three samādhis.
That the Capable One (*Śāstṛ*) is likewise firm refers to the Buddha’s voice and the wisdom of one beyond training (*aśaikṣajñāna*).
One who practices non-duality builds a lecture hall; one who provides for a wife and children is not a bhikṣu.
One who does not alter their anger toward sentient beings—the Capable One—constantly protects all beings.
Regarding the construction of a lecture hall through non-dual practice, this has already been explained in the parable of the hunter.

As for constructing a lecture hall through non-dual practice: it is the hunter’s dwelling within the assembly of those who dwell in seclusion, while the bhikṣu dwells within the assembly of the assembly.
The conduct of a hunter dwelling in seclusion is not the practice of a bhikṣu; a bhikṣu guards noble conduct. To support a wife and children is not the way of a bhikṣu;
the hunter and his family are not the concern of a bhikṣu, who sustains himself solely through the accumulation of the Dharma.
"He who does not change his anger toward sentient beings" refers to a hunter who does not change his habit of killing;
"the Able One who always protects sentient beings" refers to a bhikṣu who harbors no intent to kill.
Regarding those who receive offerings from others before, during, or after [the meal], he harbors no heart of resentment; the Muni likewise protects them.
Those who eat before do not eat at all; those who eat during eat only half; those who eat after leave the remainder of the food uneaten.
Receiving alms from others, the bhikṣu obtains food.
Furthermore, he harbors no resentment; he neither reviles nor harms their physical form. He does not put on a forced smile, nor does he speak untruthfully, saying:
"If I do not receive material goods, I shall never depart from this Dharma."
Furthermore, he spoke thus:

"Those who receive excellent, subtle food at the beginning, those who receive middling food in the middle, and those who receive inferior food at the end—having received such faithful offerings from others, one should not utter harsh words;
nor should one avoid places where one receives inferior food, nor cling to the words spoken regarding such places, nor go repeatedly to those places to beg until they are completely exhausted."
Furthermore, it is said:
"Evil cannot corrupt his mind, nor does the pleasant give rise to attachment.
Some say that the foremost [state] is when yakṣas are neither pure nor impure.
Why is this liberation called "the good" when there is nothing remaining?
Some say it is "the foremost"; this is the pure teaching of the yakṣas, just like the heaven of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Why is this liberation described as such? Because it is without remainder, the wise explain it through skillful means as purity.
Hunger and thirst are the foremost illness; conditioned existence (*saṃskāra*) is the foremost suffering.
One who knows this as it truly is realizes that Nirvāṇa is the foremost bliss.
Regarding hunger and thirst as the foremost illness, it has already been explained in the section on the bestowal of predictions upon those who have severed their hands.
For such a person who has severed their hand, the pain is not as great as that of one suffering from hunger and thirst.
Regarding conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) as the foremost suffering, those formations are of various kinds.

If one knows this as it truly is, there is the supreme bliss of nirvana; being able to know such conduct, one does not accomplish verbal actions that are to be performed, and thus one possesses bliss.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Hunger and thirst are the foremost of diseases; one is constantly bound by them until they can no longer be cured.
To know as it truly is that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are the foremost of sufferings—this is what constitutes knowing these conditioned phenomena."

Regarding the statement that "nirvāṇa among all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) is the supreme bliss," it means that cessation is bliss, and the absence of objective referents (*anālambana*) is bliss—the eternal bliss.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Hunger and thirst are the foremost of diseases"; this refers to the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
That action is the foremost suffering is the condition of ignorance giving rise to volitional formations (*saṃskāra*).
The experiencing of various afflictions is called the truth of origination (*samudaya-satya*).
To know this truly as it is is the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
Nirvāṇa is the supreme bliss; it is the Truth of Cessation.
The robes of a brahmin are modesty and shame; A brahmin’s hands are pure;
Water flows constantly and never stagnates; And the tongue serves as his cleansing bath.
Regarding the "shame and modesty" as the robe of a brahmin, this was already explained by the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana during his prophecy:
just as clothing is used to cover and conceal the private parts, so too do shame and modesty cover and conceal the private parts.
"The brahmin whose hands are pure" is like one who has already purified the sacrificial fire; I am likewise, practicing pure conduct and the conduct of renunciation.
"Water flows constantly without ceasing, and the tongue is used for rinsing" is like using a rinsing vessel to wash away an impure container.
My tongue is likewise so; it removes defiled conduct day and night without rest.
In making offerings to the fire, there is a constant mindfulness;
relying upon the internal mind, one diligently performs the sacrifice day and night, never losing the proper measure of the precepts.
Regarding those who maintain constant mindfulness while making offerings to the fire: they cease and contemplate that burning fire of wisdom.
By relying on the internal mind, and because they rely upon and depend on that mind, they are able to extinguish it.
Practicing discipline day and night, not losing the regulation of the sense faculties, and remaining within to contemplate the mind so that it is trained—this is called "concealment."
Furthermore, it is said:
"The hidden places" refer to body, speech, and mind;
"the trainer of discipline" refers to the complete possession of all precepts.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The robe of the brahmin of shame and modesty manifests the arising of wholesome conduct.
The hands of the brahmin are pure; water flows from them constantly without ceasing."
The tongue’s virtuous conduct is called bathing; the tongue’s good deeds constitute its purification.
The second verse refers to the mind’s virtuous conduct.
One who possesses these three types of virtuous conduct is named a *brāhmaṇa*.
One who transcends shame constantly reviles others; how much more so me?
Even if you were essential to me, I would still not engage in unwholesome conduct; know that such a person is not mine.
"One who transcends shame" refers to one who feels no shame where there ought to be shame.
One should know that he is not even a kinsman; how much less could he be a kinsman to others?
He who constantly reviles those who are not his kin should be known as an enemy dwelling within my domain.
I shall tell you the essential point: regarding all that is defiled and impure, even if one follows sentient beings with care, one should know this to be deceitful corruption.

Furthermore, as for not engaging in improper conduct, if one has close and affectionate relations with others, one should not give rise to affliction toward them; one should know that the skillful means employed therein require careful vigilance against resentment.
The mind does not depart from desire, and mindfulness never finds satiety;
observing those who are able to depart from it, they are endowed with the perfection of wisdom.
Regarding "the mind does not depart from desire," this has already been explained in the *Bodhisattva-avyākaraṇa* (The Bodhisattva’s Bestowal of Prophecy).
Even when mental intentions and desires arise, there is no satiety, and one is unable to depart from that craving.
One who can depart manifests the exhaustion of the perception of desire; as they sequentially observe the moment of that exhaustion, they are said to be "one who can depart."
He who possesses wisdom and is thus sufficient contemplates the impurity of desires;
he who clearly and truly perceives this is praised by the Venerable One as one who transcends the heavens.
Regarding "clearly and correctly seeing": "clear" refers to the truth of suffering and the truth of origination; "superior" refers to the truth of the path and the truth of cessation.
Furthermore, it is said:
there are three truths—the truth of suffering, the truth of origination, and the truth of the path—while "superior" is the truth of cessation.
Furthermore, it is said:
Truth is the equal truth, the supreme ultimate truth.
Liberation is liberation from both sides; yet in liberation, one may still see bondage.
The noble and holy do not see liberation; they are liberated from folly and delusion.
This was already explained in the *Ekaputrapratyaya-nirdeśa*.
Regarding liberation from both self and other: one is liberated from false speech, yet remains defiled by killing.
One who is liberated yet again sees bondage means that although one has attained liberation from one harm, one is subsequently defiled by another.

As for the noble ones (ārya) who do not attain liberation: while they have seen the truths and attained liberation from delusion, they do not attain liberation from those fetters; thus, they attain liberation through the view of annihilationism (ucchedadṛṣṭi).
Those bound by the view of permanence attain liberation through such hearing and reflection;
likewise, they attain liberation from the view of a self-existent body (satkāyadṛṣṭi), which is otherwise a bondage resulting from doubt and grasping.
One attains liberation from sensual desire, yet remains bound by craving for form.
One attains liberation from craving for form, yet remains bound by craving for the formless.
Whether regarding the long or the short, the coarse or the subtle, the beautiful or the ugly—these are all conditioned formations.
One who does not take what is not given in the world is therefore called a brahmin.
If asked whether [the self] exists within the long and the short, the answer is:
neither the long nor the short is established.
"In that regard, if one observes even slightly, there will be length; if one observes even slightly, there will be shortness.
This is the Tathāgata’s instruction.
Furthermore, the coarse is also not accomplished."
Question:
Why is it that the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are also not established? Answer:
Within that state, it is not said that there is a measure that can be grasped, nor is there any coming.
If one commits taking what is not given, that act is both coarse and unaccomplished; therein, too, there is no exhaustive measure, yet there is pure conduct and some slight accomplishment.
Question:
What are those who have accomplished pure conduct?
Answer: [As follows:]

It is not by refraining from taking what is not given that one achieves purity or impurity within those forms; rather, it is through the practice of those [virtuous] deeds that one accomplishes them. This is the extensive teaching and admonition regarding the tongue.
Therefore it is said: "A brahmin is one who is fully endowed with all practices; such a person is called a brahmin."
Some say this:
"Those who give rise to the fetters of taking what is not given—these fetters are all [the marks of] a Brahmin.
Though unwholesome, there is that which is wholesome; one should rely upon the family of the Three Buddhas."
Not abiding [in liberation], they benefit sentient beings; they speak while relying on existence.
That which is unwholesome yet possesses wholesomeness—within that unwholesomeness, one ultimately gives rise to another realm.
He first extinguishes his former perceptions and subsequently attains other perceptions.
One who constantly relies on the family of the Three Buddhas does not rely on a mother’s womb.
One who does not abide in benefiting sentient beings passes away from another family and grows up within a mother’s womb.
He said: "One relies upon existence; the mind-born existence is virtuous conduct.
If one frequently changes worlds, there is nothing superior even in this world.
It is eternally extinguished, free from smoke and gloom; therein lies bliss and non-harming."
Among these, Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra seeks that which calculates; he knows and extinguishes the world.
The various sense bases (*āyatana*) that differ from those external ones are internal.
Furthermore, he speaks thus:
That which is different is heaven; that which is not different is hell.
Furthermore, it is said:
that which is different corresponds to the realms of form and formlessness; that which is not different corresponds to the realm of desire.
These numbers are impermanent, suffering, empty, and non-self; they are the specific and universal characteristics of cause and effect.
There is nothing superior, let alone anything that could surpass them in this world. Ignorance perceives what is known, as it is said: "One who is stained by attachment is bound by Māra."

"Breathing" (*śvasita*) refers to the cessation and stilling of the three fires; it is the eternal, perpetual quiescence characterized by extinction. It is the permanent extinction of the obscuration of smoke, wherein the manifestation of being entangled in hatred is exhausted.
Furthermore, it is said:
"The internal conditions for the exhaustion of all fetters are without the obscuration of smoke, as described regarding the sphere of craving."
There is awareness and the cessation of it, as well as the absence of smoke and obscuration; this is as described regarding both awareness and smoke.
"Without harm" means that the three harms are seen to have been exhausted.
"Without expectation" means that the expectation for gain and the expectation for life are seen to have been exhausted.
Furthermore, there is currently the exhaustion of craving, by which one is able to transcend.
Though liberated, one may fall back; though fallen, one may return through greedy attachment.
Having returned to the place of joy, one dwells well in a secure and virtuous state.

Regarding "liberated yet falling back": one who is liberated is freed from the desire realm and has also severed the fetters (*saṃyojana*) and underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) of the desire realm; however, because craving for the form and formless realms has not been exhausted, they fall back into those realms and are reborn there.

Regarding "those who, through greedy attachment, return again": they are unable to successively eliminate and exhaust the fetters associated with the desire realm; thus, those fetters remain present within them. Being defiled by attachment to the means [of practice] therein, they cannot uproot and depart from the various fetters and latent tendencies of the desire realm, and so the fetters and latent tendencies of the desire realm arise once more and return to the desire realm.
"Having returned to the place of joy and happiness" means that the Buddha’s disciples have returned to the state of peace and security, free from the afflictions of birth, aging, sickness, and death.
"The place of joy and happiness" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path.
Regarding "dwelling well in the good, delighting in the bliss of samādhi, and wandering therein, one returns forever to the place of peace and happiness," it is further explained as follows:

"Falling from liberation and falling again" refers to one who, though having attained liberation as a *srotāpanna*, falls into hell; having fallen there, they return again due to attachment to heavenly pleasures.
If craving for the desire realm has not been exhausted, one returns to the human world.
One who returns to this place of joy has no fear and no anxiety of falling into hell.
"Joy" refers to the path of the noble ones; for those who dwell well in goodness, they transcend all fetters and return to nirvana.
Furthermore, it is said:
"Falling and falling again" refers to the view of annihilationism, which falls into the permanence of existence.
"Greedy attachment and returning again" refers to the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals.
One practices the path for liberation from the views of eternalism and nihilism;
the same applies to the others.
Seeing pride give rise to a mind of faith, one observes the sequence of verses and so forth.
The hungry ones rely upon desire and the truths; [this is] for the sons who fulfill their vows through liberation.
The fourth section, the Gāthā-khaṇḍa compiled by the Venerable Vasumitra Bodhisattva, is hereby completed.
The *Vasumitra-śāstra*, Fascicle Ten.
